docs.title: ProxiPort
docs.text:
A self-hosted remote-management server. ProxiPort gives you a small REST API, an SSH-over-WebSocket tunnel transport, and an agent that idles on a remote machine and brings tunnels up on demand. It is fully open source, top to bottom — no proprietary plugin host, no closed frontend, no capability gates.

ProxiPort is maintained by Proximile LLC and licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later.

docs.title: Try the public demo
docs.text:
A live demo runs at https://demo.proxiport.net/. Sign in with demo / demo — the SPA login page shows the same banner. Three pre-registered agents appear in Inventory. The demo guest has a read-only profile, and a small set of endpoints (the admin-only user-management and agent-credential routes, plus the request-IP echo) are walled off at the edge, so it's safe to poke at without exposing operator-side state. The whole DB and agent fleet reset every hour.

The demo is for evaluation only; do not rely on it. To run your own server, see Install.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The upstream rport project was MIT-licensed when CloudRadar GmbH released it in 2020 and remained MIT under RealVNC Limited's stewardship through 2023. In September 2023 RealVNC closed the source. The community fork openrport carried the FOSS lineage forward for about eighteen months and has been effectively unmaintained since mid-2025.

ProxiPort continues that work. We:

  • removed the closed-source plugin scaffolding (plus/) and every capability gate it fed,
  • wrote a new SvelteKit frontend from scratch to replace the proprietary Vue/Nuxt SPA the upstream shipped only as compiled bundles, and
  • rebranded the tree so users do not confuse this with either the RealVNC closed product or the now-stale openrport fork.

The REST API, the chisel-based SSH-over-WebSocket transport, the agent protocol, and the operational model are all kept as-is — they are the value of the original project and we are not trying to rewrite them.

See origin for the full provenance and a precise statement of what was and was not forked from upstream.

docs.title: Anonymous transport (Tor / VPN)
docs.text:
The agent makes one outbound connection to the server and carries everything — the control channel, every tunnel, every command result — over it. Anything that carries that single TCP connection therefore carries the whole agent, so routing it through Tor or a VPN needs no special protocol support: it needs a proxy and a policy.

The transports key is that policy. It is an ordered list of egress paths. The agent tries them strictly in order and keeps the first that connects.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• The agent runs on a host whose address should not be visible to the network between it and the server.
  • The server is published as a Tor onion service and has no clearnet address at all.
  • The agent sits behind a VPN and must not fall back to the local connection when the VPN drops — or must, but visibly.

If none of these apply, leave it unset. An agent with no transports behaves exactly as it always has.

docs.title: The list is the policy
docs.text:
transports supersedes the older single-valued proxy key, and the two cannot both be set: the agent refuses to start if they are. If your config already has proxy = "...", delete it and put that URL in the list as its first entry. When transports is unset, an existing proxy keeps working as before.

There is no allow_fallback switch, and nothing is ever appended to the list for you. The agent dials the open internet if and only if you wrote the word direct into the list yourself.

[client]
  # Tor, falling back to the clear internet if the tor daemon is down.
  transports = ["socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050", "direct"]

[client]
  # A VPN, then Tor, and never the clear internet. If both are down the
  # agent retries them forever and does not connect.
  transports = ["socks5h://gluetun:1080", "socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050"]

Removing direct is how you fail closed. An agent that cannot reach its server is a recoverable operational problem; an agent that quietly revealed the address you were hiding is not.

Accepted entries:

Entry Meaning direct Dial the server with no proxy. Must be the last entry. socks5h://host:port SOCKS5. The proxy resolves the hostname, which is what makes .onion work. socks://, socks5:// Accepted spellings of the same thing. http://host:port HTTP CONNECT.

Credentials may be embedded (socks5h://user:pass@host:1080). They are never sent to the server. In the agent's log the password is masked (user:xxxxx@host:1080); the username is shown. An entry the agent rejects at startup is quoted verbatim in the error, password included, so get the entry right before you put a real password in it.

Anything else — an unknown scheme, a typo, https:// — stops the agent at startup with an error naming the entry and its position. An unusable entry is never skipped, because skipping it would silently shorten the policy you wrote.

docs.title: Order of attempts
docs.text:
Entries are tried transport-major: every server over the first transport before any server over the second.

transports      = ["socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050", "direct"]
server          = "primary.example.com:80"
fallback_servers = ["secondary.example.com:80"]

gives the order: primary over Tor, secondary over Tor, primary direct, secondary direct. Server redundancy never buys itself with anonymity — a dead primary alone cannot drop you to the clear internet while the secondary is still reachable over Tor.

transport_dial_timeout (default 45s) bounds how long each attempt may take to reach the server: the TCP connection, any proxy hop, and the WebSocket upgrade. A path that fails at those stages is abandoned within that time. A whole sweep of such failures therefore takes at most len(transports) × (1 + len(fallback_servers)) × transport_dial_timeout; keep that inside your watchdog window if you run one. The SSH handshake that follows a successful upgrade is not bounded by this timeout. A handshake that fails moves on to the next entry right away, but a peer that accepts the upgrade and then stalls the key exchange can hold an attempt for longer.

After a sweep fails the agent backs off exactly as before (5s to 10m) and sweeps again. server_switchback_interval (default 2m) retries the preferred combination — first transport, main server — while connected to any other, so a transient Tor or VPN outage heals itself. Set it to 0 to stay put.

docs.title: What advances the chain, and what does not
docs.text:
Only a failure of the path advances to the next entry: a refused connection, a SOCKS or CONNECT failure, a timeout, a broken handshake.

A credential rejection does not. The agent uses one credential for every server and every transport, so a rejection at one entry is a rejection at all of them, and walking the list could only end in dialing the clear internet because auth has a typo in it. The sweep stops and the agent backs off instead.

docs.title: Running over Tor
docs.text:
Run a tor daemon — the system package or a sidecar container — and point the agent at its SOCKS port:

[client]
  server      = "yourserveraddress.onion:80"
  transports  = ["socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050"]
  fingerprint = "SHA256:..."

Two constraints are enforced for you:

  • A .onion server is never dialed directly. Handing a .onion name to the host resolver would disclose it to whoever runs that resolver, so such a candidate is skipped rather than attempted.
  • A .onion server requires a pinned fingerprint. No CA issues certificates for .onion names, so the connection is ws:// with no TLS and the SSH host-key pin is the only thing authenticating the server. The agent refuses to start without it.

Publish the onion service with a standard torrc mapping in front of the server's existing listener — the server needs no configuration change and no code change:

HiddenServiceDir /var/lib/tor/proxiport/
HiddenServicePort 80 127.0.0.1:80

The target must be the host and port the server's [server] address listener actually binds: 0.0.0.0:80 in the seeded config, so 127.0.0.1:80. If you moved the listener, or left address unset (the built-in default is 0.0.0.0:8080), use that port instead.

Add the onion to the server's url list after the clearnet address, for example url = ["https://proxiport.example.com", "http://yourserveraddress.onion"]. Order matters: the first entry is the address the pairing dialog writes into new agents' server key, so if the onion comes first, every pairing-generated installer (clearnet agents included) gets the onion. Configure onion agents' server by hand as shown above.

docs.title: Running over a VPN
docs.text:
There are two shapes, and they are not equivalent.

A proxy the VPN exposes (for example gluetun with its SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy enabled) is a normal chain entry and can fail over:

transports = ["socks5h://gluetun:1080", "socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050"]

A network-namespace VPN — running the agent inside the VPN container's namespace, or behind a host WireGuard interface — is invisible to the agent. Every dial it makes is already inside the tunnel, so the correct configuration is simply direct (or no transports at all). This is a robust and common deployment, but the agent cannot fail over out of it, because the namespace is fixed before the process starts. If you need failover, use a proxy the VPN exposes.

Note that gluetun's Shadowsocks listener is not a SOCKS5 proxy despite the name — it speaks the Shadowsocks protocol and this agent cannot use it. Use gluetun's SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy.

docs.title: Installing with the pairing script
docs.text:
The one-shot installer the pairing service renders (see Install) can write the policy for you. Two switches build the chain, in the order given, and the installer follows the same chain for its own connection test and downloads:

Switch Effect -o Reach the server through the tor daemon on the agent host, socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050. Shorthand for -e socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050. -e <entry> Add one entry: a proxy URL (socks5h://host:port, http://host:port) or direct. Repeatable; direct must be last.

The switches need curl on the agent host: wget cannot use a SOCKS proxy, so with -o, -e, or a .onion server address the installer stops if curl is missing.

# Tor, fail closed.
curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050 https://pairing.proxiport.net/<code> -o proxiport-installer.sh
sudo sh proxiport-installer.sh -o

# A VPN sidecar's proxy, then Tor, then — visibly — the open internet.
sudo sh proxiport-installer.sh -e socks5h://gluetun:1080 -o -e direct

Alongside transports the installer sets require_fingerprint = true and updates_interval = 0, comments out an ip_api_url it finds in an existing config, skips the geolocation lookup that would otherwise label the new client with a city, and waits up to 90 s for the first "Connected to" line before it judges the agent log, since a Tor circuit takes a moment. When no -o or -e switch is given, a server address that ends in .onion implies -o. If you pass -e, the chain is exactly the entries you list, so include a Tor proxy yourself (-o, or -e for a tor daemon at another address). A .onion server is never tried over direct.

In the web UI, the dialog that creates a client credential offers the same switches as toggles: connect through Tor, a proxy to try before Tor, and whether to allow the open internet as the last resort. With a proxy chosen, the line that fetches the installer gets --proxy as well, so the pairing request stays off the open internet too.

The Windows installer has no equivalent yet; set transports in proxiport.conf by hand there.

docs.title: What this does and does not cover
docs.text:
The chain covers the agent's connection to the server. It is not a whole-host anonymiser, and the following are outside it:

  • Package-manager refreshes. updates_interval (default 4h) shells out to apt-get update, dnf check-update, zypper refresh or the Windows Update client. These are subprocesses; no setting in this file can route them. Set updates_interval = 0 on an agent that must not originate direct traffic.
  • ip_api_url. The external-IP lookup builds its own connection and cannot traverse the chain. The agent refuses to start with both set.
  • Server-issued commands and scripts. If [remote-commands] or [remote-scripts] is enabled, the server can run programs on the host, and those programs make their own network calls. The server is inside your trust boundary; the chain hides the agent from the network in between, not from the server.
  • Tunnel traffic to local targets. A tunnel to 127.0.0.1:5432 or a LAN host is dialed on the local stack, deliberately — reaching those is what the agent is for.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] direct omitted from transports unless a clear-internet fallback is genuinely acceptable.
  • [ ] fingerprint pinned, and require_fingerprint = true.
  • [ ] ip_api_url unset.
  • [ ] updates_interval = 0.
  • [ ] [remote-commands] and [remote-scripts] disabled unless needed.
  • [ ] Alerting on the literal string ANONYMITY DOWNGRADE: in the agent log. That line is emitted on every connection that uses direct after an earlier transport failed — a successful clearnet connection on an agent configured for Tor is itself the incident.
  • [ ] transport_dial_timeout × entries × servers inside your watchdog window.

See also: IP-address determination for the external-IP lookup this feature disables, and client authentication for the fingerprint pin that a .onion endpoint depends on.

docs.title: API authentication
docs.text:
The ProxiPort REST API supports three credential flows for human users and one for programmatic clients. They share a backing user store: a single inline credential, a JSON file, or a database table.

This page covers how the API authenticates an HTTP request, how to enable a TOTP second factor, and how to delegate authentication to a reverse proxy. For agent (chisel) authentication see client authentication.

docs.title: HTTP basic with username + password
docs.text:
Every endpoint accepts a Basic Authorization header. The server checks the credentials on each request:

curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients | jq

When any second factor is enabled ([api] totp_enabled = true or a two_fa_token_delivery method), basic auth with a password stops working on every endpoint except /login. The workaround for script integrations is the personal API token below.

docs.title: JWT bearer token
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/login with basic auth returns a short-lived JWT. The default lifetime is 10 minutes; request a longer one with ?token-lifetime=<seconds>, up to 90 days (7776000). A larger value, or one that is not an integer, is rejected with HTTP 400. The SvelteKit SPA asks for 24 hours.

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login?token-lifetime=3600' \
  | jq -r .data.token)

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients | jq

The JWT is HMAC-signed with [api] jwt_secret from proxiportd.conf. Pin a long random value before exposing the API — if the secret is left unset, the server generates a fresh one at every restart and every existing session is invalidated.

Login tokens are not bearer tokens

When a second factor is enabled, /login returns an intermediate token that is only accepted by POST /verify-2fa (and, for a user who has not enrolled a TOTP secret yet, by POST /me/totp-secret, so they can enroll). The final bearer token comes back from /verify-2fa once the TOTP or delivered code is validated.

docs.title: Personal API token
docs.text:
Each user can mint named, scoped API tokens. They authenticate via HTTP basic with the username + token in place of the password, so they work even when a second factor is enabled:

The token is the <prefix>_<secret> string returned by POST /api/v1/me/tokens — use it verbatim (the leading prefix_ is required; a bare secret without it does not authenticate):

curl -s -u admin:Ab3xK9pq_e83d40e4-e237-43d6-bb99-35972ded631b \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients | jq

Each token has a scope and an expiry date. If you leave out expires_at, the token expires one year after it is created. There are three scopes:

  • read+write — any request.
  • read — GET requests only, and not /ws, /ws-ticket, /me/totp-secret, or individual vault values under /vault/{id} (the vault listing is still readable).
  • clients-auth — only the /api/v1/clients-auth routes that manage agent credentials. Only an administrator can mint one; anyone else gets 400.

Mint read or read+write tokens from Admin → API Tokens in the SPA sidebar (also API tokens in the user menu at the top right). Mint any scope, including clients-auth, via POST /api/v1/me/tokens. List tokens with GET /api/v1/me/tokens, and rename one or change its expiry with PUT /api/v1/me/tokens/{prefix} (body: name, expires_at). Revoke one with DELETE /api/v1/me/tokens/{prefix}; it stops authenticating on the next request. The token is a random secret stored as a bcrypt hash and checked against the database on every request, so once its row is deleted it no longer matches.

docs.title: User stores
docs.text: Exactly one user store is active at a time. Combining the three modes is rejected at startup.

docs.title: Inline single user
docs.text:
The simplest setup: pin one credential in proxiportd.conf:

[api]
  auth = "admin:supersecret"

This mode has no SPA-managed user list, no multi-user support, and no TOTP. It is useful for an initial install or a single-operator deployment. Move to the JSON file or the database before sharing the server.

docs.title: JSON user file
docs.text:
Point [api] auth_file at a writable JSON file:

[api]
  auth_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/api-auth.json"

The file is a list of users with bcrypt-hashed passwords:

[
  {
    "username": "alice",
    "password": "$2y$10$ezwCZekHE/qxMb4g9n6rU.XIIdCnHnOo.q2wqqA8LyYf3ihonenmu",
    "groups": ["Administrators"]
  },
  {
    "username": "bob",
    "password": "$2y$10$ezwCZekHE/qxMb4g9n6rU.XIIdCnHnOo.q2wqqA8LyYf3ihonenmu",
    "groups": ["operators"],
    "two_fa_send_to": "bob@example.com",
    "totp_secret": ""
  }
]

Generate bcrypt hashes with htpasswd -nbB '' 'your-password' | cut -d: -f2. The file is read on start and on kill -SIGUSR1 <pid> — edit it and reload, or use the SPA to manage users (which writes the file in place).

The server needs read+write access to the file when the SPA is the source of truth, so chown proxiport /var/lib/proxiport/api-auth.json after creation.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
To integrate with an existing identity store or to manage thousands of users efficiently, point [api] at a set of database tables and configure [database] with the connection:

[database]
  db_type = "sqlite"
  db_name = "/var/lib/proxiport/database.sqlite3"

[api]
  auth_user_table = "users"
  auth_group_table = "groups"
  auth_group_details_table = "group_details"

The schema for SQLite:

CREATE TABLE users (
  username TEXT NOT NULL,
  password TEXT NOT NULL,
  password_expired BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  two_fa_send_to TEXT,
  totp_secret TEXT
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_username ON users (username);

CREATE TABLE groups (
  username TEXT NOT NULL,
  "group" TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX groups_username_group ON groups (username, "group");

CREATE TABLE group_details (
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  permissions TEXT DEFAULT '{}',
  tunnels_restricted TEXT DEFAULT '{}',
  commands_restricted TEXT DEFAULT '{}'
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX group_details_name ON group_details (name);

two_fa_send_to and totp_secret are needed only when the matching second factor is enabled. Personal API tokens are stored by the server itself, not in these tables.

The MySQL equivalents use VARCHAR and InnoDB; see proxiportd.example.conf for the [database] connection options.

Seed the first user:

INSERT INTO users (username, password)
  VALUES ('admin', '$2y$05$zfvuP4PvjsNWTqRFLdswEeRzETE2KiZONJQyVn7T3ZV5qcYAlmNWO');
INSERT INTO groups (username, "group") VALUES ('admin', 'Administrators');

docs.title: Managing users in the SPA
docs.text:
Admin → Users and Admin → User Groups in the SPA sidebar (/settings/users and /settings/user-groups) manage the user store from the web UI, backed by the same POST/PUT/DELETE /users and PUT/DELETE /user-groups endpoints. What you can do depends on which store is active:

Store Add / edit / delete users Edit group permissions Inline single user — — JSON user file Yes — (every user is a full admin) Database Yes Yes

On the inline single-user store both pages are read-only: the API rejects user and group writes, and the SPA shows the current account alongside a note explaining why. Switch to the JSON file or the database (above) to manage more than one operator.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: Admin → Users lists every account. New user and Edit set the username, password, and group membership; Delete removes the account; and — when TOTP authenticator 2FA is enabled — Reset 2FA clears a user's enrolled TOTP secret so they re-enroll on next login (out-of-band email/push 2FA has no per-user secret to reset). Tick a group to assign it, or type a new name to create one on the spot. Passwords must meet the server's minimum length, and Require password change forces a reset at next login. Out-of-band 2FA (email/push) also needs a delivery address per user.

docs.title: User groups and permissions
docs.text:
A user's permissions are the union of the permissions of its groups — there are no per-user grants. Each group toggles eight areas: tunnels, commands, scripts, scheduler, monitoring, auditlog, uploads, and vault. The built-in Administrators group grants all eight and cannot be edited.

Admin → User Groups shows each group's permissions. In the database store the checkboxes are editable and Save writes them back. Delete (DELETE /user-groups/{group_name}) removes the group's permission set and takes the group off every user who had it. The built-in Administrators row has neither button. In the JSON-file store the checkboxes are read-only, because that store grants every user the full permission set. Create a group by assigning its name to a user on the Users page, then set what it grants here.

Group-permission editing needs the database store

Fine-grained per-group permissions require the auth_group_details_table. The JSON file has no place to store them, so file-store deployments treat every user as an administrator.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text: ProxiPort supports two second-factor flows. Both need users in the JSON file or the database. With the inline single-user auth setting, two_fa_token_delivery is refused at startup. totp_enabled = true is accepted, but the inline user cannot be updated, so it can never enroll and every login stops at the TOTP step. Move to auth_file or auth_user_table before you turn on TOTP.

docs.title: TOTP authenticator app
docs.text:
The recommended setup. Set [api] totp_enabled = true and restart. Each user is prompted to enroll on next login — the SPA renders a QR code; scan it with any RFC 6238 app (Aegis, Google Authenticator, 1Password, etc.). The server generates the secret and a PNG of the QR code and returns both once, in the enrollment response (secret and base64 qr); the SPA displays that image along with the secret for manual entry. The secret is then kept in the user store (database or auth_file) and is not shown again.

When users live in the database (auth_user_table) and a [key_provider] is configured, the totp_secret column is encrypted at rest under the server DEK (enc:v1:… on disk), and any existing plaintext secret is re-encrypted on the next boot. Secrets stored via the JSON auth_file are not covered by this — that file is read as-is.

[api]
  totp_enabled = true
  totp_login_session_ttl = "600s"
  totp_account_name = "ProxiPort"

Run multiple servers with distinct totp_account_name values so the authenticator app can tell them apart.

To enroll programmatically:

# Step 1: get a login token (cannot be used as a bearer token).
LOGIN_TOKEN=$(curl -s -u alice:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

# Step 2: create a TOTP secret (returns secret + base64 PNG of QR).
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOGIN_TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/me/totp-secret

# Step 3: validate a code from the app to finish enrollment.
curl -s -X POST \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/verify-2fa \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOGIN_TOKEN" \
  --data-raw '{"username":"alice","token":"123456"}'

The secret is returned once

Step 2 is the only response that carries the shared secret and the QR image. GET /api/v1/me/totp-secret reports enrollment status only — {"enrolled": true} for an enrolled account, or 404 when no secret exists yet — so a leaked session or a read-scoped API token cannot lift the secret and keep minting codes after the session is revoked. Capture the secret at enrollment time, or reset the factor and enroll again.

Removing your own factor with DELETE /api/v1/me/totp-secret requires the account password in the request body:

curl -s -X DELETE \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{"old_password":"password"}' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/me/totp-secret

Changing your own two_fa_send_to delivery address takes the same old_password step-up, for the same reason: both are one step away from moving the second factor to an attacker's device.

Admins can reset a user's TOTP from Users in the SPA, or by DELETE /api/v1/users/<username>/totp-secret.

docs.title: Out-of-band code delivery
docs.text:
For sites that prefer email or push, set two_fa_token_delivery to smtp, pushover, a URL, or the path to an executable (URL delivery also needs [api] base_url set, or the server refuses to start). The user's two_fa_send_to field carries the destination address:

[api]
  two_fa_token_delivery = "smtp"
  two_fa_token_ttl_seconds = 600

Configure [smtp] or [pushover] to match, or set base_url for URL delivery. The flow mirrors TOTP: /login returns a login token, the server sends a code, and the user posts {username, token} to /verify-2fa to get the final JWT.

docs.title: Login throttling and second-factor limits
docs.text:
Failed authentication is rate-limited on two axes. Both are on by default; neither needs configuring to be effective.

Per-IP. [api] max_failed_login consecutive failures from one source address ban that address for ban_time seconds. A successful authentication clears the counter for that address.

Per-account. Each failed login also puts the source IP and username pair on a short deny list for [api] user_login_wait seconds (default 2). Further attempts at that account from that address get 429 Too Many Requests until the wait expires, which slows online guessing against a single account. The key includes the address, so a failed login from one host never locks the account out for users on other hosts. Spraying one password across many accounts from a single host is caught by the per-IP limit above.

[api]
  user_login_wait = 2.0
  max_failed_login = 10
  ban_time = 600

Second factors carry their own limits, independent of the settings above:

  • A pending login accepts at most five wrong second-factor codes. On the fifth the pending session is discarded and the user starts over from /login with their password.
  • A TOTP code is accepted once. The ±1-step skew keeps a code usable for about 90 seconds, so a code that was shoulder-surfed or phished within that window would otherwise still work a second time; the server records the step it accepted and refuses that step and any earlier one.
  • Out-of-band codes are not re-sent while the outstanding one still has more than 30 seconds to live. Repeating /login returns the same delivery target instead of mailing or pushing another code, so the endpoint cannot be used to flood a user's inbox or phone.

Sessions are invalidated when the password behind them changes — whether the user changes it themselves, an admin changes it from Users, or it is changed during login. Anyone still holding a bearer token minted under the old password is logged out.

Changing a password at login with 2FA on

/login accepts a new_password alongside the current one. When a second factor is enabled the new password is held and applied only after the factor is validated, so knowledge of the current password alone cannot change it.

docs.title: Delegated authentication
docs.text:
The server can treat any request that arrives with a configured header as pre-authenticated. The reverse proxy decides whether to allow the request; ProxiPort takes the username from a header value and issues a JWT against the matching user record.

[api]
  auth_header = "Authentication-IsAuthenticated"
  user_header = "Authentication-User"
  create_missing_users = true
  default_user_group = "operators"

user_header defaults to Authentication-User and must not be set to an empty value. create_missing_users is off by default. When it is on, a username the server has not seen before gets a new account in default_user_group, which defaults to Administrators — set it on purpose, or every user the proxy lets through becomes a full administrator. Delegated authentication needs a JSON user file (auth_file) or a database user table (auth_user_table); the server refuses to start if auth_header is combined with the inline single-user auth.

The pre-auth flow still goes through /login, so the proxy needs to inject the header on that endpoint. Once the SPA holds a JWT, every subsequent call uses the bearer token and the headers are ignored.

Lock down the trust boundary

Anyone who can set auth_header on a request to the API server can impersonate any user. Bind ProxiPort to localhost (or to a dedicated network interface only the reverse proxy can reach) and refuse the header at the public edge.

docs.title: Command-line user management
docs.text:
The proxiportd user subcommand writes directly to whichever store [api] points at, bypassing the API. Use it for break-glass password resets when no admin can log in:

sudo -u proxiport proxiportd user change -u alice -p \
  -c /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf

Run it as the proxiport system user, not root, or the JSON file's permissions will end up unreadable by the daemon.

With the JSON file store, the running daemon keeps its own copy of the user list, so it does not see the change until you reload it: kill -SIGUSR1 <pid>, or restart the service (on Windows, restart is the only option). With the database store, the change takes effect immediately.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• Pin [api] jwt_secret to a long random value, and store it encrypted — anyone who reads it in the clear can forge admin sessions. See encrypting the config secrets.
  • Switch off the inline single-user mode as soon as you have more than one operator.
  • Enable totp_enabled = true if you can.
  • Leave max_failed_login and ban_time at their defaults or tighter — see login throttling.
  • Sit the API behind TLS — see HTTPS.
  • Restrict the username/password basic-auth flow at the reverse proxy if you only intend to allow bearer tokens.
  • Review changes on the Audit page in the SPA. Most administrative changes are recorded there: users, groups, API tokens and TOTP, session revocation, client deletion, client ACLs, client credentials, client groups, tunnels, commands, scripts, the library, the vault, schedules and uploads. Logins, logouts and 2FA verification are not recorded, and neither are changes to stored tunnels or client attributes, or pairing requests. To review a user's active API sessions, use GET /api/v1/users/{user_id}/sessions (admin only).

See also: operator runbook — rotating credentials.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
ProxiPort is a three-tier system: an agent running on each managed host, a server running somewhere the agent can reach, and a web UI served by the server for human admins. There is no required cloud component and no required third-party service.

+---------+      WebSocket (SSH inside)       +-----------+
| agent   |       (port 80 by default)        | server    |
+---------+   <----------------------------   |           |
              chisel control channel          |           |
                                              |           |
+---------+      HTTPS                        |           |
| admin   |       (typically 443)             |  REST API |
| browser |   <----------------------------   |  + SPA    |
+---------+      SvelteKit SPA + REST         +-----------+
                                                    |
                                                    | SQLite files in
                                                    | data_dir (opt.
                                                    | SQL auth tables)
                                                    v
                                              +-----------+
                                              | datastore |
                                              +-----------+

proxiportd terminates TLS on the API listener — point it at a cert_file + key_file pair, or turn on the built-in ACME client for automatic Let's Encrypt certificates. The agent listener is plain WebSocket carrying an SSH session with its own encryption and a host key the agent checks against its configured fingerprint; put a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, Traefik) in front of it if you want TLS on that port as well. See HTTPS for the full deployment matrix.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
A single Go binary, proxiportd. Responsibilities:

  • terminate the chisel control channel from agents on [server] address (0.0.0.0:80 in the seeded config; SSH-over-WS carries its own encryption so no TLS at this layer)
  • serve the REST API and the SvelteKit SPA on [api] address (127.0.0.1:3000 in the seeded config; production setups switch this to one of the three TLS profiles in HTTPS)
  • persist clients, tunnels, scripts, commands, schedules, monitoring data and audit records to SQLite files under [server] data_dir; agent credentials and API users/groups can optionally live in tables in an external SQLite or MySQL/MariaDB database ([database], with auth_table / auth_user_table) instead of auth / auth_file
  • enforce auth (SSH password authentication for agents inside the tunnel-port WebSocket; JWT for the API; optional TOTP second factor)
  • multiplex tunnel sessions per connected agent

The server is the only piece that holds state. Agents are otherwise stateless beyond their own configuration.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
A single Go binary, proxiport (the agent). Responsibilities:

  • open and maintain a chisel WebSocket control channel to the server
  • present an identity (client ID + auth credentials) to the server
  • accept tunnel connections from the server: the server opens each tunnel's public listener, and for every connection it accepts, the agent connects to the requested local or LAN target over TCP or UDP (if tunnel_allowed permits it) and relays the bytes
  • execute commands and scripts dispatched by the server (when enabled in the agent config) and stream their output back

Agents do not require an inbound port. Beyond the connection to their server they make only a small number of outbound calls, all of which are off by default or can be disabled: the optional external-IP lookup (ip_api_url, see IP-address determination) and the periodic package-manager refresh (updates_interval). If the agent's egress must be constrained or routed over Tor or a VPN, see Anonymous transport, which lists every path that stays outside it.

docs.title: Tunnel transport
docs.text:
ProxiPort uses the chisel SSH-over-WebSocket transport, inherited from the upstream fork. Each chisel session is one TLS-or-not-TLS WebSocket carrying SSH framing, inside which tunnel sub-channels are multiplexed.

For production deployments, serve the API over TLS: supply cert_file + key_file (or enable_acme) under [api]. The agent listener has no TLS settings of its own — the SSH session inside the WebSocket is encrypted end to end and the agent checks the server's host key against its configured fingerprint — so it can stay plain, or sit behind the same nginx, Caddy, or Traefik front-end as the API if you want one TLS surface; both shapes are described in HTTPS.

docs.title: What an agent connection is allowed to do
docs.text:
The agent transport is an SSH connection in which the agent is the client and proxiportd is the server, so an agent can open SSH channels on it. Since 0.8.7 the server accepts exactly three channel types and rejects everything else with SSH_OPEN_UNKNOWN_CHANNEL_TYPE:

Channel Purpose session fetch one staged file, over SFTP, during a file push stdout / stderr stream a running command's output back

Two consequences are worth stating plainly, because earlier versions did not hold them:

  • The server never dials on an agent's behalf. Any other channel type used to be handed to the inherited chisel TCP-stream handler, which connected to the address in the channel's open request and piped bytes to it. Tunnel traffic does not use this path — tunnels are listeners the server opens and the agent connects back to.
  • The SFTP endpoint serves one file, to one agent, for the duration of one push. It is not a filesystem: the server records the staged path when it asks a specific agent to collect it, and refuses every other path, directory listings included. Writes, renames and deletes are refused outright.

If you have built something that relied on opening another channel type over the agent connection, it will now be rejected and logged. Nothing shipped with ProxiPort does.

docs.title: Datastore
docs.text:
ProxiPort keeps its operational state (clients, tunnels, client groups, jobs and schedules, scripts and commands, notifications, API tokens and sessions, monitoring data and the audit log) in SQLite files under [server] data_dir. SQLite is the only backend for this state; one server with up to a few hundred connected agents is the intended scale. An optional [database] connection (db_type = "sqlite" or "mysql", MySQL or MariaDB) can hold the agent-credential table (auth_table) and the API user and group tables (auth_user_table, auth_group_table). Nothing else goes there: even with MySQL configured, all other state stays local to the server, so there is no multi-server or HA deployment mode.

The vault — an encrypted KV store for documents and per-client secrets — uses a separate SQLite file with passphrase-derived encryption. The passphrase is supplied at vault unlock time and is not persisted server-side.

An optional [key_provider] adds at-rest field encryption for the recoverable secrets the server must read back on its own: the vault's stored values and verifier, the totp_secret of database-backed API users, and — in proxiportd.conf itself — key_seed, jwt_secret, and the stored credentials. A data-encryption key (DEK) held only in RAM (loaded from a file or env var; default: none) wraps them so they are enc:v1:… ciphertext on disk; reads fail closed if the DEK is absent or wrong, and the server refuses to start rather than run without a secret it cannot decrypt. This is a second layer independent of the vault passphrase, aimed at a stolen disk, snapshot, or config file. See encrypting the config secrets.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text: The web UI is a SvelteKit single-page app served as static assets from the server's doc_root. It talks to the same REST API that scripts and API-token clients use. Agents never touch the REST API; they connect over the SSH-over-WebSocket control channel on the agent listener ([server] address). There is no separate Node runtime in production.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Three layers:

  1. SSH password authentication on the chisel agent port. The agent opens the WebSocket, checks the server's host key against its configured fingerprint, then presents its credential as the SSH password before the control channel comes up. Credentials are [server] auth = "<client-auth-id>:<password>" (or an auth_file / auth_table if you prefer).
  2. JWT bearer on the REST API. Login is HTTP-Basic to /login, which returns a short-lived JWT (default 10 minutes, configurable via ?token-lifetime=). The SPA requests a 24-hour lifetime by default.
  3. TOTP second factor is optional; when enabled, /login returns a short-lived intermediate token, and the SPA POSTs the TOTP code to /verify-2fa to obtain the final JWT.

All authentication endpoints (basic auth, /login, /verify-2fa) feed a ban list keyed on the source IP plus username, with a 2-second penalty ([api] user_login_wait) after a failed attempt, which is what produces the 429 too many requests response under brute force or session-expiry cascades. A separate per-IP ban list ([api] max_failed_login / ban_time) also counts failed attempts.

docs.title: What changed from openrport
docs.text: ProxiPort imports the openrport Go server and agent tree at the MIT-licensed state of the fork (see origin for the full lineage). This page is the concrete, behaviour-oriented diff for anyone migrating from rport or openrport.

docs.title: The plus/ plugin scaffolding
docs.text:
openrport's source tree contained a directory called plus/ whose sole function was to load a separately-distributed proprietary plugin binary (the "Plus" plugin) that gated several enterprise features. The Plus binary itself was never in any public source repository — it was distributed by the previous upstream maintainer under a proprietary licence, behind a paywall.

ProxiPort deletes plus/ entirely along with every IsPlusEnabled capability gate. We do not ship the proprietary binary, do not load it, and do not reimplement Plus features as a licence-gated commercial add-on. Features that previously lived behind the gate (OAuth/OIDC, RBAC, alerting, …) will be reimplemented in the open under AGPL.

User-visible effect: API endpoints that returned a Plus status (GET /api/v1/plus/status, etc.) are gone; the corresponding settings in proxiportd.conf are accepted but no longer have any effect; the SPA does not show Plus-only configuration pages.

docs.title: The proprietary Vue/Nuxt frontend
docs.text:
Upstream rport/openrport shipped a web frontend, but only as a prebuilt JavaScript bundle. The source for that frontend was never released as FOSS. Because the source was never available, we could not have forked it, and we made no attempt to.

The frontend in frontend/ is original work: a SvelteKit SPA written from scratch in TypeScript against the existing REST API. It is AGPL-licensed along with the rest of the tree.

User-visible effect: the operator-facing web UI looks different. Functional surface area is broadly the same — clients, tunnels, commands, scripts, schedules, monitoring, library, vault, users, client-auth, client-groups, API tokens, audit log — but the rendering is now Tailwind/Svelte rather than Vue/Nuxt, and some pages are still being reimplemented. Most notably, the top-level Scripts page (running one script on many clients at once) is not implemented yet. The per-client Scripts tab works; to run on several clients, use the Commands runner and pick an interpreter. Document authoring, the Documentation page and some profile preferences are also still placeholders (see open issues for the running list).

docs.title: The tacoscript interpreter
docs.text:
Upstream let you set interpreter: "tacoscript" on a command or a script, which made the agent hand the file to a tacoscript binary — a separate third-party tool that neither rport nor ProxiPort ever installed for you.

ProxiPort removes it in v0.2.0. It was a menu item that could not work: both places the SPA offered it were command forms, and the server rejected tacoscript for commands outright, so choosing it returned 400. tacoscript is no longer an accepted interpreter value and is gone from the API schema and the SPA.

If you actually run tacoscript, nothing stops you: the server does not validate the interpreter of a script, so an alias or an absolute path (/usr/local/bin/tacoscript) still works. The only change is that ProxiPort no longer writes the script with a .yml extension for you.

docs.title: Some upstream API quirks
docs.text:
We have fixed a small number of inherited bugs where the upstream API behaviour was clearly unintended. These changes are intentional deviations from upstream, and the SPA is the only first-party consumer that depended on them:

  • GET /api/v1/schedules used to return a double envelope {"data":{"data":[…],"meta":{…}}} because the handler re-wrapped the manager's already-wrapped payload. ProxiPort returns the single-envelope {"data":[…],"meta":{…}} like every other list endpoint. The SPA accepts either shape, so older third-party clients written against the buggy response are not broken.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
Configuration and behaviour that rport / openrport never had. All of it is opt-in: an upstream config that leaves these sections out behaves as before.

  • End-to-end encrypted forwarding ([e2e] in proxiport.conf). Tunnel traffic can be encrypted between the endpoints so the server only relays ciphertext. See end-to-end encrypted forwarding.
  • Tor / VPN egress for the agent (transports in [client]). An ordered list of SOCKS proxies and/or direct that the agent tries when it dials the server, with transport_dial_timeout per attempt. See anonymous transport.
  • Per-client tunnel defaults ([tunnels] in proxiport.conf). Default options for the permanent tunnels in remotes, which any single entry can override. See the comments in proxiport.example.conf.
  • At-rest encryption of server secrets ([key_provider] in proxiportd.conf). Vault values, the totp_secret of database-backed users and the secrets in proxiportd.conf itself can be stored as ciphertext under a key held only in memory. See encrypting the config secrets.
  • A tamper-evident audit log. With a key provider configured, audit entries carry a keyed HMAC chained to the previous entry, so a removed or altered entry can be detected. See tamper-evidence.

docs.title: Kept as-is
docs.text:
The pieces that gave rport / openrport their value are kept exactly:

  • the chisel-based SSH-over-WebSocket tunnel transport,
  • the REST API surface (/api/v1/*),
  • the agent control-channel protocol,
  • the proxiportd.conf / proxiport.conf TOML config formats (option names and tags are structurally compatible with upstream's rportd.conf / rport.conf — see migration for details),
  • the optional [database] connection (SQLite or MySQL/MariaDB) for the agent-credential and API user/group tables; all other server state is kept in SQLite files under data_dir (see architecture),
  • the BDD test harness shape,
  • the systemd unit conventions (unit layout, ExecStart … -c <conf>). The units now run under new accounts, proxiport for the server and proxiport-agent for the agent; see migration for the chown steps.

docs.title: Renamed
docs.text: Upstream ProxiPort rportd / openrportd proxiportd rport (agent) / openrport (agent) proxiport /etc/rport/ /etc/proxiport/ /var/lib/rport/ (server) /var/lib/proxiport/ /var/lib/rport/ (agent) /var/lib/proxiport-agent/ systemd unit rportd.service proxiportd.service systemd unit rport.service (agent) proxiport.service rport system account (server) proxiport rport system account (agent) proxiport-agent (a separate account from the server's) rportd.conf proxiportd.conf rport.conf proxiport.conf

docs.title: Planned (not yet shipped)
docs.text:
These are tracked, not promised. Filed here so contributors can see the direction of travel before any code lands.

  • OIDC / OAuth login. First-class identity-provider login as an open-source replacement for the upstream Plus plugin's SSO. See API authentication for the current local-user model the OIDC flow will sit alongside.
  • Extended group permissions (RBAC). Per-group policy file (YAML) layered on top of the existing client groups and permissions model, so operators can express "this group can run scripts on hosts tagged prod but not infra" without code changes.
  • Alerting / notification dispatch. SMTP, Slack, and generic webhook sinks for the monitoring rule engine, replacing the proprietary alerting that used to ship with the upstream Plus plugin.
  • Sandboxed noVNC demo. The public ProxiPort demo will gain a pre-opened noVNC tunnel terminating at a network-jailed Firefox container that can reach only a baked-in offline Wikipedia mirror — so visitors can exercise the proxy feature end-to-end without ProxiPort itself operating an unrestricted web kiosk.

docs.title: Licence change
docs.text:
The combined work changes from MIT (upstream openrport / rport) to AGPL-3.0-or-later (ProxiPort). The inherited MIT code stays under MIT — see LICENSE-MIT for the verbatim original notice and origin for the rationale.

If you contribute to ProxiPort, your contribution is licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later (inbound = outbound). See CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Client attributes file format
docs.text:
ProxiPort lets you label each agent with two kinds of attribute:

  • Tags — single-dimension labels, e.g. ["linux", "edge", "vm"].
  • Labels — 2-dimensional key/value pairs, e.g. {"country": "France", "city": "Lille", "datacenter": "OVH"}.

Both are reported back to the server and can be filtered through /api/v1/clients?filter[tags]=... / ?filter[labels]=.... Tags can also select agents into a client group through its tag param; labels cannot. Use them to slice the fleet by environment, geography, role, or any other organisational dimension.

There are three places attributes can live. They are mutually exclusive — when more than one is configured, the rules below decide which wins.

docs.title: 1. Tags and labels inline in proxiport.conf
docs.text:
The simplest setup. Under [client] in proxiport.conf:

[client]
  tags = ["linux", "edge", "vm"]

[client.labels]
  country = "France"
  city = "Lille"

Labels go in a [client.labels] table of string keys and string values.

The values are read once at agent start. To change them, edit the file and restart the agent.

docs.title: 2. A separate attributes file
docs.text:
The format ProxiPort recommends for anything beyond a couple of unchanging tags. Point attributes_file_path at a JSON file:

[client]
  attributes_file_path = "/var/lib/proxiport-agent/client_attributes.json"

JSON example:

{
  "tags": ["linux", "edge", "vm"],
  "labels": {
    "country": "France",
    "city": "Lille",
    "datacenter": "OVH"
  }
}

The file must be JSON, whatever its extension. If it cannot be read or parsed, the agent prints error reading attributes_file and ignoring attributes_file, then starts with the inline values from proxiport.conf. On Windows, point the path at the location of your choice, e.g. C:\Program Files\proxiport\client_attributes.json.

This file is read only at agent start. Edit the file and restart the agent for changes to take effect — unless you are managing it through the API (see below), in which case the agent re-reads after each successful API update.

docs.title: 3. Through the API
docs.text:
Once attributes_file_path is set on an agent, the PUT /api/v1/clients/<id>/attributes endpoint accepts the entire new attribute document and pushes it to the agent, which rewrites its local file. GET /api/v1/clients/<id>/attributes returns the server's current copy of the agent's {tags, labels}.

The SPA shows the current attributes, read-only, under the client's Meta-Data tab (Inventory → client → Meta-Data; the vault must be unlocked). Editing is through the API only.

Three preconditions:

  • attributes_file_path must be set and point to a writable file.
  • The file must be writable by the agent's OS user.
  • The agent must be currently connected. Attributes are persisted on the agent only — the server has no offline buffer. An update against a disconnected agent is rejected.

If the agent is not connected, or is paused, both GET and PUT return 404. If the agent receives the update but cannot apply it (for example attributes file path not set or can't write attributes to file), PUT returns 409 Conflict with the agent's error message. A successful update returns 200.

Partial updates are not supported. The PUT request must include the entire {tags, labels} document; whatever you send replaces what was there.

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "tags": ["linux","edge","vm"],
    "labels": {
      "country": "France",
      "city": "Lille",
      "datacenter": "OVH"
    }
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/alpha-prod/attributes

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
If attributes_file_path is set and the file reads and decodes successfully, its contents win: the inline [client] tags and [client.labels] values are both replaced, even if the file leaves one of them out. If the file cannot be read or decoded (it is missing, has bad permissions, or is not valid JSON), the agent prints error reading attributes_file ... and ignoring attributes_file to stderr at startup and keeps the inline values. These messages go to stderr, not the agent log file. To go back to the inline form, comment out attributes_file_path and restart the agent.

The API only manages the file form. It cannot edit [client] tags or [client.labels].

docs.title: Filtering by attribute
docs.text:
The clients list endpoint accepts filters on both shapes:

# All agents tagged "server"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients?filter[tags]=server' | jq

# All agents whose city label equals "Lille"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients?filter[labels]=city:%20Lille' | jq

Wildcards are supported with *:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients?filter[tags]=ser*' | jq

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients?filter[labels]=*:%20Lille' | jq

URL-encode the space as %20. The filter is case-insensitive, like the client-groups matcher.

In a client-group definition only tags are usable, through the tag param key (it matches both inline tags and attribute-file tags, with the same wildcard syntax). Client-group params has no labels key, and a group definition with a labels entry is rejected with HTTP 400 (Invalid JSON data.), so labels can be used only to filter the /clients list.

docs.title: Choosing tags vs. labels
docs.text:
Use tags when the dimension is binary: the host is or is not in that category. linux, windows, vm, bare-metal, prod, staging. The matcher is set-membership.

Use labels when the value carries information of its own: country=France, datacenter=OVH, kernel=6.8. The matcher is key/value with wildcard glob.

A reasonable shape: tags for "is this in the set?" filters, labels for "what's the value?" annotations. Either works for a small fleet; both pay off as the fleet grows.

docs.title: File layout reference
docs.text:
The attributes file is a single JSON object with two optional top-level keys, in any combination:

Key Type Notes tags list of strings Case-preserved; matched case-insensitively. labels object of string→string Both keys and values are case-preserved; matched case-insensitively.

Both keys may be omitted (a file with neither is legal but pointless). Extra top-level keys are ignored — safe to add a comment field for operator notes without breaking parsing.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Restart on file edit. When you edit the file directly, the agent picks it up only on restart. API-driven updates are picked up immediately because the agent writes the file from its own process.
  • No server-side store. Attributes live on the agent. A disconnected agent's attributes are unknown to the server until it reconnects. The server caches the last-known value for display, but updates must wait for the agent to come back.
  • Permissions. The file must be writable by the agent's OS user for API updates to work, but readable by any other tooling you expect to consume it (e.g. a separate config-management runner).
  • Versioning. If you check in the attributes file alongside the agent's configuration management, the API may overwrite it from the SPA. Pick one source of truth.

See also: client groups and permissions for how tags and labels map to access-control decisions, monitoring for the per-agent metrics each agent reports, and the agent's proxiport.example.conf for every other [client] setting.

docs.title: Client authentication
docs.text:
The "client" in this page is the agent — the proxiport binary running on a managed host. Each agent presents its credential as the SSH password inside the chisel control channel it opens to proxiportd, after checking the server's host key against its configured fingerprint. The server checks the credential against one of three stores: a single inline credential, a JSON file, or a database table.

For human user authentication (the REST API and the SPA), see API authentication.

docs.title: Credential stores
docs.text: Exactly one store is active. Combining them is rejected at startup.

docs.title: Inline single credential
docs.text:
The simplest setup: pin one pair in the [server] section of proxiportd.conf:

[server]
  auth = "clientAuth1:a-strong-password"

Not recommended past the first install

A single shared credential means every agent uses the same password. Rotating it requires updating every agent at once, and revoking one compromised host means revoking them all. Move to the JSON file or the database before adding the second agent.

In this mode the credential is read-only: POST and DELETE on /api/v1/clients-auth return 405, and the Client Access page in the SPA offers no create or delete. The listing itself still works — the page loads, and GET /api/v1/clients-auth returns the credential's ID. Only the write operations are disabled.

docs.title: JSON credential file
docs.text:
Point [server] auth_file at a JSON map of client-auth-id → password:

[server]
  auth_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/client-auth.json"

{
  "alpha-prod": "ph2eePh1Bei4iezi",
  "bravo-staging": "iN4eithoG2ohgheo",
  "ops-laptop": "Eech9ieshaeYohth"
}

This is the mode the SvelteKit SPA expects. The Client Access page reads and writes this file in place, so the file must be writable by the daemon's system user:

sudo chown proxiport /var/lib/proxiport/client-auth.json
sudo chmod 0640 /var/lib/proxiport/client-auth.json

Deleting a credential from the Client Access page also removes any clients still bound to it — including disconnected ones — so the credential and its bound agents are cleared together once you confirm. A bound agent cannot reconnect afterward; add a fresh credential to pair a replacement.

The server caches each credential it looks up for 60 minutes. A new ID added to the file on disk is picked up by the next agent that connects. A password changed or an entry removed by editing the file directly can keep authenticating for up to an hour, until the cached entry expires or the server is restarted. Changes made through the Client Access page or the API take effect immediately.

If you would rather have an external tool own the file, set auth_write = false and the API will reject every write attempt (creating or deleting a credential) with HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed and the error code ERR_CODE_CLIENT_AUTH_RO:

[server]
  auth_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/client-auth.json"
  auth_write = false

docs.title: Database table
docs.text:
To share the credential store with an external provisioning system, point [server] auth_table at a table in the [database] connection. The same table schema works for SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB:

CREATE TABLE clients_auth (
  id       VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

[database]
  db_type = "sqlite"
  db_name = "/var/lib/proxiport/database.sqlite3"

[server]
  auth_table = "clients_auth"

auth_write applies here too — set it to false to make the API read-only for an externally-managed table.

docs.title: Empty credentials are rejected
docs.text:
An empty client-auth ID or password is refused in both directions:

  • The server refuses to store one. Creating or updating a credential with a blank ID or a blank password fails with an error rather than writing the blank, and the at-rest hash upgrade skips a credential it would otherwise have to hash from nothing.
  • The server refuses to accept one. An agent presenting a zero-length password is rejected during the handshake before the stored credential is consulted, and a stored credential that is somehow empty matches nothing.

Both halves matter because the credential comparison is constant-time, and a constant-time comparison of two empty strings succeeds. A blank on either side is treated as a failure explicitly rather than left to the comparison to decide.

docs.title: How an agent presents its credential
docs.text:
The agent reads its credential from one of three places, in this precedence order (highest first):

  1. The --auth command-line flag.
  2. The PROXIPORT_AUTH environment variable. RPORT_AUTH is accepted as a lower-precedence alias for compatibility with the upstream name.
  3. The [client] auth setting in proxiport.conf.

The environment variable and config setting both take the client_id:password form; the flag takes the same value. The fingerprint has the same three sources — --fingerprint, PROXIPORT_FINGERPRINT (alias RPORT_FINGERPRINT), then [client] fingerprint — in the same order.

The agent logs which state it resolved on startup: Client credential loaded for client id "<id>" when a credential is present (the password is never logged), or a clear no client credential configured error when none of the three sources supplied one.

The on-disk form in proxiport.conf:

[client]
  server = "proxiport.example.com:80"
  auth   = "alpha-prod:ph2eePh1Bei4iezi"
  fingerprint = "SHA256:<server-host-key-fingerprint>"

The port must match proxiportd's [server] address (port 80 in the example config). If the agent listener sits behind a TLS reverse proxy on 443, write the value with a scheme, server = "https://proxiport.example.com", so the agent connects over wss:// rather than plain ws://.

The fingerprint value pins the server's host key. When it is set, the agent refuses to talk to a server whose key does not match. proxiportd logs two fingerprints on startup, Fingerprint (SHA-256, pin this) and Fingerprint (MD5, deprecated), and the SPA's Info page shows them too. Pin the SHA-256 value (it starts with SHA256:), which the agent matches in full. The legacy MD5 colon-hex form is still accepted but is deprecated, and it is only prefix-matched, so a shortened MD5 pin matches more than one key.

If fingerprint is left empty, the agent accepts whatever host key the server presents and logs the fingerprint to pin. Set require_fingerprint = true in [client] to make a missing pin a hard error instead.

docs.title: Managing credentials via the API
docs.text:
The /api/v1/clients-auth endpoints list, fetch, create and delete client credentials. Every route, the listing included, requires an administrator account (a member of the Administrators user group); other users and their API tokens are refused. Listing and fetching work with any credential store. Create and delete also need auth_file or auth_table to be active and auth_write to be true. The examples below assume admin is an administrator:

# List
curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients-auth | jq

# Create
curl -s -X POST \
  -u admin:password \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"id":"delta-edge","password":"foB3ainai9ouQu0o"}' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients-auth

# Delete (force=true also removes clients still bound to it)
curl -s -X DELETE -u admin:password \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients-auth/delta-edge?force=true'

Without ?force=true, a delete is refused with HTTP 409 (ERR_CODE_CLIENT_AUTH_HAS_CLIENT) while any client, connected or not, is still bound to the credential.

The same operations are available on the Client Access page in the SPA, which only administrators can use: add a credential with + Add credential and delete one from its row. Credentials cannot be edited; to change a password, delete the credential and add it again. The password is shown only when you create it and cannot be retrieved later. If a pairing service is configured, the page then gives you Linux and Windows installer one-liners to copy. If the pairing request fails, it shows a [client] snippet to paste into the agent's config instead.

docs.title: Multi-use credentials and client identity
docs.text:
By default every agent that successfully authenticates presents its own client ID. This is the [client] id setting in proxiport.conf if one is configured. Otherwise it is the machine ID (/etc/machine-id on Linux, the ComputerSystemProduct UUID on Windows), because use_system_id = true is the default. If use_system_id = false and no id is set, the server assigns a random ID for each connection, so the ID (and the client's history) changes every time the agent restarts. Two agents may share one client-auth credential as long as their IDs differ.

To force a one-to-one relationship between credentials and clients, disable auth_multiuse_creds:

[server]
  auth_multiuse_creds = false

With multi-use off, a second agent that tries to register with a credential already in use is rejected. Set equate_clientauthid_clientid = true alongside it to also stop the agent needing its own id value — the client-auth ID becomes the client ID, which simplifies fleet provisioning at the cost of losing the credential/identity split.

docs.title: Disconnecting a compromised agent
docs.text:
1. Delete its credential from the Client Access page in the SPA (which applies force once you confirm the delete), or through the API with force:

    curl -s -X DELETE -u admin:password \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients-auth/<id>?force=true"

    This closes the agent's live session, removes the client records bound to the credential, and deletes the credential. 2. The agent's reconnect attempts then fail, so it stays disconnected. 3. If the host is reachable, also stop proxiport.service and remove the stale binary + config so the credential is not re-issued by automation.

Removing the row by editing the JSON file or the database table by hand does not drop a session that is already connected. With the file store, a credential that was looked up recently can also keep authenticating for up to 60 minutes (see JSON credential file).

Rotating one credential out of many does not affect other agents.

docs.title: Upgrading to 0.8.6 — the API served agent credentials
docs.text:
Affects every version through 0.8.5, on all three credential stores.

An agent sends its whole configuration to the server when it connects, and servers before 0.8.6 stored that configuration verbatim and served it back through the REST API. The stored copy included the agent's own auth credential and any proxy credential, so GET /api/v1/clients/<id> returned an agent's connection password to any authenticated API user — a read-only account included — for every client that account could see, and GET /api/v1/clients?fields[clients]=client_configuration returned it for the whole visible fleet in one request. A reader could then connect to the server as that agent.

0.8.6 stops the agent sending those fields at all, so nothing new is stored, and the server deletes them from records written by older versions the first time it starts. Backups taken before the upgrade still contain them.

Treat every agent credential that existed on an affected server as disclosed to every account that had API access, and rotate it:

  1. Upgrade the server to 0.8.6 and restart it.
  2. Issue a fresh credential per agent — see managing credentials via the API.
  3. Update each agent's auth = and restart it.
  4. Delete the old credential rows.

The same applies to any credential written into an agent's proxy setting, and to tunnel HTTP basic-auth passwords: auth_password was returned by the same endpoints and is now redacted from the client payload.

If you are also upgrading past the 0.8.5 advisory below, one rotation covers both — do it once, after the upgrade to 0.8.6.

docs.title: Upgrading to 0.8.5 — reading a credential destroyed it
docs.text:
Affects 0.2.0 through 0.8.4 on the inline and auth_file stores. Reading a credential through the API blanked the stored copy, and the blank then authenticated any agent that presented an empty password.

Reading GET /api/v1/clients-auth (which the Client Access page issues when it loads) or GET /api/v1/clients-auth/<id> wrote an empty password over the server's own copy of the credential. Two consequences followed:

  • Agents stopped connecting. Every reconnect failed against the blanked credential, so the fleet drained away with no error that pointed at the cause.
  • Anyone could connect. A client-auth ID with a blank password accepted an empty password from an unauthenticated caller, admitting them as an agent for that ID. With equate_clientauthid_clientid = true they took over the client ID outright.

On auth_file the damage persisted: the successful empty login triggered the at-rest hash upgrade, which wrote the hash of the empty password back to the file over the real credential.

The auth_table (database) store is not affected — it builds a fresh credential for each query, so nothing the API did could reach the stored row.

If you ran an affected version with the inline or auth_file store, treat every agent credential as having been reachable without authentication:

  1. Upgrade the server to 0.8.5 or later and restart it.
  2. Issue a new password for every client-auth ID, keeping the IDs so the client rows survive (see operator runbook — rotating credentials).
  3. Update each agent's [client] auth and restart it.
  4. If your auth_file contains an entry whose password is empty or is the bcrypt hash of an empty string, that credential was blanked in place — replace it rather than trying to recover it.

Nothing in the server records which credentials were read, so there is no way to narrow this to a subset after the fact. Rotate all of them.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• Use the JSON file or database mode. Avoid the inline credential beyond the initial install.
  • Issue one credential per agent. Long random passwords (32+ chars).
  • Pin [server] key_seed so the host-key fingerprint stays stable across server restarts; otherwise every agent fails the next fingerprint check. The seed is the host identity — store it encrypted so a copy of the config cannot be used to impersonate the server. See encrypting the config secrets.
  • The client listener carries SSH inside the WebSocket, so the credential and everything after it are encrypted and the host key is checked against the agent's fingerprint. To wrap that port in TLS as well, put it behind a reverse proxy. The client listener has no TLS option of its own: the TLS keys under [server] (tunnel_proxy_cert_file, tunnel_proxy_key_file, tunnel_enable_acme, tls_min) apply only to the built-in tunnel proxy at tunnel_host, not to this port. See HTTPS.
  • Watch for repeated failed-auth log lines and ban offending IPs at the firewall. The server has two built-in throttles, and neither replaces fail2ban. client_login_wait (default 2 s) refuses further logins for a client auth ID for that long after a failed attempt; it is enforced in the SSH handshake per client auth ID, not per IP. max_failed_login / ban_time (defaults 5 / 3600 s) bans a source IP at the HTTP layer with status 423. It counts distinct failing credentials from that IP, so an agent that keeps retrying the same wrong credential does not ban itself.

See also: operator runbook — rotating credentials and install — agent.

docs.title: Client groups and permissions
docs.text:
ProxiPort has two related but distinct grouping models:

  • Client groups label sets of agents (the managed hosts) so that operators can run commands, push files, or grant access against a meaningful set rather than enumerating client IDs every time.
  • User groups label sets of operators (humans + API tokens) and carry the permissions that gate which API endpoints — and therefore which SPA sections — each operator can use.

These compose: a user has effective rights on an agent only when at least one of their user-group function permissions is allowed and at least one of their client permissions covers that agent.

For the user side of the auth story, see API authentication. For the agent-side credentials, see client authentication.

docs.title: Client groups
docs.text: A client group is identified by an id string and is defined by a set of params. Every known agent, connected or disconnected, is evaluated against the params of every group. A disconnected agent stays known until keep_disconnected_clients expires. Matching agents are listed in the group's client_ids field at read time, limited to the agents the requesting user has access to.

docs.title: Matching modes
docs.text:
Each params value can be either an exact-match list (case-insensitive) or a list with wildcard glob patterns (also case-insensitive):

{
  "params": {
    "client_id": ["alpha-prod", "bravo-staging"]
  }
}

{
  "params": {
    "os_family": ["linux*", "*win*"]
  }
}

When multiple parameters are given, an agent is in the group only if all of them match. Within one parameter that takes a list of values on the agent side (tag, ipv4, ipv6, etc.), it is enough for one value to match. Roughly: AND across keys, OR within each key.

The explicit and/or object form is accepted on tag only; every other key takes a plain list of values, matched as OR:

{
  "params": {
    "tag": { "and": ["Linux", "Datacenter-3"] }
  }
}

Means the agent must carry both tags. or works the same way and matches if any one tag is present.

docs.title: Available parameter keys
docs.text:
• client_id
  • name
  • os, os_arch, os_family, os_kernel
  • hostname
  • ipv4, ipv6
  • tag (single-dimension labels)
  • version
  • address
  • client_auth_id
  • connection_state (connected or disconnected)

For 2-dimensional labels (e.g. country=France), use client attributes.

docs.title: Managing groups via the API
docs.text:
Creating, updating and deleting client groups requires membership of the Administrators user group; other users get an error on those calls. Any authenticated user can read groups, but each group's client_ids lists only the clients that user may access, and for a user who is not an administrator the list call (GET /api/v1/client-groups) also leaves out groups that contain none of their clients.

A group id must be non-empty, at most 30 characters, and use only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _, - and *. On PUT, the body's id must equal the id in the URL, or the request is rejected with 400. POST returns 201 Created, while PUT and DELETE return 204 No Content; none of the three returns a body.

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

# Create
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "id": "linux-edge",
    "description": "Linux hosts on the edge fleet",
    "params": {
      "os_family": ["linux*"],
      "tag": ["edge*"]
    },
    "allowed_user_groups": ["ops"]
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/client-groups

# Read
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/client-groups/linux-edge | jq

# Update (full replacement; partial PATCH is not supported)
curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{ "id": "linux-edge", "description": "...", "params": { ... }, "allowed_user_groups": ["ops"] }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/client-groups/linux-edge

# Delete
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/client-groups/linux-edge

The Client Groups page in the SPA lists each group with its description, client count and allowed user groups. It is read-only: create, update and delete groups through the /api/v1/client-groups API shown above.

docs.title: Where groups show up
docs.text:
• The multi-client command endpoint (POST /api/v1/commands) and the Schedules page accept group_ids for fan-out; the Commands page in the SPA targets clients individually. See command execution.
  • The multi-host script endpoint, POST /api/v1/scripts, accepts group_ids the same way — see scripts. The SPA's Scripts page does not have multi-target selection yet.
  • The file-push endpoint accepts repeated group_id form fields — see tunnel hosting → file reception.
  • Creating, updating and deleting a group is recorded in the audit log under application client.group, with the group ID as affected_id. The audit log has no filter that scopes entries to a group's members; to filter by host, use client_id or client_hostname.
  • User-group permissions can grant access to a client group as a unit (see below), so adding a host to the right group automatically gives the matching operators access.

docs.title: User groups and function permissions
docs.text:
Every API endpoint that does something interesting is gated by a named function permission. A user-group record carries the set of permissions it grants; a user is in zero or more groups; the effective permission set is the union of their groups' grants.

There is no negative-permission mechanism. If group-A grants tunnels and the user is also in group-B, you cannot use group-B to revoke tunnels. Build the group set so that each grant is intentional.

docs.title: The function permissions
docs.text:
• tunnels — open, close, list tunnels.
  • scripts — run, store, list scripts.
  • commands — run, store, list commands.
  • vault — read, write, list vault items.
  • scheduler — create, run, list schedules. A schedule runs a command or a script, so it also needs the matching commands or scripts permission (see below).
  • monitoring — read monitoring data (graph metrics, metrics, processes, mountpoints) and trigger an OS-updates status refresh on an agent (POST /api/v1/clients/<id>/updates-status). The refresh trigger is available even when monitoring is disabled.
  • uploads — push files to agents.
  • auditlog — read the audit log.

The Administrators user group bypasses every check — its members have every function and every client.

docs.title: Scheduling is not a way around commands and scripts
docs.text:
A schedule is a command or a script with a cron expression attached, so it is gated by the same permission the equivalent direct call is:

Schedule type Permissions needed command scheduler and commands script scheduler and scripts

The check applies both when the schedule is created or repointed and again each time the cron fires, so revoking commands or scripts from a group stops the schedules its members have already stored — you do not have to hunt down and delete each one. The account and its client access are untouched, which makes this the right way to withdraw execution from an operator while an investigation runs.
