docs.title: Manual install — Windows and macOS
docs.text:
The agent registers itself with the platform's service manager (the Service Control Manager on Windows, launchd on macOS) through its built-in --service subcommand. --service accepts install, uninstall, start and stop; alongside it, only --config and --service-user are honoured.

On Windows, download proxiport_<ver>_windows_x86_64.zip from the release page, unzip it to C:\Program Files\proxiport\, and create proxiport.conf next to the binary from proxiport.example.conf. Fill in the three fields described under Configure the agent, and under [logging] swap the Linux log_file line for the commented C:\Program Files\proxiport\proxiport.log one (the agent does not start if it cannot open its log file). Then, in an elevated PowerShell:

& "C:\Program Files\proxiport\proxiport.exe" --service install --config "C:\Program Files\proxiport\proxiport.conf"
& "C:\Program Files\proxiport\proxiport.exe" --service start

On macOS, unpack proxiport_<ver>_darwin_<arch>.tar.gz, install the binary and a config the same way, and run sudo proxiport --service install --config <path-to-proxiport.conf> followed by sudo proxiport --service start. Point [client] data_dir and [logging] log_file at directories that exist on that platform.

docs.title: Configure the agent
docs.text:
Edit /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf and set three fields:

[client]
  server      = "your-proxiport-server.example.com:80"
  auth        = "<client-auth-id>:<password>"
  fingerprint = "<server-host-key-fingerprint>"
  • server — the address the agent dials. Port should match what the proxiportd [server] listener was bound to; the seeded default is 80.
  • auth — pull the first credential off the server with sudo cat /var/lib/proxiport/initial-client-auth, or any later credential you've created. Both halves of <id>:<password> go in.
  • fingerprint — the proxiportd host-key fingerprint. The server logs it every time it starts (look for the line Fingerprint (SHA-256, pin this):), and the SPA's Info page shows it too. It stays the same across restarts as long as key_seed does not change. Without it, the agent will accept whatever public key the server presents — fine for testing, never for production. Prefer the SHA-256 value (starts with SHA256:): the agent matches it in full, in constant time. The legacy MD5 colon-hex form still works but is deprecated.

Then start the service:

sudo systemctl enable --now proxiport

The agent connects, registers, and waits for tunnel-open requests from the server. It reconnects automatically.

Refresh the SPA. The new agent shows up in the inventory.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Install the new package over the old one. The binaries, the unit files and the bundled SPA are replaced. Your databases and the other server state in /var/lib/proxiport are not moved, and your settings are kept. The package changes only these things, and only where they still need it:

  • [api] doc_root in proxiportd.conf, if it is still the shipped default (see Upgrading to v0.11.1 or later).
  • The two installer credential files under /var/lib/proxiport, if still present, are handed to proxiport:proxiport with mode 0600.
  • When the agent package is installed, /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf is set to root:proxiport-agent 0640, and its old default log_file = "/var/log/proxiport/proxiport.log" and data_dir = "/var/lib/proxiport" lines are repointed to /var/log/proxiport-agent and /var/lib/proxiport-agent; the agent's state.json and log file move with them.
Debian / UbuntuFedora / RHEL / openSUSE 
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/proximile/proxiport/releases/latest/download/proxiportd_<version>_linux_x86_64.deb
sudo dpkg -i proxiportd_<version>_linux_x86_64.deb

sudo rpm -Uvh proxiportd_<version>_linux_x86_64.rpm

A service that was running is restarted automatically at the end of the upgrade; one that was stopped stays stopped. Check it came back:

systemctl status proxiportd
proxiportd --version

Upgrading from v0.8.3 or earlier

Packages up to v0.8.3 disabled and stopped both services during every upgrade, including unattended ones, and never restarted them — the server stayed down until someone noticed. Upgrading to v0.8.4 still runs the old package's hook, so re-enable it once, after which upgrades keep the service running:

sudo systemctl enable --now proxiportd

Upgrading from v0.9.x or earlier to v0.10.0: shrink the monitoring log file

Before v0.10.0 the server rewrote monitoring.db on every start, which left a write-ahead log (monitoring.db-wal) next to it as large as the database itself — gigabytes on a busy fleet. v0.10.0 stops the rewrite, but it only shrinks a log that is already there after its first daily compaction, which happens once the server has run for 24 hours without a restart. Shrink it once, by hand, right after the upgrade:

ls -la /var/lib/proxiport/monitoring.db*      # note the -wal size
sudo systemctl stop proxiportd
sudo -u proxiport sqlite3 /var/lib/proxiport/monitoring.db \
    'PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);'
sudo systemctl start proxiportd
ls -la /var/lib/proxiport/monitoring.db*      # -wal is now small

The command prints 0|0|0 on success. A first value of 1 means the server was still running and nothing was shrunk: stop it and run the command again. It needs the sqlite3 command-line tool (sudo apt-get install sqlite3, or sudo dnf install sqlite). The data stays intact: the log is folded into monitoring.db before it is truncated. Releases after v0.10.0 do this themselves every time the server starts, so upgrading straight to one of them needs no manual step.

Upgrading an agent from v0.9.x or earlier

v0.10.0 gave the agent its own account, proxiport-agent, and moved its default data_dir from /var/lib/proxiport to /var/lib/proxiport-agent. The packages create both. An agent that was installed by hand, runs as some other account and has no data_dir line of its own falls back to the new default after the upgrade and refuses to start with an error containing failed to create data_dir "/var/lib/proxiport-agent" and permission denied. Either set data_dir in [client] to the directory that account already owns, or move the agent to the proxiport-agent account as shown under Manual install — tarball.

Downgrading uses the same commands with the older package: sudo dpkg -i with the older .deb, or sudo rpm -Uvh --oldpackage with the older .rpm (plain rpm -Uvh refuses to replace a newer version). The client database schema is versioned and migrated forward on start, so a downgrade across a schema change is not supported — snapshot /var/lib/proxiport first if you intend to go back. Going back below v0.11.1 also needs doc_root set back by hand (see the next section).

docs.title: Upgrading to v0.11.1 or later
docs.text:
v0.11.1 moves the bundled web UI out of the server account's data directory into a root-owned tree, so that a process running as the server account can no longer rearrange what the next package upgrade unpacks as root.

  • The SPA now lives at /usr/share/proxiport/docroot (root-owned, read-only for the daemon). The old /var/lib/proxiport/docroot is removed by the package manager; anything else left there is unused.
  • If [api] doc_root in /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf is still the shipped default "/var/lib/proxiport/docroot", the package rewrites it to the new path. Any other value is left alone; if it still points at the old path the upgrade prints a warning and the web UI stays dark until you set doc_root = "/usr/share/proxiport/docroot" and restart proxiportd.
  • Debian and Ubuntu print dpkg: warning: unable to delete old directory '/var/lib/proxiport': Directory not empty once during this upgrade. That is expected: the old package listed the data directory, the new one does not, and the directory holds your state.
  • The upgrade restarts a running proxiportd at the end, as before. On Debian and Ubuntu the old UI files are gone from the moment the package is unpacked until that restart, so the web UI returns 404 for a few seconds during the upgrade.
  • To downgrade to v0.11.0 or earlier afterwards, set doc_root back to "/var/lib/proxiport/docroot" first; the older package installs the UI there again but does not edit the configuration.

docs.title: Upgrading from a v0.1.2 install
docs.text:
v0.1.3 changes two things that already-running v0.1.2 installs do not pick up automatically — the package postinstall deliberately leaves an existing /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf alone.

  • [api] address default moved from 0.0.0.0:3000 to 127.0.0.1:3000. v0.1.2 servers that have always relied on the example config will still listen on 3000 publicly until you switch them onto one of the three public-listener profiles above. Until then, the API is reachable on plain HTTP, which is exactly what the v0.1.3 defaults are meant to stop.
  • Random secrets and initial credential files are only generated on first install. If you set key_seed / jwt_secret / [api] auth yourself when bringing v0.1.2 up, nothing to do. If you left them at the example placeholders (<YOUR_SEED>, <YOUR_SECRET>, admin:foobaz, clientAuth1:1234), generate replacements manually before upgrading — openssl rand -hex 32 for the seed, openssl rand -base64 24 for the JWT secret, anything strong for the auth strings.

Otherwise the upgrade is dpkg -i / rpm -Uvh of the new package and systemctl restart proxiportd. Config schema is unchanged.

docs.title: Migrating from rport or openrport
docs.text:
ProxiPort's config file format is intentionally compatible with the upstream rportd.conf and rport.conf. Tags and option names are unchanged where the underlying behaviour is unchanged.

To migrate:

  1. Stop the upstream service (rportd or openrportd).
  2. Install ProxiPort using the Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora/RHEL, or tarball path above.
  3. Copy your existing rportd.conf to /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf.
  4. Start proxiportd.
  5. On each agent, replace the upstream binary, copy the config to /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf, and start proxiport. Re-issue the fingerprint if the server's host key has changed.

The datastore schema is forwards-compatible from the openrport tree; ProxiPort runs any pending migrations on first start.

docs.title: What does not change from upstream
docs.text:
• Config file format — TOML, structurally compatible with rportd.conf / rport.conf.
  • Tunnel transport defaults — chisel over WebSocket. Serve it over TLS in production (built-in cert_file/enable_acme on the server, or an external reverse proxy — see HTTPS).
  • Datastore — SQLite by default, MySQL supported.
  • REST API surface — the same /api/v1/* routes and request/response conventions, with the deliberate exceptions listed in What changed from openrport. A few endpoints are new (for example POST /api/v1/pairing). The OpenAPI spec is in the repository under api-doc/.

docs.title: IP-address determination
docs.text:
The server records two IP addresses per agent:

  • the transport IP that the server observes the chisel WebSocket connection coming from, and
  • one or both of the agent's external IPv4 / IPv6 addresses as reported by the agent itself.

The transport IP is always known — it's the TCP source the kernel sees on the agent listener. The external IP is optional and is collected by the agent calling an HTTP IP-discovery API. This page covers when each value is right, why they can disagree, and how to configure the external-IP discovery.

docs.title: Why both values exist
docs.text:
Three common deployments produce three different "the IP" answers:

  1. Direct internet exposure. The server is on the public internet, the agent dials it directly. The transport IP equals the agent's public IP. They always agree.
  2. Reverse proxy in front of the server. The proxy terminates TLS; from the server's perspective every agent appears to come from 127.0.0.1. The transport IP is useless for identifying the agent's network.
  3. Agent behind a CGNAT or a corporate egress proxy. The server sees the gateway IP, not the agent's. Even if the server reads X-Forwarded-For, that header only carries the closest hop the proxy can see, not the original interface IP on the agent host.

The external-IP discovery exists for cases 2 and 3. The agent makes a small outbound HTTPS request to an IP-discovery API, the API echoes back the source IP it observed, and the agent reports that to the server. Because the agent's outbound HTTPS connection traverses the same NAT boundary as a real user request, the IP it gets back is the one inventory tools and ACLs usually want.

docs.title: Enabling the discovery
docs.text:
Off by default, for privacy. Each refresh interval the discovery makes up to two outbound requests to a server you do not control: one over IPv4, then one over IPv6. They use whatever scheme ip_api_url names; a plain http:// URL is accepted and sends the request unencrypted. Decide whether that is acceptable for your deployment before turning it on.

This call does not use the agent's proxy

The lookup builds its own HTTP connection and deliberately dials IPv4 and IPv6 separately, so it does not go through proxy or transports. On an agent routed over Tor or a VPN it would announce the host's real address — which is the one thing that setup exists to hide. With proxy set the agent ignores ip_api_url and logs a warning; with transports set it refuses to start. See Anonymous transport.

In proxiport.conf under [client]:

[client]
  ip_api_url   = "https://api64.ipify.org?format=json"
  ip_refresh_min = 30

ip_refresh_min is the refresh interval in minutes. The default is 30; lower values produce more accurate state at the cost of more outbound calls.

docs.title: Supported IP-discovery APIs
docs.text:
The agent accepts only one response shape: a JSON object with an ip string field:

{"ip": "203.0.113.42"}

Any extra fields are ignored. A plain-text body holding just the address is rejected: the lookup fails, the agent logs Failed to determine IP addresses, and no addresses are reported. Services that return plain text by default (such as https://ifconfig.me/ip, or api.ipify.org without ?format=json) must be used in their JSON form, for example https://api64.ipify.org?format=json. Other examples: https://api.my-ip.io/ip.json, https://api.myip.com, https://api.seeip.org/jsonip.

Verify the URL works over both IPv4 and IPv6 before deploying it. On each refresh ProxiPort makes one IPv4 call and then one IPv6 call, and both must succeed. If either call fails (the endpoint does not answer over that family, or the host has no connectivity for it), the agent logs Failed to determine IP addresses and reports nothing for that refresh, not even the address that worked. A host with no IPv6 connectivity therefore never reports an external IP. Both commands below must print a JSON object with an ip field:

curl -4 -s 'https://api64.ipify.org?format=json'; echo
curl -6 -s 'https://api64.ipify.org?format=json'; echo

ProxiPort does not operate a first-party IP-discovery service.

docs.title: Running your own IP API
docs.text:
A small PHP file on a webserver of yours is enough:

<?php
header('Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8');
echo json_encode(['ip' => $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']]);

To gate access with HTTP basic auth, embed the credential in the URL:

[client]
  ip_api_url = "https://probe:longpassword@ip.example.com/"

Running your own endpoint avoids two failure modes of the public services: throttling (a public service can rate-limit or block your agents in bulk) and disappearance (the service can go down or stop being free). It also keeps the discovery traffic inside your network boundary.

docs.title: What the server does with the values
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/clients returns both kinds of address on each client record:

  • address — the transport-level IP the server saw the connection come from (host only; the port is not stored).
  • ipv4 and ipv6 — arrays of the addresses the agent found on its own (non-loopback) network interfaces, as sent when it connects. Discovered external addresses never appear here.
  • ext_ip_addresses — the result of external-IP discovery, for example {"ipv4": "203.0.113.7", "ipv6": "2001:db8::7", "error": "", "updated_at": "..."}. Here ipv4 and ipv6 are single strings, not arrays. The value is null when discovery is disabled or has not reported yet. A failed lookup is logged on the agent and not sent, so the value keeps the last successful result. To choose it with the fields query option, use the name ip_addresses.

The SPA's per-client detail page shows the transport address and the interface addresses in its Network card. It does not show the discovered external addresses yet; read them from the API (ext_ip_addresses).

The "Only my current IP address" preset on the tunnel-create form uses the address the server saw the request come from (GET /me/ip). That is the operator's IP, not the agent's, so the agent's discovery setting does not affect it. Behind a reverse proxy this address comes from X-Forwarded-For only when the proxy is listed in [api] trusted_proxies (see below). Otherwise it is the socket peer.

docs.title: Forwarded-for handling on the server
docs.text:
This takes two settings, one on each side. Forwarding the header from the proxy is not enough on its own: the server ignores X-Forwarded-For unless the socket peer is listed in [api] trusted_proxies, and that list is empty by default.

Without it the audit log records the proxy's address — usually 127.0.0.1 — for every operator action, and GET /me/ip returns the same, so the "Only my current IP address" tunnel ACL preset writes an ACL for the loopback rather than for the operator. Neither failure is reported: the header is simply not read.

1. Tell the server which peers may speak for someone else, in proxiportd.conf:

[api]
  ## CIDRs or addresses of the reverse proxies in front of this server.
  ## Empty (the default) means X-Forwarded-For is never trusted.
  trusted_proxies = ['127.0.0.1/32', '::1/128']

Use the address the proxy connects from, which for a proxy on the same host is the loopback the API is bound to. Keep this list as small as it can be: anything in it can claim to be any client.

2. Configure the proxy to send the header. For nginx:

proxy_set_header X-Real-IP        $remote_addr;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For  $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

A Caddy reverse proxy adds X-Forwarded-For by default.

X-Forwarded-For from outside the trusted network must be stripped at the edge — otherwise a client can spoof its source IP for audit log entries. Most reverse proxies do this by default; double-check yours.

With built-in TLS (no proxy in front) leave trusted_proxies unset. The connection's remote address is the operator's address, and an empty list is what stops a client from claiming otherwise.

To check it is working, make any state-changing API call through the proxy and read the remote_ip on the resulting audit-log row: it should be your address, not the proxy's.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• Decide whether the privacy tradeoff of outbound IP discovery is acceptable. If not, leave it off and rely on the transport IP.
  • If you enable it, prefer a small endpoint you operate, ideally on HTTPS with basic auth, to keep the metadata trail inside your network.
  • Always set the refresh interval to a value that won't get you throttled — 30 minutes is the default and is rarely the bottleneck.
  • If you front the server with a reverse proxy, do both halves: set [api] trusted_proxies to the proxy's address and configure the proxy to forward X-Forwarded-For. Either one alone leaves the audit log recording the proxy instead of the operator. With built-in TLS the connection remote address is used directly, no header configuration is needed, and trusted_proxies should stay empty.

See also: client attributes for tagging agents by location/role/datacenter, and operator runbook — tunnels for the single-IP ACL preset that uses the operator's request address.

docs.title: Migrating from rport or openrport
docs.text: ProxiPort is config-format-compatible with upstream rport and openrport. The migration is a stop / replace / restart, not a schema rebuild.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
1. Stop the upstream service. 
    sudo systemctl stop rportd   # or: openrportd
  2. Back up the existing state. The datastore lives in /var/lib/rport/ (or /var/lib/openrport/): 
    sudo tar -czf rport-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz \
  /etc/rport /var/lib/rport
  3. Install ProxiPort server packages. See install.
  4. Copy the config across. 
    sudo cp /etc/rport/rportd.conf /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf
    The option names are the same. Only the file path and the systemd unit name change — but a few values need a look. [api] doc_root must point at ProxiPort's web UI (/usr/share/proxiport/docroot for a package install; an upstream value such as /var/lib/rport/docroot leaves the UI dark), and any cert_file, key_file or auth_file path that still names /etc/rport or /var/lib/rport must follow the files. The same goes for [logging] log_file and, if set, [api] access_log_file: an upstream value under /var/log/rport is read-only under the packaged systemd unit, which allows writes only to /var/lib/proxiport and /var/log/proxiport. proxiportd exits at startup if it cannot open its log file, so point them at /var/log/proxiport/proxiportd.log and /var/log/proxiport/api-access.log.
  5. Move the existing datastore into place. The packaged unit only lets proxiportd write under /var/lib/proxiport and /var/log/proxiport (ProtectSystem=strict), so move the old directory there and hand it to the proxiport account (upstream ran as rport): 
    sudo mv /var/lib/rport /var/lib/proxiport
sudo chown -R proxiport:proxiport /var/lib/proxiport
    Make sure [server] data_dir in /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf is /var/lib/proxiport. If you must keep the data somewhere else, point data_dir at it and add that path with a systemd drop-in (sudo systemctl edit proxiportd, then under [Service] add ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/rport). Without the drop-in the server cannot write its databases there.
  6. Start the service. 
    sudo systemctl enable --now proxiportd
sudo systemctl status proxiportd
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/proxiport/proxiportd.log
    Pending schema migrations run automatically on first start, and the server writes them to the file set by [logging] log_file, along with its host-key fingerprint. If the unit fails to start, sudo journalctl -u proxiportd -n 50 shows why. That includes a config error or a log_file the proxiport account cannot write, such as one that still points at the old upstream log directory.

Existing agents reconnect against the same client-auth credentials and the same host-key fingerprint, so the inventory comes back populated without any per-agent touch:

7. Disable the old unit so it does not race ProxiPort on reboot. 

sudo systemctl disable rportd

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Each agent needs the binary swapped and the config relocated. The control protocol is unchanged — agents register against the same client-auth credentials.

  1. Stop the upstream agent. 
    sudo systemctl stop rport   # or: openrport
  2. Install the ProxiPort agent package (see install).
  3. Move the config. 
    sudo cp /etc/rport/rport.conf /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf
sudo chown root:proxiport-agent /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf
sudo chmod 0640 /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf
    The ProxiPort agent runs as its own account, proxiport-agent, so point [client] data_dir at a directory that account owns (/var/lib/proxiport-agent in the packages) rather than at the old /var/lib/rport.
  4. Re-issue the host-key fingerprint if the server's host key changed. If you reused the same key_seed in proxiportd.conf, the fingerprint is unchanged — keep fingerprint = "..." as it was. If the server now has a different key, copy the new fingerprint from /var/log/proxiport/proxiportd.log on first start.
  5. Start. 
    sudo systemctl enable --now proxiport

docs.title: What is config-compatible
docs.text:
• [server] block options: address, key_seed, auth_file, data_dir, keep_lost_clients, tunnel_*, used_ports, excluded_ports.
  • [api] block options: address, auth, auth_file, auth_user_table, auth_group_table, auth_group_details_table, jwt_secret, doc_root, cert_file, key_file, access_log_file, user_login_wait, max_failed_login, ban_time, totp_enabled, totp_login_session_ttl, totp_account_name. (auth_group_details_table is required for per-group permission editing in the database store; see API authentication.)
  • [logging], [database], [caddy-integration], [monitoring], [notifications], [pushover], [smtp] blocks — same option names as upstream. (There is no separate [client-auth] block — client-authentication options live under [server]: auth, auth_file, auth_table, auth_multiuse_creds, equate_clientauthid_clientid.)
  • The schedule, command, script, library and user-auth tables: same schema, read as-is. The audit-log and vault tables are read as-is too, and ProxiPort extends them automatically on first start. The audit log gains seq, mac and prev_mac columns for its tamper-evidence chain, plus corrected indexes. The vault status table gains a kdf column and drops dec_check, and the vault is re-keyed to Argon2id on its next unlock. Because of these changes, rolling back to openrport needs the backup from step 2 (see Rollback).

docs.title: What is intentionally not migrated
docs.text:
• Anything plus/ produced. OAuth/OIDC sessions issued via the upstream Plus plugin will not work after migration. Affected users will need to log in via local password + (optional) TOTP, which is the AGPL-supported path.
  • Alerting state. The upstream alerting feature was Plus-gated. Alert definitions in the database are ignored. They will start working again when alerting is reimplemented in the open.
  • The Vue/Nuxt frontend. Users do not need to migrate anything — the SvelteKit SPA is served by the new server out of the box.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If the migration fails and you need to roll back:

sudo systemctl stop proxiportd
sudo systemctl enable --now rportd

The datastore is forwards-compatible from openrport, so rolling back in the other direction (after ProxiPort ran migrations on the schema) may not work cleanly. Restore from the backup taken in step 2 above.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
The proxiport agent can sample basic host metrics — CPU, memory, disk fill, network throughput, and a running-process list — and ship them to the server, where they are persisted to monitoring.db and charted in the SPA's per-client Monitoring tab.

Monitoring is enabled by default on both ends. Operators who want to keep the agent footprint minimal, or who already run a dedicated monitoring stack (Prometheus, Netdata, Grafana Agent, etc.), can turn it off without losing tunnel or command functionality.

docs.title: What is sampled
docs.text:
The agent collects, on every interval:

  • CPU usage as a percentage across all cores.
  • Memory usage as a percentage of total.
  • IO wait as a percentage of CPU time (CPU iowait share). Only Linux agents report it; on macOS and Windows the operating system exposes no iowait counter, so the value is always 0.
  • Filesystem fill for every detected mount point or volume.
  • Network bandwidth on up to two named interfaces (net_lan, net_wan).
  • Process list sorted by PID descending; the top N are reported.

No application-level metrics (request counts, queue depth, etc.) are collected. This is host telemetry, not APM.

docs.title: Server configuration
docs.text:
Under [monitoring] in proxiportd.conf:

[monitoring]
  enabled = true
  data_storage_duration = "7d"

enabled is the system-wide kill switch. Setting it to false overrides every agent's monitoring setting — no samples are accepted or stored. The monitoring read endpoints (/clients/{id}/graph-metrics, /graph-metrics/{graph}, /metrics, /processes, /mountpoints) then answer 404 with "monitoring disabled. re-enable to view monitoring statistics."

data_storage_duration (7d default) is the retention window. Use d for days or h for hours, and quote the value. The minimum is 1h: a shorter value stops the server at startup with "monitoring results must be stored for at least 1 hour". A background task runs every 2 minutes and deletes rows older than the window. After a pass that deleted rows, the task runs a VACUUM to shrink monitoring.db, at most once every 24 hours. The older integer key data_storage_days is deprecated but still honoured: when it is set above 0 it takes precedence over data_storage_duration.

Database growth

monitoring.db can grow quickly. Each connected agent at the default 60-second interval writes a row roughly every minute across CPU, memory, IO, every mounted filesystem, every monitored network adapter, and the top-N processes. A fleet of a few hundred agents at the default retention will easily push past a gigabyte. Pick data_storage_duration deliberately, and put monitoring.db on a volume with room to grow. To keep the file outside the main data_dir, replace it with a symlink before first start. The packaged systemd unit runs with ProtectSystem=strict and lets the service write only under /var/lib/proxiport and /var/log/proxiport, so also add the target directory with a drop-in (systemctl edit proxiportd, then [Service] / ReadWritePaths=/path/to/target-dir). Otherwise SQLite cannot write there. Do not put the target under /home: the unit sets ProtectHome=true, which hides that tree from the service.

docs.title: Client configuration
docs.text:
The [monitoring] block in proxiport.conf controls what the agent sends:

[monitoring]
  enabled = true
  interval = '60s'

  fs_type_include = ['ext3','ext4','xfs','jfs','ntfs','btrfs','hfs','apfs','exfat','smbfs','nfs']
  fs_path_exclude = []
  fs_path_exclude_recurse = false
  fs_identify_mountpoints_by_device = true

  pm_enabled = true
  pm_kerneltasks_enabled = true
  pm_max_number_processes = 500

  net_lan = ['eth0', '1000']
  #net_wan = ['eth1', '1000']

interval is the sample period, written as a quoted duration string (e.g. '60s', '5m') like the other duration keys. A bare integer is decoded as nanoseconds, not seconds, so write interval = '5m', not interval = 300. Values below 60 seconds are clamped up to '60s' — the storage rate is the bottleneck, not the collection rate.

fs_type_include whitelists filesystem types the agent will report. fs_path_exclude lists mountpoints, drive letters or globs (e.g. ['/mnt/*', 'h:']) to skip. Each entry must match a whole mountpoint. With fs_path_exclude_recurse = true, an entry can also be any directory, and every mountpoint beneath it is excluded too. This is useful for excluding bind mounts, tmpfs, or container overlay paths.

net_lan and net_wan are optional, and each takes a [device_name, max_speed_mbit] pair. Leave a key out if you don't want that card monitored. When you set one, the device name must be non-empty and the max speed must be a whole number of at least 1. Otherwise the agent fails config validation and does not start. The agent uses the max speed to compute a usage percentage. On Windows discover the device name with Get-NetAdapter.

To disable monitoring on a single agent — for example a tiny edge device where samples cost meaningful CPU — set:

[monitoring]
  enabled = false

The agent then sends no samples, so the per-client Monitoring tab shows an empty state.

docs.title: SPA
docs.text: The per-client Monitoring tab plots CPU and memory utilisation for the last 6, 12 or 24 hours (the chart cannot cover the full retention window). It also shows the most recent process snapshot, or the snapshot nearest a sample you select on the chart. The tab does not show filesystem fill levels. Query them from /api/v1/clients/<id>/mountpoints.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
The raw rows are exposed via /api/v1/clients/<id>/metrics. Rows come back newest first; use sort=timestamp for ascending order. Select a time range with filter[timestamp][since]= / filter[timestamp][until]= (RFC3339) or filter[timestamp][gt]= / filter[timestamp][lt]= (unix epoch). Choose columns with fields[metrics]= followed by any of timestamp, cpu_usage_percent, memory_usage_percent or io_usage_percent (all four are returned by default). The endpoint is paginated with page[limit] and page[offset]. The default limit is 1 row, so a query without page[limit] returns only the latest sample; the maximum is 120. Other query parameters are ignored. Filesystem and process snapshots are at /api/v1/clients/<id>/mountpoints (max limit 100) and /api/v1/clients/<id>/processes (max limit 10), with the same timestamp filters. Use it to feed another visualisation system, to export to a long-term store, or to script alerting on top of ProxiPort without modifying the agent.

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/alpha-prod/metrics?filter[timestamp][since]=2026-05-17T00:00:00Z&page[limit]=120&sort=timestamp' \
  | jq

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: monitoring.db is one of the SQLite files listed in the operator runbook backups section. Treat it like any other datastore — snapshot it with the filesystem-stop-the-world technique or use SQLite's .backup command for a hot copy. Losing the file resets the charts to empty but does not break anything else; the agents continue sending samples to a fresh monitoring.db on next start.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
ProxiPort itself does not evaluate thresholds against the metrics yet. Until alerting lands as an OSS module, wire one of these:

  • Run a small cron job that queries /api/v1/clients/<id>/metrics, checks against your thresholds, and pushes to your notifier of choice (Alertmanager, Pushover, Slack webhook).
  • Use the agent's command/script channel to invoke the host's own monitoring agent (node_exporter, telegraf, …) and rely on that pipeline for alerting. ProxiPort then sits alongside the existing observability stack rather than replacing it.

Alerting based on monitoring thresholds is planned but not yet shipped — tracked as an OSS reimplementation of upstream functionality previously gated behind a proprietary plugin. See Changes from openrport.

See also: architecture — datastore, operator runbook — backups, client attributes for labelling agents with tags and labels, so you can find the agents you want (the inventory search matches tags; /api/v1/clients accepts filter[tags] and filter[labels]) before opening each one's Monitoring tab.

docs.title: Operator runbook
docs.text: Short reference for keeping a ProxiPort server healthy. Not a full admin guide — see install and migration for the first-run setup.

docs.title: Service control
docs.text:
# Server
sudo systemctl status proxiportd
sudo systemctl restart proxiportd
sudo tail -f /var/log/proxiport/proxiportd.log
sudo journalctl -u proxiportd -n 50   # startup failures

# Agent
sudo systemctl status proxiport
sudo systemctl restart proxiport
sudo tail -f /var/log/proxiport-agent/proxiport.log

Both programs log to the file set by [logging] log_file, and only to stdout (and so to the journal) when log_file is left empty. With the shipped configs the journal shows service start/stop and errors printed before the log file is open.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
Purpose Path Server config /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf Server data /var/lib/proxiport/ Server SPA files /usr/share/proxiport/docroot/ (root-owned, read-only for the daemon) Server logs (default) /var/log/proxiport/proxiportd.log ([logging] log_file; journald only if it is left empty) Agent config /etc/proxiport/proxiport.conf Agent binary (.deb / .rpm package or tarball) /usr/bin/proxiport, unit at /lib/systemd/system/proxiport.service Agent binary (pairing installer) /usr/local/bin/proxiport, unit written by proxiport --service install Agent data /var/lib/proxiport-agent/ ([client] data_dir) Agent log (default) /var/log/proxiport-agent/proxiport.log ([logging] log_file; journald only if it is left empty)

Use the binary path that matches how the agent was installed when you write sudoers rules, watchdog units or command allow-lists.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
The server keeps everything that matters in two places:

  • SQLite databases under /var/lib/proxiport/. The set as of this writing: clients.db, monitoring.db, library.db, auditlog.db, api_sessions.db, api_token.db, client_groups.db, jobs.db, notifications.db, and the vault store at vault.sqlite.db. All of them except the vault store are created, with their schema, the first time the server starts (auditlog.db only while the audit log is enabled); vault.sqlite.db appears once the vault is initialised. When the audit log rotates it also leaves auditlog.<timestamp>.db files in the same directory, so include those too. Back the directory up with a stop-the-world snapshot or with the SQLite .backup command for hot backups.
  • /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf — the config with the pinned key_seed, jwt_secret, and admin credentials. Treat it as a secret in its own right, or encrypt those settings — see encrypting the config secrets.
  • The at-rest DEK key file (if [key_provider] type = "file" is configured) — losing it makes all of this unreadable: the encrypted totp_secret column, the entire vault, any encrypted config setting, stored command and script output in jobs.db, and the process and mountpoint data in monitoring.db (see What else the key provider encrypts). Back it up out-of-band, not only inside the data_dir tarball, and ideally keep it off the disk that holds the databases.

User auth lives either in a JSON file ([api] auth_file = "...") or in user and group tables ([api] auth_user_table / auth_group_table) in the separate [database] connection — a MySQL/MariaDB database or the stand-alone SQLite file named by [database] db_name, not one of the per-feature files above. Back up whichever one you use alongside the SQLite files.

Tarball both directories for the simplest backup. Restore by stopping the service, replacing the directories, and starting again.

The [database] section (db_type = "mysql" or "sqlite") holds only the optional API-user (auth_user_table) and client-auth (auth_table) tables. It does not replace the SQLite files in data_dir, which still need the backup described above. If you configured it, back that database up too: with your usual MySQL tooling for MySQL/MariaDB, or by copying the SQLite file it points to, which may live outside data_dir.

The vault is a special case. It is encrypted at rest with a passphrase that is never written to disk (and, when a [key_provider] is configured, additionally wrapped under the server DEK), so a server restart always re-locks it — back up vault.sqlite.db alongside the other databases and remember that restoring it requires re-entering the passphrase through the SPA before the documents and per-client secrets are readable again. If a key provider was enabled, the restored server must also present the same DEK, or the vault fails closed.

docs.title: Encrypting the config secrets
docs.text:
proxiportd.conf holds the two most valuable secrets on the box: key_seed, from which the SSH host key every agent pins is derived, and jwt_secret, which signs every API session. Anyone who reads the file in the clear can stand up a server your agents will trust and mint admin tokens for your API — from a copy, off your machine, without touching the running service.

Configure a key provider (the [key_provider] section of proxiportd.example.conf) and those settings can live in the config as ciphertext instead.

With type = "file", create the key so that only its owner can read it:

(umask 077 && openssl rand -base64 32 > /etc/proxiport/dek.key)
chown proxiport /etc/proxiport/dek.key

The umask 077 is not optional. Without it the default root umask leaves the key 0644 inside a world-traversable /etc/proxiport, which hands every local account the one key whose whole job is to make a read of the config and the databases useless. The server refuses to start on a key file that is readable by anyone but its owner, and names the chmod that fixes it.

Encrypt a value with:

proxiportd -c /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf secret encrypt

It prompts for the value without echoing it (or reads it from a pipe), and prints an enc:v1:… string. Paste that in place of the plaintext:

[server]
  key_seed = "enc:v1:0nQxk2…"

[api]
  jwt_secret = "enc:v1:kZ0m9y…"

The same works for [server] auth, [api] auth, [database] db_password, [smtp] auth_password, and the [pushover] credentials. Settings without the enc:v1: prefix are still read as plaintext, so a config can be migrated one value at a time, and nothing breaks if you encrypt none of them.

Two things follow from the DEK being the only way back:

  • Keep the DEK off the machine. A type = "file" key sitting next to the config it protects stops nobody who steals the disk. Prefer type = "env" with the key injected at start (systemd EnvironmentFile on a tmpfs, a secrets manager, your orchestrator).
  • A value the server cannot decrypt stops the server. Wrong DEK, missing DEK, corrupted ciphertext — proxiportd refuses to start rather than run with a regenerated jwt_secret (which would silently invalidate every session) or a different host key (which would break every agent's fingerprint check). Fix the key, don't work around it.

docs.title: What else the key provider encrypts
docs.text:
Enabling a [key_provider] also encrypts the recoverable operational data the server stores, transparently — you read and write it through the API exactly as before, and only the on-disk databases hold ciphertext:

  • Command and script output (jobs.db): stdout, stderr and error text are encrypted. The command itself and the one-line summary stay in the clear so the schedules "last run" view works without the key.
  • Monitoring data (monitoring.db): the process list and mountpoint blobs (which can carry command-line arguments and filesystem layout) are encrypted.
  • Vault secrets and TOTP enrolment seeds, as covered in vault.md and the two-factor docs.

On the first boot after you enable a key provider, existing plaintext rows are re-encrypted in place. A stolen database read under the wrong key (or with none) fails closed — it never returns the ciphertext as if it were the value. As with the config secrets, this protects a stolen disk, not a live host that also holds the DEK.

File pushes are staged briefly on disk before agents pull them; that staging directory ({data_dir}/filepush) is created owner-only. For the strongest guarantee, mount it on a tmpfs so payloads never touch persistent storage.

docs.title: Rotating credentials
docs.text:
• Admin password. Edit /etc/proxiport/proxiportd.conf, change the [api] auth = "admin:<new-password>" line, restart the service. Or, if running a multi-user setup with auth_file, edit that JSON file or the corresponding DB row.

The Users page surfaces a banner whenever auth is pinned in the config ([api] auth = "admin:...") rather than user-managed — rotating in that mode is a config edit + restart, not a SPA action.

- JWT secret. [api] jwt_secret = "<long-random-string>" — rotating this invalidates every issued session immediately. All users will be redirected to /auth. - key_seed. Rotating the seed changes the server's SSH host key. Every connected agent will fail the fingerprint check until its proxiport.conf is updated. Avoid rotating unless the seed is compromised; coordinate with all agent operators.

Both of these can be stored encrypted — rotate by writing the new value's enc:v1:… form into the config, exactly as above. - client-auth credentials. Used by agents to register. Change via [server] auth = "<id>:<password>" (single credential), or via the JSON file pointed at by [server] auth_file, or via the table named in [server] auth_table. Push the new credentials to each agent and restart it.

When the credentials come from auth_file or auth_table (and [server] auth_write has not been set to false), they can also be managed from the SPA at Client Access. The single [server] auth credential is read-only there:

  • API tokens. For programmatic API consumers, mint scoped API tokens at API Tokens rather than reusing a human's username/password. Tokens carry a lifetime and an explicit scope (read, read+write, …) and are revocable independently.

Send a token as HTTP basic auth — your username, with the token as the password (curl -u <username>:<token> …) — not as a Bearer header; see API authentication.

  • TOTP second factor. TOTP needs a user store the server can write the enrolled secret to: a JSON auth_file or the database user table, each with a totp_secret field (see API authentication). It does not work with the single static [api] auth = "user:password" credential. With such a store in place, set [api] totp_enabled = true in proxiportd.conf, restart, and each user is prompted to enroll on their next login. The user scans the SPA's QR with any RFC 6238 TOTP app:

Admins can require an existing user to re-enroll from the Users page:

Once enabled at the server, the Info page reflects the new posture:

Each user's profile shows their TOTP enrollment state and lets them remove their authenticator. Removing it asks for the account password; a user who cannot supply it needs an admin to use Reset 2FA on the Users page instead:

docs.title: Capacity and limits
docs.text:
• Connected agents per server. The agent inventory (clients.db) and the other operational databases (jobs, monitoring, audit log) are always SQLite files under [server] data_dir. SQLite handles a few hundred agents comfortably on modest hardware; to support more, give the server faster storage and more CPU. The [database] section (db_type = "mysql") moves only the API-user and client-auth tables to MySQL/MariaDB, not the agent store.
  • Tunnel ports. [server] used_ports controls the pool of ports the server may allocate for tunnels. Default 20000-30000. Expand if you run out.
  • Per-user session lifetime. ?token-lifetime=<seconds> on /login; defaults to 10 minutes; the SPA asks for 24 hours.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Package installs (.deb / .rpm, the common case): install the new package over the old one, exactly as in Upgrading. The package restarts a running proxiportd itself, runs schema migrations on that first start, and since v0.11.1 moves the web UI to /usr/share/proxiport/docroot and rewrites a default doc_root for you (see Upgrading to v0.11.1 or later for what it prints and what to check). Tail the logs afterwards.

Tarball installs:

  1. Stop the service.
  2. Replace the binary at /usr/bin/proxiportd (where the tarball steps put it) and the web UI under /usr/share/proxiport/docroot, both root-owned.
  3. Start the service. Schema migrations, if any, run on first start.
  4. Tail the logs to confirm.

For the agent, the same shape applies on each managed host; agents installed through the pairing service update with its update script.

docs.title: Tunnels
docs.text:
A tunnel is a per-session listener on the server that forwards traffic back to a TCP port on the agent. Open one from a client's Tunnels tab.

The ACL is enforced at the server's listener, not at the agent — denied traffic never crosses the chisel session. Only my current IP address is the default preset and uses the address the API saw the request come from. Behind a reverse proxy that is the proxy's own address unless the proxy is listed in [api] trusted_proxies and sends X-Forwarded-For — both halves are needed, see IP-address determination. With built-in TLS the connection IP is used directly.

Tunnels also accept inactivity / lifetime caps, after which the server closes the listener and notifies the agent.

You can save a tunnel definition into the Stored tunnels library to re-open it later in one click.

The global Tunnels page is the operator's at-a-glance view across every connected agent.

docs.title: Finding and reusing tunnels from the API
docs.text:
The per-client endpoint GET /api/v1/clients/{id} includes that client's active tunnels by default. The list endpoint GET /api/v1/clients returns a lean projection — id, name, hostname — so request the tunnels field explicitly when you want it across the fleet:

GET /api/v1/clients?fields[clients]=id,name,tunnels

This is the same field-projection the list endpoint uses for every optional attribute: ask for a field and you get it; a client with no open tunnels reports an empty list. Each tunnel object carries the id you delete it by (DELETE /api/v1/clients/{id}/tunnels/{tunnelID}), so you never have to remember the id from when you created it.

docs.title: Tunnels survive an agent restart
docs.text: When an agent drops and reconnects under the same client id, the server re-establishes that client's tunnels automatically — including a manually pinned local port — and the restored listener starts carrying traffic again with no operator action. Because the tunnel is still there, opening a new tunnel to the same agent-side port returns ERR_CODE_TUNNEL_TO_PORT_EXIST. Reuse the existing tunnel (look it up as above) rather than recreating it; delete it by id first only if you genuinely want a fresh listener.

docs.title: Commands and scripts
docs.text:
ProxiPort can run ad-hoc commands or multi-line scripts against any connected agent and show the output once each run finishes. What an agent will run is decided by the [remote-commands] block in its proxiport.conf. With the stock config, remote commands are enabled (enabled = true) but filtered: only commands given by absolute path under /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin or C:\Windows\System32 pass the default allow list, and the default deny list rejects shell metacharacters. Set enabled = false to turn command execution off entirely. Agents installed through the pairing service have remote commands disabled unless the installer was run with -x, which enables them with an unrestricted allow list.

When a command is allowed, the SPA polls the job and, once it finishes, prints stdout / stderr under the form followed by a --- status=successful --- (or failed / cancelled) line. If the command fails, its error (for example exit status 127) also appears in the Error column of the Recent commands table.

Scripts are the same control surface with a multi-line editor and a free-text Interpreter field, which starts out as /bin/bash; enter any interpreter path (for example /usr/bin/python3) or an interpreter alias defined in the agent's config. The agent writes the body to a tempfile, executes, and reaps the process.

Script execution is off by default on the agent and is separate from the command allow list. Set enabled = true under [remote-scripts] in the agent's proxiport.conf and restart the agent; until then every script run is rejected. Scripts also need remote commands to be enabled. An agent installed with the pairing installer's -x switch already has scripts enabled. See Scripts.

For repeated patterns, save commands and scripts into the Library:

The Library stores command and script bodies for reuse; it has no run action of its own. To run a command against several agents at once — useful for one-shot fleet work — use the Commands page: tick the target agents and type the command, or paste a saved entry's body from the Library.

The global Scripts page is the same concept for whole-fleet script runs. It is still being reimplemented from the upstream shape — at the moment it is a stub whose button opens the Commands page, where you can pick an interpreter to run a script body across several agents. To run a script on a single agent, use the Scripts tab on that agent's page.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text: For recurring runs, create a schedule: a cron expression, the target agents (or client groups), and the command or script body to run. The body is entered on the schedule itself; schedules do not reference Library entries, so changing a Library entry does not change a schedule. The scheduler is in-process; no external cron is needed.

docs.title: File transfer
docs.text: From a client's Files tab, upload a file from your browser to a chosen path on the agent, with optional mode, owner and group, and options for an atomic (sync) write and force-overwrite. The transfer goes over the same chisel session as everything else.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
Every state-changing API call writes an auditlog.db row with the user, client (if any), action, timestamp, and the request payload. The per-client view filters the same table down to events touching one agent:

The global Audit page is for cross-cutting queries — who created which tunnel, who rotated which credential. Reading a vault secret — the one high-value read worth tracking — is recorded too, as a read action (never the secret itself).

docs.title: Tamper-evidence
docs.text:
When a key provider is configured, each audit entry carries a keyed HMAC chained to the previous entry (the key is derived from the server DEK and is never stored in the audit database, so someone who has only the database files cannot recompute it; anyone who can read the DEK — the key_file, or the running server's environment or memory — can). Editing or deleting a row after the fact breaks the chain. Check it with:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://<server>/api/v1/auditlog/verify | jq

A "Valid": true response means every entry verifies; a break reports the sequence number and kind (mac — a row was edited, link/gap — a row was removed or reordered). This detects tampering on the box; it does not stop a host with the DEK from forging new entries — ship entries to an off-host, append-only sink for that. Rotation starts a fresh chain per auditlog.<timestamp>.db file.

docs.title: User and group admin
docs.text:
User groups gate which API endpoints (and therefore which SPA sections) each user can reach. The built-in Administrators group has every permission set and cannot be edited or deleted. To add a group, give a user its name on the Users page (type it in the group field and click Add group); the group then appears on User Groups, where you tick only the columns the role needs. Permissions can be edited only with database-backed users and an [api] auth_group_details_table; otherwise the page is read-only. A user's effective permissions are the union across its groups.

Client groups are rule-based sets of agents: a group's params match client attributes such as client ID, name, hostname, OS or tags, and every agent that matches belongs to the group. Groups are created and changed through the API (see Client groups and permissions); the SPA's Client Groups page lists them read-only. You can target a group by passing group_ids to the multi-client command and script API calls, or in a schedule's "Target groups" field. The ad-hoc Commands page selects targets per client only, and the audit log has no group filter.

Each user has a profile page (Settings → Profile) that shows their username, group membership and 2FA recipient, and manages their own TOTP second factor. The web UI has no self-service password change. An administrator sets a user's password from Settings → Users, or a user can change their own through the API with PUT /api/v1/me (password plus old_password). With static [api] auth, the password is whatever the config file sets.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• 429 too many requests or 423 Locked after failed logins. Failed password logins are throttled per source IP plus username: after a failed basic-auth or /login attempt for a username, further attempts for that username from the same address get 429 for [api] user_login_wait seconds (default 2). Requests with an expired or invalid session token, or with no credentials, just get 401 and add nothing to that throttle, but every unauthorized request counts against the per-IP limit: after [api] max_failed_login failures (default 10) the address is refused with 423 Locked for [api] ban_time seconds (default 600). The SPA stops sending API calls once its token is gone; if you write your own client, stop retrying on the first 401 and re-authenticate, so a burst of rejected calls does not lock out your own address.
  • Agent refuses to connect with "fingerprint mismatch". Either the server's key_seed changed or the agent's fingerprint = "..." value is stale. Compare the fingerprint printed in the server log at startup against the agent config.
  • SPA shows the vault as locked even after entering the passphrase. Vault passphrases are not persisted server-side — they live in memory for the life of the process. A server restart re-locks the vault. Enter the passphrase again via Settings → Vault.

  • Server exits with "is still the placeholder from proxiport.example.conf". Since 0.8.8 proxiportd refuses to start while [api] jwt_secret, [server] key_seed, [server] auth or [api] auth still holds the value the example config ships. Those values are published in the project repository, so they are not secrets — a placeholder jwt_secret in particular becomes the token signing key, and anyone who can reach the API can mint an admin token with it. The .deb and .rpm postinstall substitutes all four on first install; a tarball, container, or hand-copied config does not. Generate them yourself:

    openssl rand -hex 32     # key_seed
openssl rand -base64 24  # jwt_secret

    Leaving jwt_secret unset is also fine — the server then mints a random one at startup, at the cost of logging every user out on each restart.

docs.title: Where to get help
docs.text:
• File a bug or feature request on the GitHub repository.
  • Private vulnerability reports go through GitHub Security Advisories — see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: What we forked
docs.text:
Specifically taken from openrport, under its MIT licence, and now part of the ProxiPort tree under AGPL-3.0-or-later (as the combined work):

  • the Go server (server/)
  • the Go agent (client/ upstream, renamed to the ProxiPort agent packaging)

The inherited MIT copyright notice for that imported code is preserved verbatim in LICENSE-MIT.

docs.title: The plus/ plugin scaffolding
docs.text:
openrport's source tree contained a directory called plus/. Its sole function was to load a separately-distributed proprietary plugin binary (the "Plus" plugin) that gated several enterprise features (OAuth/OIDC, RBAC, alerting, etc.). The Plus binary itself was never in any public source repository — it was distributed by the previous upstream maintainer under a proprietary licence, behind a paywall.

We deleted the plus/ scaffolding from ProxiPort along with every IsPlusEnabled capability gate. We do not ship the proprietary binary, we do not load it, and we do not reimplement Plus features as a license-gated commercial add-on. Features that previously lived behind the gate (OAuth/OIDC, RBAC, alerting, …) will be reimplemented in the open under AGPL.

docs.title: The proprietary Vue/Nuxt frontend
docs.text:
The upstream rport / openrport projects shipped a web frontend, but only as a prebuilt JavaScript bundle. The source for that frontend was never released as FOSS. We could not have forked it even if we wanted to, because the source was not available.

The frontend in ProxiPort's frontend/ is original work: a SvelteKit SPA written from scratch by Proximile LLC, in TypeScript, against the existing REST API. It is AGPL-licensed along with the rest of the tree.

docs.title: Why AGPL?
docs.text:
The upstream rport / openrport tree is MIT-licensed and remains so as imported — the inherited MIT notice in LICENSE-MIT is the authoritative attribution for that code. The MIT licence permits relicensing of the combined work as long as the original notice is preserved, which it is.

We chose AGPL-3.0-or-later for the combined work for two reasons:

  1. Network-use protection. ProxiPort is a server. AGPL is the licence specifically designed to ensure that users interacting with a modified server over the network get the right to its source. Permissive licences (MIT, Apache) do not give that guarantee, and the one thing we are not interested in repeating is the cycle of FOSS server projects being closed-sourced once they reach a useful state.
  2. No closed forks of ProxiPort itself. If someone wants to build commercial features on top of ProxiPort, they may, but the AGPL ensures their modifications to ProxiPort itself flow back. The inherited MIT code is unaffected — anyone who wants the permissively-licensed upstream remains free to take it directly from openrport.
