docs.text: If you find a file in this tree that is not FOSS, is missing attribution, or you believe is licensed incorrectly, please open an issue. Attribution bugs are bugs and we will fix them.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Scripts are the multi-line cousin of commands. Where a command sends a single line for the agent's shell to evaluate, a script sends a body of code plus an interpreter — the agent writes the body to a tempfile, runs the interpreter against it, and reaps the process.

This lets you ship a bash heredoc, a Python script, or a PowerShell function to one or many agents and stream the output back, without keeping the script on disk on every host.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The operator POSTs the base64-encoded script body to /api/v1/clients/<id>/scripts along with an interpreter and the usual command options.
  2. The server forwards the body to the agent via the chisel channel.
  3. The agent decodes the body, writes it to a random tempfile under {data_dir}/scripts/, and invokes the interpreter against the file.
  4. stdout/stderr stream back over the same channel.
  5. The agent deletes the tempfile when it stops supervising the job, whatever the exit code. That happens when the process exits or when timeout_sec elapses, whichever comes first. A script still running at the timeout is not killed: the job is reported with status unknown, and the process keeps running after its tempfile is gone.

The end-to-end model is the same as command execution; the only differences are that scripts can hold multiple lines and that the agent's [remote-scripts] switch must also be enabled (in addition to [remote-commands]).

docs.title: Enabling script execution on the agent
docs.text:
[remote-commands]
  enabled = true

[remote-scripts]
  enabled = true

Script execution requires command execution. If [remote-scripts] enabled = true while [remote-commands] enabled = false, the agent refuses to start and logs config validation failed: remote scripts execution requires remote commands to be enabled. Enable both switches, or leave [remote-scripts] disabled.

The allow/deny filter does not apply to scripts

A script body and its interpreter are not matched against [remote-commands] allow or deny. The filter applies to the command path only. A script job runs the interpreter the operator chose, with the body the operator sent, and the only agent-side control over that is [remote-scripts] enabled.

So narrowing allow does not narrow what scripts can do. If an operator should not be able to run arbitrary code on a host, do not give them the scripts permission, and leave [remote-scripts] enabled = false on that agent.

Earlier releases of this page said the opposite. It was wrong: the agent has never applied the filter to script jobs.

docs.title: The scripts directory
docs.text:
The agent writes each job to {data_dir}/scripts/ and then runs it. The path is not configurable — it is data_dir with scripts appended — and two properties of that directory decide whether jobs run at all. Ordinary commands are written there as well as scripts, so the directory has to be right even if you never run scripts.

It must have mode exactly 0700 and be owned by the agent's own account. Anything written there is executed as the agent, so a scripts directory other accounts can reach is a way to run code as that account. Every job checks this before it runs, and while the mode is not exactly 0700 (stricter modes like 0500 fail too) or the owner is a different account, every command and script job fails with:

scripts directory /var/lib/proxiport-agent/scripts must be read-writable
only by proxiport-agent[997]. Change directory mode from 0755 to 0700.
Your setup is insecure

When [remote-scripts] is enabled the agent also runs this check at startup, but there it only logs the error and keeps running; jobs keep failing until the directory is fixed.

You normally never see this. When the directory is missing, the agent creates it with mode 0700 at startup, wherever data_dir points, and the pairing installer also creates it at 0700. The error appears only when the directory already exists with another mode, for example one created by hand with a plain mkdir or changed later. Fix it with chmod 0700 on the directory, or remove the directory and let the agent recreate it.

Its filesystem must allow execution for shebang scripts. A body that starts with #! is executed directly from the file the agent writes, so on a data_dir mount carrying noexec — common for /var or /tmp on a hardened host, and the default for a Docker tmpfs — those script jobs fail with:

failed to start a command: fork/exec
/var/lib/proxiport-agent/scripts/<uuid>: permission denied

A body without a shebang is run as <interpreter> <file> (/bin/sh when no interpreter is given) and still works, because reading a file needs no execute bit. Ordinary commands run the same way. If shebang scripts fail this way while commands and shebang-less scripts do not, check the mount options on data_dir.

docs.title: Running a script
docs.text:
Bodies are base64-encoded because the JSON payload would otherwise break on embedded newlines, quotes, and special characters:

SCRIPT=$(printf '#!/bin/bash\nset -euo pipefail\nuptime\nfree -h\n' | base64 -w0)
TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)
CLIENT=alpha-prod

JOB=$(curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw "{
    \"script\": \"$SCRIPT\",
    \"interpreter\": \"/bin/bash\",
    \"timeout_sec\": 30
  }" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/$CLIENT/scripts" \
  | jq -r .data.jid)

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/$CLIENT/commands/$JOB" | jq

Note that the result is fetched from the commands endpoint, not a separate scripts endpoint. Scripts are commands under the hood.

docs.title: Request fields
docs.text: Field Type Notes script string (required) Base64-encoded body. interpreter string Default /bin/sh on Unix, cmd on Windows. See aliases below. cwd string Working directory on the agent. is_sudo bool Prefix with sudo -n on Unix. timeout_sec int Agent-side supervision timeout.

docs.title: Multi-host execution
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/scripts fans a single script out to many agents:

curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw "{
    \"script\": \"$SCRIPT\",
    \"interpreter\": \"/bin/bash\",
    \"client_ids\": [\"alpha-prod\",\"bravo-staging\"],
    \"group_ids\": [\"edge-fleet\"],
    \"execute_concurrently\": true,
    \"abort_on_error\": false,
    \"timeout_sec\": 60
  }" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/scripts

The response carries the parent jid. There is no scripts read endpoint: multi-host script jobs share the commands job store. Poll GET /api/v1/commands/<jid> for the rolled-up status and GET /api/v1/commands/<jid>/jobs for the per-host results. Both routes need the commands permission, and only the user who started the job or an admin can read it.

Concurrency and abort-on-error semantics are the same as command fan-out.

docs.title: Interpreters and aliases
docs.text:
The server can ship any interpreter the agent can locate. Common shapes:

  • Bash / sh / zsh — /bin/bash, /bin/sh, /usr/local/bin/zsh. The agent invokes the interpreter against the tempfile path.

    On Linux and other non-Windows agents, if the script body begins with #!, the agent runs the tempfile directly and the shebang line picks the interpreter. The interpreter field is then ignored (sudo -n is still put in front when sudo is requested). On Windows the interpreter field is always used.

  • Python — /usr/bin/python3. Use #!/usr/bin/env python3 in the body if you want it to work across hosts with different paths (see the shebang note above).

  • PowerShell — powershell (Windows PowerShell 5.x) or a full path like C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe. ProxiPort appends -Noninteractive -executionpolicy bypass -File and writes the tempfile as .ps1 when the resolved interpreter path contains powershell (case-insensitive) after alias expansion. That covers powershell and the default PowerShell 7 install path, which matches because of its PowerShell directory, not because of pwsh.exe. A pwsh.exe installed somewhere whose path does not contain powershell (for example C:\tools\pwsh\pwsh.exe, or bare pwsh) is not recognised as PowerShell: it gets no flags and its script is written as a .bat file.
  • CMD — cmd on Windows. The agent writes a .bat tempfile.

For brevity, define aliases in the agent's proxiport.conf under [interpreter-aliases]:

[interpreter-aliases]
  pwsh7 = 'C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe'
  bash  = 'C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe'

Now "interpreter": "pwsh7" in the API call resolves to the full path.

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
The Saved scripts tab of the SPA's Library page (sidebar → Library) is a convenience wrapper around /api/v1/library/scripts. (The separate sidebar Scripts item is not the library.) A library entry stores the same fields as an ad-hoc request (name, interpreter, sudo flag, cwd, timeout and the body) plus an optional list of tags. If timeout_sec is omitted or 0, the server stores 60. The tab creates, edits and deletes entries; it does not run them. To run one, send its body as an ad-hoc script.

A schedule is not linked to a library entry. It stores its own copy of the command or script body and its run options. You can paste a library entry's body into a schedule, but later edits to the entry do not change the schedule.

Manage library entries via the API:

# Create
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "name":"current_directory",
    "interpreter":"/bin/sh",
    "is_sudo":false,
    "cwd":"/root",
    "script":"pwd",
    "tags":["maintenance"],
    "timeout_sec":60
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/library/scripts

# List, sort by newest first
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  'https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/library/scripts?sort=-created_at' \
  | jq

# Update (full replacement; partial updates are not supported)
curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{ "name":"...", "interpreter":"...", "is_sudo":false, "cwd":"...", "script":"...", "tags":[...], "timeout_sec":... }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/library/scripts/<script-id>

# Delete
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/library/scripts/<script-id>

The list endpoint accepts sort= and filter[<field>]= on id, name, created_by, created_at, updated_by, updated_at, interpreter, is_sudo, cwd, script and tags. Use fields[scripts]= to limit the returned fields; it accepts the same names plus timeout_sec. Results are paginated with page[limit] (default 20, maximum 100) and page[offset].

docs.title: WebSocket execution
docs.text:
For live stdout, the server exposes WS /api/v1/ws/scripts. Send one JSON message using the multi-host body of POST /api/v1/scripts (script, interpreter, and at least one of client_ids, group_ids or tags, plus optional cwd, is_sudo, timeout_sec, execute_concurrently, abort_on_error). There is no per-client socket, so target a single host with client_ids: ["<id>"]. As output is produced, the server sends frames of the form {"jid", "client_id", "client_name", "result": {"stdout", "stderr", "summary"}}, with the new chunk in result.stdout or result.stderr and the other fields empty. When each client's job finishes, it sends that job's full JSON.

Use this path from your own clients or the test harness below when you want output as it is produced. The SPA does not use it: it starts the script with POST /clients/{id}/scripts and polls GET /clients/{id}/commands/{jid}, showing the output once the job finishes.

To enable the test harness UI at /api/v1/test/scripts/ui, set enable_ws_test_endpoints = true in [api]. The test UI is the easiest way to confirm a script body, interpreter, and target host combination before wiring it into the SPA library or a scheduled job.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Scripts run as the agent's OS account (proxiport-agent on a packaged install, not the server's proxiport account). With is_sudo: true, the agent writes the body to {data_dir}/scripts/<random-uuid> and runs sudo -n <interpreter> <that file>, or sudo -n <that file> when the body starts with a shebang. The file name changes on every run, so a sudoers rule cannot name one particular script. A NOPASSWD rule for <interpreter> {data_dir}/scripts/* lets every script the server sends run as root through that interpreter. Grant it only if you accept that, and limit who may send sudo scripts on the server side.
  • The body lands on disk briefly under {data_dir}/scripts/. If the host has FIM (file-integrity monitoring), expect events from that directory during script execution.
  • The send_back_limit cap from [remote-commands] (default 4 MiB per stream) applies. Long-running, chatty scripts should redirect to a logfile on the host and tail it via another mechanism.

See also: command execution, client groups and permissions, operator runbook — schedules.

docs.title: Tunnel hosting
docs.text:
A ProxiPort tunnel is a server-side listener that forwards traffic to a TCP port on an agent. Everything in this document is about how operators publish those listeners — on what port, on what hostname, with what protocol on top — so users can reach them in a browser or an SSH client.

ProxiPort can present a tunnel as:

  • a raw TCP port on the server itself (the default, fine for SSH, databases, anything that already has its own client);
  • a subdomain on a wildcard hostname routed by an embedded Caddy instance (HTTPS-on-443 access to internal web UIs, RDP-via-browser, VNC-via-browser);
  • a NoVNC-wrapped VNC tunnel that renders a remote VNC server inside an HTML5 browser tab;
  • an RDP-via-browser tunnel that proxies through an Apache Guacamole guacd daemon;
  • a target for inbound file pushes that uses the same chisel channel to drop files onto the agent host.

This page covers all five. For tunnel ACLs, timeouts, and the basic SPA flow, see operator runbook — tunnels.

docs.title: Tunnels on random subdomains
docs.text:
The default tunnel scheme allocates a random port from [server] used_ports (default 20000-30000). That works fine until you have to dial through a firewall that blocks outbound traffic to non-default ports.

The subdomain hosting feature lets you publish each HTTP-based tunnel on https://<random>.tunnels.example.com:443 alongside the random port. Same tunnel, two access paths. The browser uses 443, which gets through most strict egress filters.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: proxiportd launches a Caddy process as a child and stops it on shutdown. It does not restart Caddy itself: if Caddy exits with an error, proxiportd exits too, and the packaged systemd unit (Restart=always) restarts proxiportd, which launches Caddy again. Caddy listens on the configured port (typically 443), terminates TLS, and routes the random subdomain to the right tunnel's internal port. All Caddy configuration is generated and pushed by proxiportd over a Unix socket — no manual Caddyfile.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Caddy installed locally. Either via the package manager or as a static binary in /usr/local/bin/caddy. A Caddy in a separate container is not supported — proxiportd needs to spawn and manage the process directly.
sudo curl -L "https://caddyserver.com/api/download?os=linux&arch=amd64" \
  -o /usr/local/bin/caddy
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/caddy
sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' /usr/local/bin/caddy

setcap is what lets the unprivileged proxiport user start a listener on 443. Without it, Caddy will fail to bind.

If Caddy is installed via the package manager, the unit usually auto-starts on boot. Disable it (sudo systemctl disable caddy) so the package's Caddy does not fight proxiportd's child Caddy.

  1. Wildcard DNS record. Create *.tunnels.example.com pointing at the server's public IP. If you would rather not use a subdomain prefix, a wildcard at the apex (*.example.com) works too.

  2. Wildcard TLS certificate. A Let's Encrypt DNS-01 wildcard:

sudo certbot certonly --manual --preferred-challenges dns \
  -d '*.tunnels.example.com'

Make the cert readable by the proxiport user:

sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live} -type d -exec chmod o+rx {} \;
sudo find /etc/letsencrypt/{archive,live} -type f -exec chmod o+r  {} \;

Caddy always serves the wildcard certificate from the cert_file / key_file paths under [caddy-integration]. proxiportd checks at startup that both files exist and load. The built-in ACME cannot issue a wildcard, so get one with a DNS-01 client as shown above and set up renewal for it. ([server] tunnel_enable_acme is a separate option. It gets a certificate for the single tunnel_host name, used by the tunnel proxy on the random tunnel ports, not by Caddy.)

docs.title: Server configuration
docs.text:
Two deployment shapes, "split port" and "shared port".

Split port keeps the API/SPA on one TCP port (say 3000) and lets Caddy run on its own port (typically 443) just for tunnels. proxiportd.conf:

[caddy-integration]
  caddy            = "/usr/local/bin/caddy"
  address          = "0.0.0.0:443"
  subdomain_prefix = "tunnels.proxiport.example.com"
  cert_file        = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/tunnels.proxiport.example.com/fullchain.pem"
  key_file         = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/tunnels.proxiport.example.com/privkey.pem"

The subdomain_prefix is the bare domain — do not include the leading *..

The [caddy-integration] address port must be different from [api] address.

Shared port runs the API and the tunnel subdomains on one TCP port (443). Caddy fronts everything; the API runs as a plain-HTTP backend behind it:

[api]
  address = "127.0.0.1:3000"
  # cert_file and key_file MUST be commented out — Caddy terminates TLS.

[caddy-integration]
  caddy            = "/usr/local/bin/caddy"
  address          = "0.0.0.0:443"
  subdomain_prefix = "tunnels.proxiport.example.com"
  cert_file        = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/tunnels.proxiport.example.com/fullchain.pem"
  key_file         = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/tunnels.proxiport.example.com/privkey.pem"

  api_hostname = "proxiport-api.example.com"
  api_cert_file = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/proxiport-api.example.com/fullchain.pem"
  api_key_file  = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/proxiport-api.example.com/privkey.pem"
  api_port = "3000"

api_port must equal the port in [api] address. Caddy will SNI-route requests for api_hostname to the API backend; everything else under the wildcard goes to a tunnel.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
When creating a tunnel from the SPA's per-client Tunnels tab, choose an HTTP or HTTPS service (directly, or as the target of a forwarding tunnel). Then tick Terminate TLS on the server using the server's certificate. This sends http_proxy=true with the create request. With [caddy-integration] enabled, the server allocates a random subdomain under subdomain_prefix and returns the resulting URL in the tunnel's tunnel_url field.

For now, the SPA's Active tunnels table shows only the random-port address (<server>:<port>, with a Copy button). To get the subdomain URL, read tunnel_url from the create response or from the client's tunnel list in the API (GET /api/v1/clients/{id}).

To inspect the live Caddy routes:

curl --unix-socket /var/lib/proxiport/caddy-admin.sock \
  -H "host:unix" \
  http://localhost/config/apps/http/servers/srv0/routes | jq

docs.title: HTTPS targets and certificate verification
docs.text:
When the reverse proxy fronts an HTTPS target it terminates the browser's TLS and opens a second TLS connection to the target. That second connection's certificate is verified — against the system trust store, or against a private CA bundle if you set one:

[server]
  # PEM bundle of CA certificate(s) to trust for tunnel targets.
  # Empty = use the system trust store.
  tunnel_proxy_target_ca_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/target-ca.pem"

Verification uses the target's real hostname for SNI: the tunnel's host_header when you set one, otherwise the tunnel's remote host. If a particular target presents a self-signed certificate you cannot add to a CA bundle — or one whose SAN does not match the hostname, such as a LAN appliance whose certificate carries no SAN at all — opt that one tunnel out with the skip_tls_verify=true query parameter when creating it. It applies only to that tunnel. In the web UI the same option is a "Do not verify the target's TLS certificate" checkbox that appears under Terminate TLS on the server once the target scheme is https.

A private CA bundle does not help a certificate that has no SAN: modern TLS verification ignores the legacy Common Name and matches only against the SAN, so a SAN-less certificate is rejected however it is trusted. Either reissue the target's certificate with the hostname in its SAN, or use skip_tls_verify for that tunnel.

If you would rather the operator's own browser validate the target certificate end to end, use a plain (non-proxied) tunnel instead: the bytes pass through untouched and your client completes the real TLS handshake with the target.

docs.title: Protecting a tunnel with HTTP basic auth
docs.text:
A tunnel served through the reverse proxy (http_proxy=true) can require HTTP basic auth. Send the credential in a JSON request body:

curl -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"auth_user":"operator","auth_password":"<password>"}' \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/<id>/tunnels?remote=0.0.0.0:8080&scheme=https&http_proxy=1&acl=203.0.113.0/24"

auth_user and auth_password are still accepted as query parameters for compatibility, but a credential in a URL is recorded by every access log, proxy cache and browser history between the caller and the API. The body form takes precedence when both are supplied.

The password is stored so the proxy can check incoming requests, but it is redacted from the client API payload and from the audit log.

docs.title: Plaintext HTTP tunnels are blocked by default
docs.text:
A tunnel whose scheme is http with no TLS in front of it carries the operator's browser ⇆ server traffic in the clear. Anyone able to observe the network path between the ProxiPort server and the browser — other hosts on the LAN, an upstream router, a hostile Wi-Fi access point, a transit provider — can read the request URLs, headers, session cookies and page contents. Because a management UI is exactly the kind of traffic worth protecting, ProxiPort refuses to open such a tunnel by default.

A tunnel is considered safe, and needs no override, when either:

  • the server terminates TLS with its own certificate — tick Terminate TLS on the server in the SPA, or pass http_proxy=true (see the reverse proxy above); or
  • TLS is carried end to end by the target — use the https scheme, and the encrypted bytes pass through the tunnel untouched.

If you genuinely need plaintext http — for instance on a trusted, isolated private network — you must opt in explicitly:

  • In the SPA: tick Allow insecure http:// without TLS on the New Tunnel form. The box appears only for an http tunnel with server TLS disabled, and the tunnel cannot be created until it is ticked.
  • Via the API: add allow_insecure_http=true to the PUT /clients/{client_id}/tunnels query. Without it the request is rejected with 400 and a message explaining the exposure.

This is the same deliberate, one-tick opt-in the UI already requires before opening a tunnel to an unrestricted IP range — an easy-to-hit safe default, with a clear escape hatch when you know what you are doing.

docs.title: NoVNC proxy
docs.text: For agents on hosts that expose a VNC server, ProxiPort can bridge to noVNC so the operator opens a browser tab and sees the remote desktop without installing a VNC client.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• noVNC JavaScript bundle on the server's filesystem.
  • TLS enabled on the tunnel proxy (tunnel_proxy_cert_file and tunnel_proxy_key_file). NoVNC depends on the same TLS-fronted reverse proxy that the subdomain feature uses.

Install noVNC:

sudo curl -L \
  https://github.com/novnc/noVNC/archive/refs/tags/v1.3.0.zip \
  -o /tmp/novnc.zip
sudo unzip -d /var/lib/proxiport /tmp/novnc.zip
sudo rm -f /tmp/novnc.zip

Point ProxiPort at the extracted directory:

[server]
  novnc_root = "/var/lib/proxiport/noVNC-1.3.0"
  tunnel_proxy_cert_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/server.crt"
  tunnel_proxy_key_file  = "/var/lib/proxiport/server.key"

Restart proxiportd. You create a noVNC tunnel through the REST API. The web UI's tunnel form has no noVNC option, and it shows the TLS-proxy checkbox only for HTTP and HTTPS tunnels. Ask for the VNC scheme with the internal proxy enabled:

curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/<client-id>/tunnels?remote=127.0.0.1:5900&scheme=vnc&http_proxy=true&acl=203.0.113.7"

The response gives the tunnel's proxy URL. Open it in a browser to get the noVNC console. If novnc_root is unset, the noVNC app files are answered with 404, so the console does not load, and the server logs novnc_root is not configured.

docs.title: RDP proxy via guacd
docs.text:
For RDP access from a browser, ProxiPort proxies the chisel tunnel through an Apache Guacamole guacd daemon on the same host:

[server]
  guacd_address = "127.0.0.1:4822"
  tunnel_proxy_cert_file = "/var/lib/proxiport/server.crt"
  tunnel_proxy_key_file  = "/var/lib/proxiport/server.key"

You do not need a full Guacamole web stack — only guacd. Run it in a container:

docker run -d --name guacd --net=host --restart unless-stopped \
  lscr.io/linuxserver/guacd

--net=host is required so guacd can reach the tunnel listener on 127.0.0.1.

proxiportd test-connects to guacd_address when it starts and refuses to start (try guacd connection: ...) if nothing is listening there. Start guacd first, then (re)start proxiportd, and if both start at boot, make sure guacd comes up before proxiportd.

Once guacd is running, an RDP tunnel created with the tunnel proxy enabled (scheme=rdp&http_proxy=true) exposes a URL like https://proxiport.example.com:<port>/ that loads the Guacamole client in the browser. The web UI's tunnel form does not offer this option yet (its TLS-termination checkbox appears only for HTTP and HTTPS services), so create the tunnel through the API:

curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/clients/<client-id>/tunnels?scheme=rdp&remote=3389&http_proxy=true&acl=203.0.113.7"

The server rejects http_proxy=true ("creation of tunnel proxy not enabled") unless the tunnel proxy is enabled, either with tunnel_proxy_cert_file and tunnel_proxy_key_file or with tunnel_enable_acme.

You can pass through Guacamole session parameters as query strings:

/?username=Administrator&width=1280&height=800&security=nla&keyboard=en-us-qwerty

The landing page does not accept a password query parameter; the operator types the password into the login form, which posts it to /createToken. Available keyboard values are the standard Guacamole layout codes (e.g. en-us-qwerty, de-de-qwertz, fr-fr-azerty).

docs.title: File reception
docs.text: A separate but related capability: pushing a file from the server's disk to one or many agent hosts over the same chisel channel that carries tunnel traffic.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
1. The operator uploads the file to the server via the multipart POST /api/v1/files endpoint, specifying target client IDs or group IDs, the destination path, and optional mode/owner/group.
  2. The server saves the file to {data_dir}/filepush/<uuid>_proxiport_filepush.
  3. Each addressed agent opens an SFTP-over-SSH session inside its existing chisel channel, downloads the file to its own {data_dir}/filepush/<uuid>_proxiport_filepush (same file name as on the server), verifies the MD5, applies any chmod/chown, and moves the file to the destination.
  4. The server tracks per-agent success/failure and surfaces it on the API and on a WebSocket subscriber stream.

A minimal upload:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F 'upload=@./hosts.allow' \
  -F 'client_id=alpha-prod' \
  -F 'client_id=bravo-staging' \
  -F 'dest=/etc/hosts.allow' \
  -F 'force=true' \
  -F 'mode=0644' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/files

Useful form fields:

Field Notes upload (required) The file body. client_id / group_id Repeatable. Picks the target agents directly or by group. Give these or tags, not both. tags Optional alternative to client_id/group_id: one JSON value such as {"tags":["linux","web"],"operator":"AND"}. It cannot be combined with them, and the tag list must not be empty. id Optional upload ID. A UUID is generated when it is omitted. It names the staged <id>_proxiport_filepush file and is reported as uuid. dest (required) Absolute destination path on the agent. Relative paths are rejected — see below. force Overwrite if the file already exists. sync Compare MD5; overwrite only if changed. Apply mode/owner if requested. mode Unix mode bits, e.g. 0644. Without it the agent creates the file with 0764 less its umask (0744 under the usual 022). Directories the agent has to create for the destination get 0755. user, group Unix owner / group, by name or numeric id. An agent running as root sets them directly; any other agent needs passwordless sudo for chown. If the mode or owner cannot be applied, the push fails and the destination is left as it was.

docs.title: File-size limit
docs.text: Server side, [api] max_filepush_size caps the single-file size in bytes (default 10 MiB). Increase it under [api] if you need to push larger payloads. The general max_request_bytes cap does not apply to this endpoint.

docs.title: The destination must be absolute
docs.text:
dest is required to be an absolute path: /etc/motd on a Unix agent, C:\ProgramData\app\config.ini or \\fileserver\share\file.txt on Windows. A relative path such as etc/motd is refused by the server and, independently, by the agent.

This matters for more than tidiness. Every entry in the server's refusal list and in [file-reception] protected is written as an absolute path, so a relative destination matches none of them — while the agent still resolves it, against the agent process's working directory. Under the shipped systemd unit that directory is /, so a relative etc/cron.d/job would have arrived at /etc/cron.d/job with every protection bypassed. Requiring an absolute path is what makes the lists below mean what they say.

A Windows path that is rooted but has no drive (\Windows\...) is also refused: it resolves against whichever drive is current, which is the same surprise in a different form.

docs.title: Protected destinations
docs.text:
[file-reception] protected is the agent's own refusal list, enforced on the agent because it is the agent's filesystem at stake. By default the agent refuses to write anywhere a pushed file could become code that runs as root:

  • executable search paths and pseudo-filesystems (/bin/**, /sbin/**, /usr/bin/**, /usr/sbin/**, /usr/local/bin/**, /usr/local/sbin/**, /lib*/**, /usr/lib*/**, /boot/**, /dev/**, /run/**, /proc/**, /sys/**)
  • anything that runs on a schedule (/etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/**, /etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly,monthly}/**, /var/spool/cron/**)
  • anything that runs at boot or defines a service (the systemd unit directories, /etc/init.d/**, /etc/init/**, /etc/rc.local, /etc/rc*.d/**, and on macOS the launchd directories and /etc/periodic/**)
  • shell and loader initialisation (/etc/profile, /etc/profile.d/**, /etc/bash.bashrc, /etc/bashrc, /etc/environment, /etc/ld.so.*)
  • accounts and authorization (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, /etc/gshadow, /etc/sudoers, /etc/sudoers.d/**, /etc/pam.d/**, /etc/security/**, /etc/ssh/**)
  • SSH keys — /root/**, /home/*/.ssh/**, /Users/*/.ssh/** — since an authorized_keys file is a login
  • package-manager hook directories (apt, yum, dnf, apk, pacman), which run as root on the next update, and network and DHCP hook directories
  • the agent's own configuration (/etc/proxiport/**)

On Windows it covers C:\Windows, C:\ProgramData, both Program Files trees and the per-user Startup folder. The full list is in the agent source (client/upload_nix.go, client/upload_win.go).

A pattern ending in /** protects that directory and everything below it. Any other pattern is a shell-style glob that matches a single path element, tested against both the target file path and its directory, so /etc/systemd/* covers /etc/systemd/system but not /etc/systemd/system/foo.service.d/override.conf — use the /** form for a directory tree. A ** anywhere else in a pattern does not cross path separators.

Setting protected replaces the default rather than adding to it, so an override must carry the built-in entries you still want:

[file-reception]
  enabled = true
  protected = ['/bin/**', '/sbin/**', '/usr/bin/**', '/usr/sbin/**', '/etc/systemd/**', '/srv/deploy/**']

To disable reception entirely, set enabled = false. The server refuses an obviously dangerous destination too, before transferring the file, but that check is a convenience — the agent's list is the enforcement.

File reception crosses the command permission boundary

A push carries a mode and an owner, and the agent will chown as root, so an operator who can write to one of these locations has code execution on the host without needing the commands or scripts permission. Treat the uploads permission as equivalent to command execution unless you have narrowed protected to an allowed directory of your own.

docs.title: Privileged writes
docs.text:
The agent runs as an unprivileged user. To let it chown a pushed file or write into a root-owned directory, add narrow sudoers rules:

# /etc/sudoers.d/proxiport-filereception
proxiport-agent ALL=NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/chown * /var/lib/proxiport-agent/filepush/*_proxiport_filepush
proxiport-agent ALL=NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/mv     /var/lib/proxiport-agent/filepush/*_proxiport_filepush *

The rules name the agent's own account (proxiport-agent since 0.10.0; proxiport is the server's) and the agent's data directory. A rule that still names proxiport grants the server, not the agent.

Limit the wildcards as much as your operational shape allows.

A failed chown or chmod does not fail the push. If the sudoers rule is missing or does not match, the agent still moves the file into place, owned by the agent's own account with the agent's mode, and reports status: "success". The failure appears only as a chown of ... failed or chmod failed note in the result's message (on WS /ws/uploads and in the audit log). Only a failed copy or move fails the push. When ownership matters, check message, not only status.

docs.title: Live progress
docs.text:
WS /ws/uploads streams per-file results as they happen. The socket does not accept a Bearer token. First call GET /api/v1/ws-ticket with your normal Bearer token, then open /api/v1/ws/uploads?ticket=<data.ticket> within 30 seconds. Each ticket works only once. Clients that can set request headers can use HTTP basic auth on the upgrade instead. Otherwise the upgrade is answered 401 ticket required. Subscribers get JSON frames like:

{
  "client_id": "alpha-prod",
  "uuid": "482ae29e-d372-4d21-8cb4-58d75482b7e1",
  "filepath": "/etc/hosts.allow",
  "size": 17118,
  "message": "file successfully copied to destination /etc/hosts.allow",
  "status": "success"
}

If setting the mode or owner fails but the file is still placed, a chmod failed: ... or chown of ... failed: ... note comes first in the message, joined with a period.

The test UI at /api/v1/test/uploads/ui (enable with enable_ws_test_endpoints = true under [api]) is the easiest way to see this in action.

For long-term auditing, the result is also written to auditlog.db and surfaces on the Audit page.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Caddy fails to bind 443. Re-run sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' $(which caddy) after every Caddy upgrade. The capability is on the binary and is lost when the binary is replaced.
  • Tunnel URL returns a Caddy 404. Caddy has no route for that subdomain. Either the tunnel was not created as a proxied tunnel (http_proxy=true, so it has no tunnel_url), or Caddy lost its routes, for example after a restart. List the live routes with the admin-socket curl shown above, and check journalctl -u proxiportd -n 100 --no-pager for failed to create downstream caddy proxy or other caddy errors. Caddy serves the static wildcard certificate from [caddy-integration] cert_file/key_file; no ACME runs for tunnel subdomains.
  • NoVNC loads but the canvas is blank. The agent could not reach the VNC port on the target host. The tunnel itself is fine; the agent-side TCP connect is failing.
  • File push reports "permission denied" on rename. The agent user can't write to dest. Either change the destination or add a sudoers rule and retry with the correct owner.

See also: HTTPS for the underlying TLS setup, operator runbook — tunnels for ACLs and the per-tunnel SPA flow, and architecture for the chisel transport details.

docs.title: Vault
docs.text:
The vault is ProxiPort's encrypted key-value store for documents and per-client secrets. It is a separate SQLite database at {data_dir}/vault.sqlite.db (the file name is fixed; only data_dir sets its location), sealed with a passphrase. The server never stores the passphrase: while the vault is unlocked, only the key derived from it is held, in the server process's memory and never on disk. If a [key_provider] is configured, every stored value is additionally envelope-encrypted at rest under a server-held key — see At-rest encryption.

A server restart always re-locks the vault, regardless of what is stored inside. An operator with the passphrase has to unlock it again through the SPA or the API before the values become readable.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Initialize. Once, the very first time the vault is used. Creates the database file and stores key-derivation parameters.
  2. Unlock. Every time the server starts. The administrator provides the passphrase; the server derives a key, validates it against the stored marker, and keeps the derived key in memory.
  3. Read/write. Any user with the vault function permission can list, fetch, store, update, and delete entries while the vault is unlocked.
  4. Lock. Optional manual seal. Wipes the key from memory. The stored data stays on disk.

Vaults created by rport or openrport. Those vaults used an unsalted SHA-256 key derivation. On the first successful unlock under ProxiPort, the server re-keys the vault to Argon2id: it derives a new salted key, re-encrypts every stored value and the verifier in a single transaction, records the new key-derivation parameters, and then compacts vault.sqlite.db. This first unlock takes longer than later ones, and the database file is rewritten. Once it has run, rport and openrport can no longer open the vault, so take a backup before the upgrade if you may need to roll back (see migration).

The administrator who runs unlock does not gain any per-entry visibility beyond what the user-group permissions would otherwise allow — locking is a global control, not a per-entry one.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text: All endpoints under /api/v1/vault-admin require the vault function permission. Status (GET /api/v1/vault-admin) needs nothing more. Initialize (POST /vault-admin/init), unlock (POST /vault-admin/sesame) and lock (DELETE /vault-admin/sesame) also require Administrators group membership, and anyone else gets a 403. Members of Administrators hold every permission implicitly.

docs.title: Initialize
docs.text:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -u admin:password \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/login | jq -r .data.token)

curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{"password":"a-vault-passphrase"}' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault-admin/init

The passphrase must be between 8 and 256 bytes. Anything outside that range is rejected with a 400 naming the limit it missed.

Earlier releases of this page published the range as 4 to 32 bytes. That was wrong in both directions: 4 bytes has never been accepted, and 32 bytes is far below the real ceiling.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault-admin | jq

{
  "data": {
    "init":   "setup-completed",
    "status": "unlocked"
  }
}

init is setup-completed or uninitialized. status is unlocked or locked, or an empty string ("") while init is uninitialized.

docs.title: Unlock and lock
docs.text:
# Unlock
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{"password":"a-vault-passphrase"}' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault-admin/sesame

# Lock (DELETE on the same path)
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault-admin/sesame

Status codes, for scripting these calls:

Call Success Errors POST /vault-admin/init 201 400 passphrase outside 8–256 bytes; 409 vault is already initialized POST /vault-admin/sesame (unlock) 201 401 wrong password provided; 409 vault is already unlocked or vault is not yet initialized DELETE /vault-admin/sesame (lock) 204 409 vault is already locked (also returned for a vault that was never initialized) any /api/v1/vault call — 409 vault is locked

A cron job that locks or unlocks should treat a 409 "already locked" or "already unlocked" as success.

If the wrong passphrase is supplied to unlock, the request is rejected and the vault stays locked. If the passphrase is lost, the data is unrecoverable — the passphrase is the only key that can recover the contents; there is no backup escrow and no support recovery path. (The optional key provider adds a second at-rest layer, but it is not a passphrase-recovery mechanism — a configured server still requires the passphrase to unlock.)

docs.title: User API
docs.text: Once the vault is unlocked, any user with the vault function permission (see client groups and permissions) can interact with /api/v1/vault.

docs.title: List
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/vault returns every entry's metadata — id, client_id, created_by, created_at, key — but not the decrypted value:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault | jq

Supports sort= (prefix with - for descending) and filter[<field>]= on id, client_id, created_by, created_at, and key. Pass -g to curl if you use the bracketed filter syntax on the URL.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/vault/<id> returns the full record including the decrypted value:

{
  "data": {
    "id": 1,
    "client_id": "alpha-prod",
    "required_group": "",
    "key": "deploy-key",
    "value": "ssh-ed25519 AAAA…",
    "type": "secret",
    "created_at": "2026-05-17T09:46:07+00:00",
    "updated_at": "2026-05-17T09:46:07+00:00",
    "created_by": "admin",
    "updated_by": "admin"
  }
}

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{
    "client_id": "alpha-prod",
    "required_group": "",
    "key": "deploy-key",
    "value": "ssh-ed25519 AAAA…",
    "type": "secret"
  }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
# Full replacement; partial PATCH is not supported
curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '{ "client_id":"alpha-prod","required_group":"","key":"deploy-key","value":"...","type":"secret" }' \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault/1

# Delete
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault/1

docs.title: Field reference
docs.text:
• client_id — Optional. Ties a document to a specific agent. Leave it empty for a global entry that is not tied to any one client. The value is matched exactly, so 0 is its own scope and does not mean global.
  • required_group — Optional. If set, only users in this user-group can read, update, or delete the entry. Use it for compartmentalised secrets in a multi-team server.
  • key — Required short identifier. Unique within a client_id scope.
  • value — Required. The encrypted body of the document. Every other column is stored in clear.
  • type — Required. One of text, secret, markdown, string; the server rejects any other value with 400. The type is stored with the entry and returned when a single entry is read, as a rendering hint for clients.

The web UI does not render entry bodies yet. Admin → Vault initializes, unlocks and locks the vault and lists entries by key; the per-client Documents tab and the Documentation page in the sidebar are placeholders that do not list vault entries. Use the /api/v1/vault endpoints to create and read entries.

docs.title: At-rest encryption (optional)
docs.text:
By default the vault contents are protected only by the passphrase described above. If a [key_provider] is configured (see the [key_provider] section of proxiportd.example.conf), the server adds a second at-rest layer: a data-encryption key (DEK) held only in RAM wraps the vault's verification marker and every stored value, so on disk they become enc:v1:… ciphertext on top of the passphrase-derived encryption. An existing vault is wrapped in place the next time the server boots.

This closes the offline-guessing path: with the DEK the attacker does not have, a stolen copy of vault.sqlite.db cannot be used to test passphrase guesses at all. The DEK is not a passphrase-recovery mechanism — unlock still requires the passphrase — and a type = file key stored on the same disk as the database gives no protection against whole-disk theft.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
vault.sqlite.db belongs in the same backup schedule as the other SQLite files (see operator runbook — backups). The encrypted file is safe to copy — the cipher text is useless without the passphrase (and, if a [key_provider] is configured, without the DEK as well). Back up the DEK/key file separately, and never inside the same data_dir tarball as the database.

Restoring a vault backup requires re-entering the passphrase on the restored server. The marker the new server checks against is part of the database, so the same passphrase used at init time will unlock the restored copy. If the backup was written with a [key_provider] enabled, the restored server must also present the same DEK (key_file/env_var); without it the vault fails closed and cannot be read.

docs.title: Clear-text backups
docs.text:
Because losing the passphrase loses the data, consider also keeping clear-text dumps of the vault outside the server. The dumps belong in a safe (encrypted disk, password manager, hardware-backed store) — never alongside the unencrypted database file.

A minimal export script. The token must be minted with the read+write scope (see API authentication): a read-scoped token can list the vault but is refused the decrypted value of every entry. Because the script runs curl -s, that failure is silent — each <id>.json would hold an error response instead of the entry.

USER=admin
TOKEN=Ab3xK9pq_e83d40e4-e237-43d6-bb99-35972ded631b   # a personal API token with read+write scope, prefix included
URL=https://proxiport.example.com/api/v1/vault
FOLDER=./vault-backup

mkdir -p "${FOLDER}"
IDS=$(curl -s -u "${USER}:${TOKEN}" "${URL}" | jq .data[].id)
for ID in $IDS; do
  curl -s -u "${USER}:${TOKEN}" "${URL}/${ID}" -o "${FOLDER}/${ID}.json"
done

tar czf vault-backup.tar.gz "${FOLDER}"

# Securely delete the per-entry files; keep only the tarball.
find "${FOLDER}" -type f -exec shred {} \;
rm -rf "${FOLDER}"

Encrypt vault-backup.tar.gz before storing it anywhere external.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• The vault is locked after every restart. This is the most common operator surprise. Bookmark the unlock URL in the SPA, or script the unlock with a credential pulled from your password manager.
  • A wrong passphrase only fails — it does not damage the data. Brute-forcing the passphrase is the only attack path against the data on disk — and a configured [key_provider] closes even that for a disk thief who lacks the DEK. Use a strong passphrase.
  • required_group is checked at every read. Removing a user from the required group immediately revokes their access to the entries that name it.
  • The vault does not auto-lock on idle. If you want a periodic lock, run a cron that sends DELETE /api/v1/vault-admin/sesame on the schedule you want, and treat a 409 (already locked) as success.
  • Vault activity is audited. With the audit log enabled (enable_audit_log, on by default), the server records vault init, unlock and lock, and every entry create, update, delete and read. Each record holds the user and the source address, plus the entry id for entry operations; a read is logged as a read action. The audit log never stores a stored value itself: create and update records keep the entry's metadata, not its value. Filter the Audit page on vault to see them.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• Pick a passphrase that survives a brute-force attempt against the on-disk file — 32 random ASCII characters is a reasonable floor, and the limit is 256 bytes, so there is a lot of room above it.
  • Store the passphrase in a password manager, not in a shell history or a script committed to version control.
  • Schedule regular clear-text backups and encrypt them at rest.
  • Use required_group to restrict per-team secrets even from other vault users.

See also: operator runbook — backups, architecture — datastore, client groups and permissions for the user-group model the vault function permission and required_group fields rely on.

docs.title: Watchdog integration
docs.text:
The proxiport agent already self-supervises its connection: a broken chisel session is retried with exponential backoff, and connection keepalives detect a peer that has silently dropped. In normal operation you do not need a watchdog.

The watchdog integration exists for the corner case where the agent process is alive but its connection logic has wedged — typically a kernel-level network issue that the Go runtime hasn't surfaced as an error. With the watchdog enabled, the agent emits a periodic heartbeat to a file (or to the systemd notify socket) that an external supervisor can use to restart the process.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Long-running agent on a host with flaky networking, where the reconnect loop has been observed to hang.
  • A deployment where agents disappear for hours and an operator notices late.
  • Belt-and-braces hardening on critical infrastructure.

If you have not seen a stuck agent, leave it off. The watchdog adds no behaviour beyond what systemctl restart proxiport would do for you on demand.

docs.title: Enabling on the agent
docs.text:
In proxiport.conf under [connection]:

[connection]
  keep_alive = '3m'
  max_retry_count = -1
  watchdog_integration = true

Two preconditions:

  • keep_alive must be greater than 0s. Disable keepalives and there are no heartbeats to emit.
  • max_retry_count must be -1 (unlimited). If the agent gives up after a bounded number of attempts, the watchdog would be the thing restarting an agent that already chose to stop — the wrong shape.

Restart the agent:

sudo systemctl restart proxiport

The agent will create state.json in its data directory.

docs.title: The state.json heartbeat
docs.text:
Path: {data_dir}/state.json, defaulting to /var/lib/proxiport-agent/state.json.

{
  "last_update":    "2026-05-17T10:37:25.643839Z",
  "last_update_ts": 1779014245,
  "last_state":     "connected",
  "last_message":   "ping to 203.0.113.7:443 succeeded within 14.682823ms"
}

The two last_update* fields are the ones a supervisor should compare against the current clock. As long as the timestamp keeps advancing, the agent is alive.

last_state carries one of:

  • initialized — the agent has just started and has not produced a connection result yet.
  • connected — the chisel session is up.
  • reconnecting — the agent is dialling the server and has not yet succeeded.

last_message is a free-text description of the most recent event, such as Connected to <ip:port> within <duration>, ping to <ip:port> succeeded within <rtt> or Retrying in <duration>... — useful for logs, not stable enough to parse.

The file is written on four events:

  1. The agent starts (last_state: initialized).
  2. A connection attempt succeeded (connected).
  3. A connection attempt failed and a retry is scheduled (reconnecting). The agent then waits before retrying. The wait grows exponentially from about 5 seconds to a fixed ceiling of 10 minutes, with jitter. If the server timed out, the wait resets to a few seconds. max_retry_interval is accepted in the config but currently has no effect on this wait. Once max_retry_count is exhausted, the agent gives up without writing the file again.
  4. A keepalive ping succeeded (connected; interval governed by keep_alive). A failed or timed-out keepalive ping does not update the file. The agent closes the connection, and the next update is the reconnecting entry written when the reconnect attempt is scheduled.

docs.title: Linux: the systemd watchdog (recommended)
docs.text:
systemd has a built-in watchdog. Add WatchdogSec=N to the agent's unit, and systemd creates a Unix socket that the agent will push heartbeats to automatically — no extra script needed. Add it with a drop-in rather than by copying a whole unit:

sudo systemctl edit proxiport

[Service]
WatchdogSec=960

sudo systemctl restart proxiport

A drop-in keeps the installed unit's ExecStart and the rest of its settings. The binary is /usr/bin/proxiport for deb/rpm and tarball installs, and /usr/local/bin/proxiport for pairing-script installs, so don't copy a whole unit with a hard-coded path from another host.

WatchdogSec must be longer than the longest gap the agent can leave between two heartbeats:

  • While connected, the agent sends a heartbeat after each successful keepalive ping. One cycle can take keep_alive + up to 5 s of jitter + up to three keep_alive_timeout waits (default 30 s each) plus about 6 s of retry back-off. With keep_alive = '3m' that is about 4m40s.
  • While reconnecting, the agent sends a heartbeat before each back-off wait. The wait grows to a fixed ceiling of 10 minutes; max_retry_interval does not cap it. The next connection attempt can then take up to 5 minutes to time out (or transport_dial_timeout when a transport chain is set).

A WatchdogSec shorter than these gaps turns a normal reconnect back-off into a kill-and-restart cycle during any prolonged outage. With keep_alive = '3m', WatchdogSec = 960 (16 minutes) rides out both.

When the agent detects the systemd notify socket (the NOTIFY_SOCKET environment variable), it logs a confirmation at debug level:

Using NOTIFY_SOCKET /run/systemd/notify for systemd watchdog integration

If 960 seconds pass with no notification, systemd kills the agent and respawns it through Restart=always. The state.json file is still written even when the systemd socket is in use, so you can read it to debug what the agent thought was happening.

docs.title: Windows: a scheduled PowerShell check
docs.text:
Windows services do not have a built-in watchdog equivalent. A scheduled task that runs every minute is the usual shape:

$stateFile = 'C:\Program Files\proxiport\data\state.json'
$threshholdSec = 960

$now = [int][double]::Parse((Get-Date -UFormat %s))
$lastUpdate = (Get-Content $stateFile | ConvertFrom-Json).last_update_ts
$diff = $now - $lastUpdate

if ($diff -gt $threshholdSec) {
    Write-Output "ProxiPort wedged. No activity for $diff seconds."
    Restart-Service proxiport
} else {
    Write-Output "ProxiPort is healthy. Last activity $diff seconds ago."
}

Save as check-proxiport.ps1, register as a scheduled task that runs every minute under SYSTEM. Keep $threshholdSec above the longest heartbeat gap described for WatchdogSec above.

docs.title: Custom supervisor
docs.text:
Any process that reads state.json once a minute, compares last_update_ts against the current Unix timestamp, and restarts the agent on excess staleness will work. The check is intentionally trivial — language and tooling are an implementation detail.

A minimal shell variant:

#!/bin/sh
threshold=960
now=$(date +%s)
last=$(jq -r .last_update_ts /var/lib/proxiport-agent/state.json)
if [ $((now - last)) -gt "$threshold" ]; then
    logger -t proxiport-watchdog "stale heartbeat; restarting"
    systemctl restart proxiport
fi

Schedule from cron, run as root.

docs.title: Verifying the integration
docs.text:
1. With the agent connected, watch state.json update:
watch -n 5 'jq . /var/lib/proxiport-agent/state.json'

The timestamp should advance on the keep_alive cadence.

  1. Block the agent's egress to simulate a network failure. The agent notices at the next keepalive: after keep_alive (plus a little jitter), a ping times out after keep_alive_timeout, and is retried up to three times. The agent then drops the connection, and state.json switches to last_state: "reconnecting". After that, a reconnecting heartbeat is written on each reconnect attempt, spaced by the agent's built-in back-off (5 seconds, growing to at most 10 minutes). The supervisor should not restart the agent yet — the agent is correctly trying.

  2. Push the agent into a wedged state. Easiest reproduction is kill -STOP $(pidof proxiport) to freeze the process. The heartbeat stops; after the threshold, the supervisor restarts proxiport. Unfreeze with kill -CONT if you do not want to exercise the full restart path during the test.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• Pick a WatchdogSec (or threshold) that is larger than the longest heartbeat gap: the 10-minute reconnect back-off ceiling plus one connection attempt, and the keepalive cycle while connected (see above). Too tight, and systemd will restart the agent during normal reconnects.
  • Leave Restart=always and RestartSec set on the unit. Without them, systemd's kill won't be followed by a respawn.
  • Monitor the restart counter (systemctl status proxiport) — a watchdog that fires constantly is hiding a real network problem.

See also: operator runbook — service control and architecture — agent.
